一句话：迁移一个场景生成器，要迁的不只是输出，还有规划、构建工具与已积累的经验。

要点：

  • 问题说得很准：把一个场景生成器搬到新游戏引擎，**不只是导出最终产物**——规划逻辑、构建工具、甚至积累下来的经验都可能依赖原来那套后端
  • SceneAgent 是一个多 agent 框架，目标是**复用构建过程与经验**，让它们跨后端迁移
  • 结构上分两层：**canonical SceneContext** 维护持续演进的世界状态；**backend adapters** 隔离坐标系约定、资产与工具差异

为什么值得看：「AI 生成的场景能不能换引擎」是落地时第一个撞上的问题：坐标系、资产格式、工具链全不一样。把「过程」而不是「产物」做成可移植，等于把生成器变成引擎无关的一层——这正是 AI 原生引擎该有的分层。

中文摘要：把一个场景生成器迁移到新的游戏引擎，远不只是导出最终产物：规划、构建工具乃至已积累的经验，都可能依赖原来的后端。SceneAgent 因此提出一个多 agent 框架，目标是复用「构建过程」以及其中积累的经验，使它们可以跨后端迁移。它的结构分两层：canonical SceneContext 负责维护持续演进的世界状态（与具体后端无关），backend adapters 则隔离各引擎在坐标约定、资产与工具上的差异。对同时维护多引擎管线、或想把生成能力产品化的团队，这种「过程可移植」的分层比任何单点生成质量都关键。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·cs.CV（English）

原文发布：2026-11-16

本期推送：2026-11-17

SceneAgent: A Multi-Agent Framework for Portable Game Scene Generation

Abstract

Moving a scene generator to a new game engine requires more than exporting its final output: planning, construction tools, and stored experience may also depend on the original backend. We present SceneAgent, a multi-agent framework for reusing the construction process and its experience across backends. A canonical SceneContext maintains the evolving world, while backend adapters isolate coordinate conventions, asset bindings, and export. Structured handoffs let fresh Builder sessions query this persistent state without inheriting the full construction transcript. Across generations, human-approved traces are distilled into asset-ID-free Layout skills and semantic Content skills that can be retrieved and recombined. We introduce GameSceneBench, comprising 69 indoor and outdoor prompts. Under a common asset and evaluation protocol, SceneAgent obtains human tie-adjusted preference scores of 78.2–89.4% against five baselines. Ablations show that reusable skills and the multi-agent protocol primarily improve prompt alignment and scene completeness, with additional runtime. Deployment in a second engine preserves the shared construction protocol and skill library while replacing backend integration components. Together, these results support separating persistent scene state, task-local reasoning, and reusable experience for portable scene construction.

1 Introduction

Constructing a 3D game environment requires coordinated design decisions: buildings must follow roads, landmarks must face useful viewpoints, and vegetation must respect occupied space. These decisions should remain useful when the engine or asset library changes. Existing LLM-based systems can construct complex scenes [16, 3], but construction decisions are often expressed through backend-specific coordinates, asset identifiers, APIs, and execution traces. An interoperable output file alone does not make these decisions reusable.

We study construction portability: retaining the planning protocol, scene-state interface, and reusable design knowledge while localizing backend-specific implementation. This requires more than a common export schema. During generation, agents need to coordinate against the same evolving world without inheriting every preceding tool call. Across generations, experience must retain useful spatial and semantic patterns without carrying over incidental asset bindings. Both world state within a run and design knowledge across runs must remain accessible through the shared interface.

We introduce SceneAgent, organized around three complementary mechanisms.

Canonical construction state. A shared SceneContext records actor transforms, bounding boxes, occupied regions, and subtask provenance in canonical coordinates. Builders query and update this state through construction tools. Adapters handle coordinate conversion, asset bindings, and export. Backend-specific capability wrappers expose native operations through the construction interface. This boundary preserves the shared protocol while making the required backend integration explicit.

Structured handoffs. An Orchestrator launches a fresh Builder session for each planned subtask. The Builder receives its objective, shared conventions, relevant skills, and compact completion reports and then queries SceneContext for additional world information. Thus, later subtasks can respect earlier construction without replaying its full transcript. Geometry checks and bounded refinement provide control points before the next handoff.

Factored experience. Human-approved traces are distilled into asset-ID-free Layout skills for spatial organization and semantic Content skills for object roles, style, and substitution. Thin recipes compose these factors with prompt-specific requirements. Backend databases supply concrete assets. The same route layout can therefore guide different scene themes, and the same theme can be realized through different layouts. Rejected traces are retained separately as failure evidence.

We evaluate SceneAgent on GameSceneBench, a benchmark of 69 indoor and outdoor prompts. Under a shared asset and rendering protocol, a blinded human study yields tie-adjusted preferences of 78.2–89.4% over five baselines. VLM comparisons favor the method in alignment, spatial plausibility, and completeness. Skill-library and single-agent ablations show the clearest gains in alignment and completeness, while quantifying the runtime cost. A second-engine deployment tests reuse of the shared protocol and skills, and cross-LLM studies examine model dependence.

Our contributions are:

  • •

    A construction-portability design that couples canonical scene state with a shared tool interface and an explicit backend integration boundary.

  • •

    A Planner–Builder protocol that coordinates fresh task-local sessions through persistent scene state and structured completion reports.

  • •

    A factored Layout–Content experience library for compositional reuse, with evaluation on GameSceneBench through baseline comparisons, ablations, and cross-engine and cross-model studies.

    • 2 Related Work

    Agentic Scene Generation and Portable Representations.

    Language models have expanded text-to-scene generation from layout prediction [4] to assembling and refining complete 3D scenes [1]. Holodeck [23] populates scenes with retrieved assets, while Holodeck 2.0 [2] adds generated assets and interactive editing. Other agentic systems combine specialized roles, tool use, and visual feedback [11, 22, 12], while SAGE [20] further introduces visual and physics critics for simulator-validated generation. The Procedural Scene Programs approach [7] instead represents scene layouts as imperative programs, placing objects relative to previously constructed elements and improving layout validity through LLM-free program search. Many existing systems realize these capabilities through specific authoring environments: SceneCraft [9] and CityX [26] generate Blender programs or procedural structures, whereas UnrealLLM [16], AutoUE [24], and LatticeWorld [3] rely on Unreal Engine facilities and tooling.

    A complementary line of work develops structured scene representations that remain editable and renderable across graphics systems. The Scene Language [27] represents structure, semantics, and visual identity through programs, words, and embeddings, supporting traditional, neural, and hybrid renderers. GenUSD [10] hierarchically plans scene layouts, generates 3D assets on demand, assembles them in Omniverse, and exports the resulting scenes in USD, thereby providing an interoperable scene output. SceneAgent focuses on portability of the construction process: agents query and update canonical world state through a shared interface, while adapters and capability wrappers handle backend realization. This complements interoperable output representations by also retaining the planning protocol and semantic experience across backend deployments.

    Long-Horizon State and Reusable Experience.

    Long-horizon agents increasingly externalize task state instead of relying on the full interaction history. Magentic-One [5] coordinates specialized agents through structured task and progress ledgers, while InfiAgent [25] reconstructs bounded reasoning contexts from persistent workspace state and a fixed window of recent actions. Another line of work distills prior trajectories into reusable knowledge: Voyager [18] stores successful behaviors as executable skills, ExpeL [28] extracts transferable insights from trajectories, and Agent Workflow Memory [19] induces reusable workflows. In 3D scene synthesis, SceneMotifCoder [15] similarly distills example arrangements into reusable visual meta-programs.

    SceneAgent brings these two forms of persistence into one construction protocol. SceneContext carries the evolving world between Builder sessions, while approved traces supply spatial and semantic guidance for later scenes. Layout and Content are stored and retrieved separately, with concrete asset mappings left to backend databases. The distinction is between reusable scene-design guidance and the backend-bound details of an individual construction trace.

    3 System Overview

    Figure 1 shows the generation and experience-update paths. Given a prompt or reference image, the Orchestrator retrieves Layout and Content skills and supplies them as read-only guidance to the Planner and relevant Builders. The Planner produces an ordered queue of semantic subtasks. For each subtask, a fresh Builder reads its task record and compact completion reports, queries SceneContext, and modifies the world through construction tools. Geometry checks diagnose the updated state and support bounded refinement. After construction, the backend adapter exports the canonical state to the target engine.

    Two forms of information persist beyond individual Builder sessions. SceneContext stores the current world within a generation, while the skill library stores reusable guidance across generations. Human review determines which completed traces enter the experience-update path. Automatic checks provide supporting diagnostics. Planning, handoffs, canonical state, and semantic skills are shared across backends. Asset configuration, export adapters, and native-capability wrappers supply backend-specific realization. The Orchestrator coordinates these stages without placing actors directly.

    4 Method

    SceneAgent separates three responsibilities: storing the constructed world, reasoning about the current subtask, and retaining experience for future scenes.

    SceneContext records what has been built, handoffs summarize task outcomes and unresolved issues, and skills provide reusable design guidance. A fresh Builder combines these sources without inheriting the full construction transcript. This division lets task-local reasoning use persistent world state and cross-scene experience, while adapters and asset databases handle backend-specific realization.

    4.1 Canonical Scene State and Backend Boundary

    The Planner expresses scene intent through semantic categories, roles, spatial relations, constraints, and gameplay affordances. Builders realize this intent in a shared SceneContext, rather than by invoking an engine directly. SceneContext stores each concrete actor in a builder coordinate system (X: left–right, Y: up, Z: forward–back), together with its asset reference, transform, bounding box, source tag, and subtask identifier. It also maintains scene bounds and an occupancy index for spatial queries. SceneContext serves as both an exportable world representation and the live coordination state: later Builders query what earlier subtasks constructed, including occupied space and provenance, without replaying their actions.

    The exported payload is actor-centric: each actor carries an asset reference, a transform, and optional appearance or collision metadata. A backend adapter converts SceneContext into the target backend’s coordinate, unit, scale, and rotation conventions, resolves backend-specific asset bindings when required, and serializes the result. For example, one adapter swaps the builder Y and Z axes, converts game units to meters, and emits quaternion rotations. The same construction state can therefore be exported through another adapter while preserving how Builders place actors and query the scene.

    Table 1 defines the portability boundary. Retargeting requires a compatible asset catalog, an adapter, and wrappers for backend-specific capabilities. The canonical coordinates, SceneContext schema, core tool interface, Planner–Builder protocol, and semantic skill libraries remain shared. Portability therefore concerns reuse of the construction process with explicit backend integration.

    From semantic design to backend assets.

    Retargeting preserves semantic roles and spatial rules while grounding them in the active backend. For a street scene, a Layout skill can specify a central route with buildings along its sides, while Content skills specify building families and supporting props. Builders retrieve candidates from the local catalog, inspect their metadata and dimensions, and place selected assets relative to SceneContext. Content skills can guide substitution when a requested object is unavailable. Placement and scene queries use the shared coordinate conventions. The adapter then converts transforms and resolves backend-specific bindings for export. This process reuses the construction strategy while allowing concrete assets and scene geometry to reflect the target catalog.

    4.2 Planning and Tool-Mediated Construction

    The Planner transforms the prompt and an optional reference image into an ordered queue of subtasks, such as ground, building, vegetation, prop, and refinement tasks. Each record specifies a semantic objective, target region, candidate content, construction guide, and shared conventions including the main axis, orientation rules, scale unit, and ground height.

    For each subtask, the Orchestrator launches a fresh Builder session. Its initial context includes the current task record, construction guide, shared conventions, selected Layout and Content skills, and compact reports from completed subtasks, while excluding raw placement and tool-call histories. When additional information is required, the Builder queries the live SceneContext as needed instead of reconstructing the world from a transcript.

    The shared construction tools cover asset retrieval and inspection, direct and procedural placement, scene queries, and targeted editing. Geometric operations use builder coordinates and read from or write to SceneContext. For example, Builders can inspect candidate assets, populate a region, query per-subtask footprints, or remove actors from an occupied area. Additional backend-local wrappers encapsulate native APIs and normalize inputs and outputs to shared conventions where possible. The supplementary material lists the construction and agent-control interfaces.

    Scene-changing operations trigger geometry checks for collisions, unsupported or out-of-bounds actors, extreme transforms, invalid assets, and density anomalies. High-confidence violations can receive conservative corrections, such as removal, clamping, or re-seating. Unresolved cases trigger a bounded number of refinement passes or return control to the user. At the end of a subtask, the Builder returns a compact report containing its completion status, summary, residual issues, and actor-count change. SceneContext, rather than the Builder conversation, carries the constructed world into the next subtask.

    For a night market, the street Builder first establishes the road. The market-stall Builder receives its completion report and queries SceneContext for road geometry and occupied regions before placing vendors along the sides. A later prop Builder can inspect the resulting footprints before adding furniture. Each handoff preserves task outcomes and access to the world while discarding the preceding Builder’s raw tool-call history.

    4.3 Factored Experience Representation

    A stored scene trace can entangle spatial organization, semantic content, and concrete asset choices. To make these decisions independently reusable, SceneAgent extracts three complementary objects:

  • •

    Layout skill: reusable spatial organization and geometric constraints, such as grouping, support, symmetry, focal placement, path structure, density gradients, and terrain constraints. It contains no concrete asset identifiers.

  • •

    Content skill: semantic roles, stylistic attributes, and substitution rules, such as object families, theme tags, and material styles. It contains no backend-specific bindings.

  • •

    Thin recipe: a scene-specific composition record that references Layout and Content skills and retains only residual details unique to the current prompt.

    • Factoring allows the same spatial organization to be paired with different content families and the same content family to be realized through different layouts, without storing a separate fused memory for every combination. A campsite layout, for example, may be paired with medieval, science-fiction, or cartoon content, while a village theme may use grid, radial, or terrain-following organization. This factorization need not perfectly decompose every scene, but keeps concrete asset IDs and backend directives separate from transferable experience.

    Example of skill composition.

    Consider a night-market scene organized around a pedestrian street. A linear Layout skill specifies a continuous route between an entrance and a terminal focus, places major regions along its sides, and preserves an unobstructed circulation corridor. A night-market Content skill supplies semantic roles such as vendors, lighting, furniture, and supporting props, together with stylistic guidance and substitution rules. For example, a missing food stall can be replaced by a canopy-and-counter assembly. A thin recipe combines these skills and adds scene-specific requirements, such as staggered vendor rows and small dining pockets. Concrete assets are subsequently resolved through the backend-specific asset database. Thus, reusable spatial rules, semantic content, and prompt-specific requirements remain separately represented.

    4.4 Quality-Gated Experience Update

    Experience is retained through a human-led quality gate, with automatic checks serving as supporting diagnostic evidence. After generation, SceneAgent packages the prompt, construction record, final SceneContext, multi-view renderings, automatic validation results, and checkpoint feedback into an experience candidate. The automatic checks expose collisions, unsupported actors, invalid transforms, and density anomalies, but do not alone determine whether to retain the experience.

    A human reviewer makes the final decision by considering prompt adherence, spatial organization, visual coherence, richness, and potential reusability. The reviewer may approve or reject the trace and optionally provide a natural-language critique or correction. Only approved traces are passed to the experience extractor, which assigns transferable spatial rules to Layout skills, semantic and stylistic knowledge to Content skills, and prompt-specific residuals to a thin recipe. Candidate skills then undergo schema validation and deduplication before insertion into the library for future reuse. Rejected traces and reviewer feedback are retained separately as failure evidence.

    At generation time, the Orchestrator retrieves a compact set of Layout and Content skills from their indexes and injects them as structured, read-only sections of the system prompts for the Planner and relevant Builder sessions. Separate indexes enable independent retrieval of spatial and semantic experience, while suppressing duplicate loads.

    Visual experience acquisition.

    Reference images or screenshots provide an additional source of reusable experience. A vision-language model interprets their semantic content, spatial relations, and construction cues, which then condition the standard Planner–Builder pipeline. The resulting scene and construction trace undergo the same human-led quality gate as text-prompted generations. Only approved traces are factorized into Layout and Content skills and inserted into the experience library after schema validation and deduplication. This route can incrementally expand the library from visual examples without changing the skill representation, retrieval mechanism, or update protocol.

    5 GameSceneBench and Evaluation Metrics

    GameSceneBench.

    We introduce GameSceneBench, a text-driven benchmark containing 69 prompts: 56 outdoor and 13 indoor scenes spanning diverse natural, built, historical, stylized, and functional environments. Prompts range from open-ended requests to detailed descriptions with required objects and spatial relations. Every method uses the same asset catalog, rendering pipeline, and camera protocol and is run independently three times per prompt. Each scene is rendered from four perspective views and one top-down view. Because multiple realizations may satisfy a prompt, we evaluate alignment, efficiency, spatial plausibility, and completeness rather than reconstruction error. The prompts, category breakdown, and rendering details are provided in the supplementary material.

    CLIPScore and runtime.

    We compute CLIPScore [8] with CLIP ViT-L/14 [14] for each prompt–view pair and average over the five views. Runtime measures wall-clock time from prompt submission to scene completion, including planning and construction but excluding offline rendering, VLM evaluation, and human evaluation. Both metrics are averaged over the three runs.

    VLM evaluation.

    We evaluate text–scene alignment (prompt satisfaction), spatial plausibility (placement, support, scale, accessibility, and overlap), and scene completeness (sufficient, nonredundant supporting content). For each method pair, prompt, and run, the two sets of five views form an anonymous 2×5 composite with randomized top–bottom order. The VLM selects top, bottom, or tie separately for each dimension. We repeat the comparison with independently randomized ordering and report tie-adjusted preference, counting a tie as half a win. For method A, the preference score is

    P_A=(W_A+0.5T)/(W_A+L_A+T)×100%,

    		(1)

    where W_A, L_A, and T count wins, losses, and ties. 50% indicates parity. Human preferences use the same definition. These judgments assess visible scene quality from the rendered views. They do not directly test physical stability or successful navigation.

    Human evaluation.

    We recruit 65 volunteers and exclude 14 who do not complete the required number of comparisons, leaving 51 participants and 1,860 judgments. Given the prompt and the same anonymous, randomized 2×5 composite, participants select the scene with better overall plausibility and consistency with the input text, or indicate no preference. Method identities are hidden, and no preference counts as half a win. Study oversight, consent, and protocol details are provided in the supplementary material.

    6 Experiments

    6.1 Experimental Setup

    Unless otherwise stated, all experiments use Engine A as the target backend and follow the GameSceneBench protocol. All methods use DeepSeek-V4-Flash [21] with a context window of up to 204,800 tokens. Pairwise VLM evaluation uses gpt-4o-2024-11-20. For SceneAgent, the Orchestrator is limited to 30 interaction rounds, the Planner to 50 rounds and 40 tool calls, and each Builder session to 40 rounds. The Planner produces 5–10 outdoor or 3–6 indoor subtasks, and the Orchestrator allows up to three automatic refinement rounds.

    For fairness, all baselines query the same Engine A retrieval service and asset catalog while retaining their own search prompts. We otherwise preserve their original planning, prompting, and construction procedures wherever possible. We evaluate AutoUE [24] through its scene-layout stage in the common Engine A pipeline. Full adaptation details are provided in the supplementary material. The experience library is frozen before evaluation and is not updated on GameSceneBench.

    6.2 Main Comparison on GameSceneBench

    We compare SceneAgent with AutoUE [24], Holodeck [23], ImperativeScene [7], Reason-3D [1], and SceneWeaver [22]. Table 2 reports the results.

    Human evaluation consistently favors SceneAgent. Across 1,860 judgments, SceneAgent wins 76.9%, ties in 12.7%, and loses 10.3%, yielding an overall tie-adjusted preference of 83.3%. It is preferred to each baseline, with scores of 78.2–89.4%. Pairwise VLM evaluation agrees in direction: SceneAgent is favored over every comparator in all three dimensions, with aggregate preferences of 72.5–86.7%.

    CLIPScore is also highest at 0.216, although the margin over ImperativeScene (0.214) is small. The preference results therefore provide complementary evidence about scene organization and content beyond global text–image similarity. These gains incur additional computation: average generation time is 203.2 seconds, lower than SceneWeaver but higher than the other baselines. Figure 2 provides representative outputs under the same asset and rendering protocol.

    6.3 Cross-Engine and Cross-Model Deployment

    Cross-engine.

    To demonstrate cross-backend portability, we deploy SceneAgent in Engine B and run all 69 GameSceneBench prompts while keeping the language model, agent protocol, SceneContext, core tools, skills, and generation budget fixed. Only the adapter, asset catalog and database, and capability-tool wrappers change. Figure 3 shows representative Engine B generations. Additional outputs and export schemas appear in the supplement. This study tests whether the shared protocol can be retargeted through the stated backend boundary. Because the asset catalogs differ, the examples provide qualitative evidence of retargeting rather than a matched quality comparison.

    Cross-LLM.

    We replace the main DeepSeek-V4-Flash backbone with Gemini 3.5 Flash [6], Hy3 [17], and Qwen3.6-35B-A3B [13], running each on all 69 GameSceneBench prompts with all other settings fixed.

    Gemini achieves a slightly higher CLIPScore than DeepSeek (0.220 vs. 0.216) but is slower (374.8 vs. 203.2 seconds). Their aggregate VLM preferences are near parity (51.2% vs. 48.9%): Gemini is favored for alignment (52.4%) and plausibility (53.0%), while DeepSeek is favored for completeness (51.9%). Figure 4 presents a qualitative comparison across all four language models for the same prompt. These deployments show that the shared protocol accommodates multiple model families. The near-parity comparison between Gemini and DeepSeek illustrates that model choice can change runtime substantially without a corresponding overall preference gain.

    6.4 Reusable Experience

    Library-size ablation.

    We construct a frozen library of 50 human-approved Layout and Content skills from development prompts disjoint from GameSceneBench. We compare no skills, a random subset of 20 skills, and the full library, with all other settings unchanged. Table 3 reports the results.

    The full library improves alignment and completeness over the no-skill variant, with preference scores of 59.7% and 63.8%, respectively. Spatial plausibility is 46.2%, giving an aggregate preference of 56.6% across the three dimensions. Thus, the clearest benefit is selecting and organizing prompt-relevant content. Additional guidance does not uniformly improve geometry. CLIPScore increases from 0.211 to 0.214 to 0.216 as the library grows from 0 to 20 to 50 skills. The full library’s aggregate preference over 20 skills is 52.1%, with similar plausibility and completeness, indicating modest additional gains in this comparison. Runtime increases from 173.3 to 203.2 seconds. This ablation measures access to reusable experience. It does not isolate factorization from alternative memory representations.

    Layout–Content composition.

    Figure 5 crosses representative Layout skills (rows) with Content skills (columns). Layout controls spatial organization, whereas Content controls semantic and stylistic realization. The examples illustrate recombination at inference time without storing each pairing separately. They illustrate the representation’s compositional use.

    Visual experience acquisition.

    Figure 6 illustrates how visual examples extend the same experience library. Gemini 3.5 Flash [6] extracts semantic, spatial, and construction cues from a reference image for the Planner–Builder pipeline. After human approval, the trace is factorized into Layout and Content skills through the standard update procedure. Later scenes reuse these skills without the source image.

    6.5 Single- versus Multi-Agent Construction

    We compare the full multi-agent SceneAgent with a monolithic single-agent variant on all 69 GameSceneBench prompts. The single-agent variant receives the original prompt and the complete construction-tool interface, and follows a plan-then-construct workflow specified in its system prompt. Unlike the full system, however, planning and construction are performed by the same agent within a single persistent interaction history. It does not instantiate separate Orchestrator, Planner, or Builder agents, nor does it use structured inter-agent handoffs or fresh task-local contexts.

    Both variants use the same language model backbone, Engine A asset catalog, retrieval service, construction tools, rendering protocol, and evaluation procedure. We do not enforce an identical number of model or tool calls, because these calls are determined by the respective execution protocols. Runtime therefore reflects the end-to-end cost of each design. Each variant is run three times on every benchmark prompt. Table 4 reports the results.

    The multi-agent system improves CLIPScore from 0.210 to 0.216. In the three VLM dimensions, it obtains tie-adjusted preference scores of 57.5% for alignment, 51.0% for spatial plausibility, and 62.4% for scene completeness. Aggregated across dimensions, it wins 54.6% of cases, ties in 4.8%, and loses 40.6%, corresponding to an overall preference score of 57.0%. The largest preference gain is in completeness, while plausibility is close to parity. Average runtime increases from 39.3 to 203.2 seconds with the additional planning, construction, and coordination stages. The result supports the integrated protocol for more complete construction, with a substantial quality–efficiency trade-off.

    The ablations consistently favor coverage of requested content, while spatial plausibility remains a challenge. The single-agent comparison tests decomposition, context management, and handoffs jointly. Attributing gains to individual mechanisms requires separate controls.

    7 Conclusion

    SceneAgent extends portability from scene output to the construction process and its reusable experience. Canonical SceneContext state connects fresh Builder sessions through structured handoffs, while factored Layout and Content skills preserve design guidance across generations. Backend adapters, asset configuration, and capability wrappers localize engine-specific implementation. On GameSceneBench, human and VLM comparisons favor SceneAgent over five baselines under a shared evaluation protocol. Ablations show the clearest benefits in alignment and completeness, and second-engine deployment demonstrates reuse of the shared protocol and skills. Persistent world state and composable experience provide a practical basis for portable scene construction.

    Limitations.

    Porting still requires backend integration and compatible assets. The cross-engine study uses different catalogs and establishes qualitative retargeting rather than matched quantitative quality. Fresh Builder sessions avoid replaying raw histories, but do not guarantee constant context size as scenes grow. Multi-agent orchestration adds runtime, and human approval limits update scalability. The ablations test the integrated protocol and experience availability, leaving individual mechanisms and alternative memory representations for further study. Finally, rendered-view preferences and geometry checks do not establish physical stability, navigability, or gameplay success. These limits motivate more efficient orchestration, geometry-aware refinement, and broader validation of experience transfer.

    LLM Usage Statement

    The research uses DeepSeek-V4-Flash for scene construction, with Gemini 3.5 Flash, Hy3, and Qwen3.6-35B-A3B in cross-model experiments; Gemini 3.5 Flash also supports visual experience acquisition. GPT-4o (gpt-4o-2024-11-20) is used for the pairwise scene evaluation described in the paper. OpenAI GPT and Codex assisted with editing and refining author-produced manuscript content. The authors remain responsible for all scientific claims, experimental results, citations, and the final manuscript.

    • Appendix A GameSceneBench Specification

    A.1 Benchmark Composition

    GameSceneBench is a text-driven benchmark for complete 3D game scene generation. It contains 69 user prompts, comprising 56 outdoor scenes and 13 indoor scenes. Each entry contains a unique scene identifier, a display name, an indoor–outdoor subset label, and the prompt supplied to every evaluated method. The prompts range from short, open-ended requests to detailed descriptions that specify required objects and spatial relations. The benchmark therefore tests both broad scene completion and instruction following under compositional constraints.

    The outdoor and indoor subsets cover the scene families summarized in Table 5. These categories summarize the types of scenes covered by the benchmark. They do not prescribe a unique layout or visual appearance for each prompt.

    Each method receives the same input prompt and produces a complete 3D scene using the common asset catalog, rendering pipeline, and standardized camera protocol. Every method is run independently three times for each prompt to account for generation variability. Because the benchmark admits multiple valid scene realizations and does not define a unique reference scene, the evaluation measures text–scene alignment, generation efficiency, spatial plausibility, and scene completeness rather than reconstruction error against a single fixed ground truth.

    • Appendix B Agent Tool Interfaces

    B.1 Builder Construction Interface

    Builder agents operate on the canonical SceneContext through the shared tool interface summarized in Table 6. The interface covers the complete construction loop: grounding assets, placing individual objects, synthesizing parametric structures, populating regions, inspecting the evolving scene, and making targeted corrections. It also provides a consistent execution boundary through which Builders can query existing scene state, validate intermediate results, and incrementally refine previously constructed content without directly accessing backend-specific APIs. Tools consume and return builder-coordinate quantities, while backend adapters handle engine-specific coordinates, units, asset bindings, command execution, and scene serialization. This separation allows the same Builder policy and construction protocol to remain unchanged across supported backends.

    Entity-First Asset Retrieval with search_modules.

    search_modules maps a natural-language asset request to a ranked list of candidates from the active backend’s asset catalog. Textual asset cards are encoded offline and stored in an approximate nearest-neighbor index, while each incoming query is encoded online and ranked by cosine similarity. The retriever follows an entity-first objective: candidates should match the requested object category before satisfying secondary attributes such as style, material, condition, or scene context. Its training data combine asset-grounded query synthesis with semantically similar hard negatives, including deceptive negatives that match the requested attributes but represent the wrong entity. A shared encoder is trained with a standard InfoNCE objective. The returned top-K candidates remain proposals rather than final bindings. Agents may inspect their metadata and thumbnails before selecting an asset.

    B.2 Agent-Control Interface

    The role-specific tools in Table 7 delimit the responsibilities of the Orchestrator, Planner, and Builders. The Orchestrator does not place actors directly, and the Planner commits semantic subtasks rather than modifying SceneContext. Final serialization is kept outside individual Builder sessions.

    The low-level export_json operation is hidden from Builder sessions and invoked through the Orchestrator’s export_scene interface. This keeps construction backend-neutral and localizes final serialization to the active backend adapter.

    Appendix C Rendering and Automated Evaluation

    C.1 Five-View Rendering Protocol

    For each generated scene, the camera rig is centered on the bounding box that encloses all valid actors. Its distance is adjusted automatically according to the scene extent. We render four perspective views distributed around the scene at an elevation angle of approximately 30^∘, together with one top-down view. The perspective views capture the scene from complementary directions, whereas the top-down view exposes the global layout, object distribution, and spatial relations. All views use a 60^∘ field of view and a resolution of 1920×1080.

    The same camera-placement and rendering procedure is used for all methods. This controlled setup reduces variation from presentation and helps isolate differences in planning and scene construction.

    C.2 CLIPScore and Runtime

    We compute CLIPScore [8] using CLIP ViT-L/14 [14]. For each generated scene, we compute the score between the input prompt and each of the five rendered views and average the five per-view scores. We then average over the three independent runs for each prompt when aggregating benchmark results.

    Runtime is wall-clock time from prompt submission to completion of the scene file. It includes planning and construction and excludes offline rendering, VLM evaluation, and human evaluation. Runtime is reported in seconds and averaged over the three independent runs.

    C.3 Pairwise VLM Evaluation

    The VLM evaluation considers three complementary dimensions:

  • •

    Text–scene alignment: whether the scene satisfies the objects, style, spatial relations, and other constraints in the prompt.

  • •

    Spatial plausibility: object placement, support, scale, accessibility, and unreasonable overlap.

  • •

    Scene completeness: whether the scene contains sufficient, nonredundant supporting content to form a coherent environment.

    • For each method pair, prompt, and run, the five views of both scenes are letterboxed into an anonymous 2×5 composite. The assignment of methods to the top and bottom rows is randomized. The VLM answers a separate pairwise question for each dimension with three possible outcomes: top, bottom, or tie. We repeat each comparison with independently randomized positions. The main experiments use gpt-4o-2024-11-20 for this evaluation.

    For a method A, the reported tie-adjusted preference is

    P_A=(W_A+0.5T)/(W_A+L_A+T)×100%,

    		(2)

    where W_A, L_A, and T denote the numbers of wins, losses, and ties for A, respectively. Thus, 50% indicates parity.

    Appendix D Human Evaluation Protocol

    Study oversight and consent.

    The human evaluation consisted of preference judgments between rendered synthetic scenes. No formal institutional ethics review was conducted because the study was limited to scene-preference evaluation. All participants were informed about the study and provided informed consent before taking part.

    We conducted a pairwise human preference study using the same anonymous 2×5 composites as in the VLM evaluation. Participants saw the input prompt and the two sets of rendered views, with method identities hidden and the top–bottom order randomized. For each comparison, they selected the scene with better overall plausibility and consistency with the input text, or indicated no preference. No preference is counted as half a win when computing the tie-adjusted score.

    The study interface offered 50 trials and required at least 30 completed comparisons, as shown in Figure 7. We recruited 65 volunteers. 14 participants were excluded because they did not complete the required number of comparisons, leaving 51 participants and 1,860 retained judgments. The judgments were approximately balanced across comparisons between SceneAgent and the five baselines.

    The instruction screen shown before evaluation is reproduced in Figure 7. It explains the blind comparison setting, response options, three evaluation dimensions, keyboard shortcuts, and completion requirement. Figure 8 shows the trial interface. The prompt and anonymous 2×5 composite occupy the main panel, while the response controls, optional notes, trial navigation, and progress indicator remain visible in a fixed side panel.

    Appendix E Baseline Adaptation & Runtime Accounting

    E.1 Baseline-Specific Adaptations

    We compare SceneAgent against five representative baselines spanning distinct paradigms of automatic 3D scene generation. AutoUE [24] prompts an LLM to author a procedural scene graph executed by a game-engine runtime. Holodeck [23] synthesizes indoor layouts through retrieval-guided constraint solving. ImperativeScene [7] expresses scene layouts as LLM-generated imperative programs. Reason-3D [1] pairs LLM-driven spatial reasoning with embedding-based asset retrieval. SceneWeaver [22] integrates LLM-based scene planning with a procedural asset-generation engine.

    These methods were originally developed around mutually incompatible asset ecosystems and rendering backends, many of which rely on proprietary, online-only, or platform-specific components. Their original pipelines therefore cannot be deployed uniformly and reproducibly in a single evaluation environment. To enable a fair comparison, we standardize three infrastructure layers across all five baselines:

  • •

    Asset retrieval: retrieval is redirected to a shared 3D asset repository accessed through a common text-based retrieval service. Each method retains its own search prompt or query formulation.

  • •

    Execution and rendering: layout execution and rendering are routed through the shared Engine A pipeline and camera protocol.

  • •

    Language model: every method uses DeepSeek-V4-Flash  [21] with a context window of up to 204,800 tokens.

    • The adaptations retain each method’s core scene-generation procedure, including its graph structure, constraint formulation, program templates, or reasoning workflow, within the common execution environment. All five baselines and SceneAgent use the same asset repository, retrieval service, rendering pipeline, and language model. This controls major sources of infrastructure variation and compares the adapted generation procedures. It does not reproduce each original system’s full native capabilities. Results should be interpreted within the common-backend setting.

    E.2 AutoUE Adaptation

    AutoUE [24] is designed for end-to-end game generation in Unreal Engine. For the common-backend comparison, we evaluate its scene-layout stage. The adaptation retains layout generation, asset grounding, and scene instantiation, while excluding Unreal-Engine-specific gameplay, interaction, and testing stages. This condition is denoted AutoUE† in the result tables.

    E.3 Runtime Boundary

    The same runtime boundary is applied to every evaluated method: measurement begins when the prompt is submitted and ends when scene generation completes. Planning, model interaction, retrieval, tool invocation, and construction are included when performed by the method. Offline rendering, VLM scoring, and human evaluation are excluded. This measures end-to-end generation cost while avoiding evaluation-time overhead.

    For SceneAgent, the Orchestrator is limited to 30 interaction rounds, the Planner to 50 rounds and 40 tool calls, and each Builder to 40 rounds. The Planner produces 5–10 subtasks for outdoor scenes and 3–6 subtasks for indoor scenes. The Orchestrator may invoke at most three automatic refinement rounds. The experience library is frozen before evaluation and is not updated using any GameSceneBench generation or feedback.

    Appendix F Complete Outcome Distributions and Cross-Engine Details

    F.1 Main Comparison on GameSceneBench

    The main paper reports the aggregate CLIPScore, runtime, and tie-adjusted preferences. Table 8 instead provides the underlying three-way outcome distributions, preserving how frequently SceneAgent wins outright, the baseline wins outright, or a comparison is judged a tie. The human-study panel also gives the exact number of retained judgments for each baseline comparison. These counts sum to 1,860.

    F.2 Cross-Engine Portability

    The cross-engine study runs all 69 prompts in Engine B with the same language model, agent protocol, SceneContext, core construction interface, skill library, and generation budget. The adapter, asset catalog and database, and capability wrappers are backend-specific. Because the catalogs differ, the study demonstrates deployment through this boundary rather than a matched quantitative comparison of engine quality. Here, abridged export payloads illustrate how canonical state is serialized for each backend.

    Backend export payloads.

    The canonical SceneContext is converted into the native import schema of each target engine. Listings  and  show abridged examples of the final files delivered to Engines A and B, respectively. Only one representative actor is shown in each listing. Thus, the listings illustrate the serialization boundary rather than reproducing the full scenes.

    Engine A stores the actor array directly. Asset identifiers are strings, positions use the engine’s centimeter convention, and each actor carries a display name, an instance name, collision and mode flags, an instance index, a quaternion rotation, scale, and optional color slots. For compactness, floating-point values are rounded in the excerpt.

    Engine B wraps scene generation in a PCGGenerate command. Its Param.Info field contains a serialized JSON object with the actor, group, and relation records. Asset identifiers are numeric, positions are converted to meters, and transform components are serialized as fixed-precision strings. The per-export AIID is generated at runtime. The listing separates the decoded Info payload solely to make the nested schema readable.

    Appendix G Reusable Experience Update

    G.1 Human-Led Quality Gate

    The main paper describes the human-led quality gate and the roles of automatic diagnostics, schema validation, and deduplication. Algorithm 1 provides the corresponding procedural specification.

    G.2 Representative Factored-Skill Examples

    Listings – show an abridged, mutually compatible triplet from the experience library. The Layout skill contains only reusable spatial organization and geometric constraints. The Content skill specifies semantic roles, stylistic attributes, and substitution rules without backend-specific asset bindings. The thin recipe references both skills while retaining only requirements specific to the target scene.

item.title: Unity CLI 1.0 出测试版：600M 条命令里 98% 由 coding agent 发起，官方给 Claude Code/Codex 写了 skills ｜ The Unity CLI 1.0 is here!
item.description:
一句话：引擎命令行工具的主要用户已经不是人，而是 agent。

要点：

  • 状态变化：Unity CLI 与 Pipeline 包（`com.unity.pipeline`）**结束 beta 进入 1.0**，面向项目、构建机与「你的 agent」；最新 Unity Hub 会自动装好 CLI
  • 官方给 agent 写了 skills：**Claude Code、Codex、Grok Build、Google Antigravity** 都有 Unity 官方插件，skills 本身开放在 GitHub 的 Unity skills 仓库，任何 agent 都能用
  • 数据很关键：自 7 月 20 日起 35 万+ 登录用户跑了 **6 亿+ 条命令，其中约 98% 来自 coding agent 与其他自动化**——典型用法是人先把 Unity 配好，然后由 agent 在运行中的 Editor 里干活

为什么值得看：这是「AI 一等公民引擎接口」最硬的一份证据：不是把 AI 加进引擎，而是**引擎把自己的命令行与包管理接口改造给 agent 用**，并且用量数据证明主要调用者已经变了。对做 AI 驱动工作流的团队，这条说明该把「终端接口 + skills」当成引擎的第一等能力来设计。

中文摘要：Unity 在 Unite Tokyo 宣布 Unity CLI 与 Pipeline 包（com.unity.pipeline）结束 beta、发布 1.0：前者从终端安装与管理 Unity Editor、模块与项目，后者让 CLI 驱动一个正在运行的 Editor，使脚本或 agent 能够打开工程、执行命令并检查结果；最新版 Unity Hub 已会自动安装 CLI。配套地，Unity 官方为 Claude Code、Codex、Grok Build 与 Google Antigravity 出了插件，给出自家团队编写的 skills，并把同一批 skills 公开在 GitHub 的 Unity skills 仓库里供任何 agent 使用。最能说明问题的是用量：自 7 月 20 日以来，35 万多名登录用户执行了 6 亿多条命令，其中约 98% 来自 coding agent 与其它自动化——人先把 Unity 配好，随后由 agent 在运行中的 Editor 里干活。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：Unity Blog（English）

原文发布：2026-11-17

本期推送：2026-11-17

On July 15, 2026, we brought Unity to the terminal. Today at Unite Tokyo, the Unity CLI and the Pipeline package (

com.unity.pipeline
) are out of beta. Version 1.0 is ready for your projects, your build machines and your agents.

How we got here

We started with a beta: one binary that installs and manages Unity Editors, modules and projects from the terminal, which we introduced in Meet the Unity CLI. Alongside it, the Pipeline package lets the CLI drive a running Editor on your machine, so a script or an agent could open a project, run a command and check the result.

Next, the Unity Hub started installing the CLI for you, so if you're on the latest Hub, you already have it. Then came official Unity plugins for Claude Code, Codex, Grok Build and Google Antigravity, which give those agents skills written by Unity's own teams. The same skills are public in the Unity skills repository on GitHub, so any agent can use them.

Along the way, we shipped more than 17 beta releases, shaped by what you told us.

Inside the Unity CLI

Since July 20, more than 350,000logged-in users have run more than 600 million commands with the Unity CLI. About 98% of those runs come from coding agents and other automation.

We looked closer at that usage in what we've learned about how developers use the Unity CLI: people set Unity up, then their agent does the work inside a live Editor.

What you told us

Many of the changes in 1.0 started as a bug report, a Discussions thread or a message from a studio using the CLI every day.

"I am not exaggerating when I say the CLI has completely changed how I work with Unity. It is incredible." Dorado Digital

"The CLI is crazy good in the most simplistic way. I'm still very much holding the reins for the moment, but it's really positive." Andy, Kwalee

Studios also sent us detailed reports: commands that said they succeeded when they hadn't, dialogs that blocked a remote session, scripts that broke when output changed shape. That feedback set the priorities for the releases that followed. You can read every change in the Unity CLI release notes or run 

unity changelog
.

What changed since launch

  • One command to set up your agent.
    unity setup
    installs the official plugin for Claude Code, Codex, Grok Build or Google Antigravity. 
    unity skill install --all
    gives Unity's skills to every agent on the machine, including VS Code, GitHub Copilot, Qwen Code and OpenCode, and 
    unity skill sync
    keeps them current. The install script now adds Unity's skills to every agent it finds.
  • No more sessions stuck on a hidden dialog. The CLI can now see the dialog an Editor is waiting on and answer it, so a script or an agent doesn't hang on a popup nobody can see.
  • Builds through the Editor you already have open.
    unity build --target
    builds in the Editor that has the project open, and 
    unity pipeline cloud-build
    sets up cloud build targets from the terminal.
  • Version control that reads like a person would.
    unity vcs
    names the asset behind each change in a scene or prefab, and can summarize a pull request without switching branches.
  • New projects that are ready from the start.
    unity projects create
    adds the Pipeline package to every new project, and can install the Editor the project needs. 
    unity open --until-ready
    waits until the Editor can take commands.
  • Output scripts can rely on. Every listing and stream now has the same JSON shape. Short flags mean the same thing in every command, 
    --project-path
    works everywhere, and the CLI never prompts in CI. Clear exit codes tell a script when the Editor is busy, when a dialog is blocking it or when the network is down. You can pin a CLI version range per project.
  • A health check for your project.
    unity projects audit
    runs Project Auditor and writes a report, with a focus such as upgrades, optimization or URP.
  • Easier to install and keep current. The CLI is a native binary on macOS, Linux and Windows, available through Homebrew, winget and APT. 
    unity self-update
    keeps your last three versions, so you can roll back. You can also keep the docs offline with 
    unity docs cache add
    .
  • Hardened for teams. Security fixes across installs, skills and project linking, so a cloned repository can't run its own programs in place of the real ones.

    • 1.0 is also a commitment: commands, flags and output stay compatible across 1.x releases. When something has to change, you’ll get a deprecation warning and time to update before anything is removed.

    Use it with your agents

    The CLI is how an agent actually works with Unity: it opens the project, runs commands in the Editor, enters Play mode and reads the result. With the official Unity plugin, the agent also gets Unity's own skills for tasks like building UI, setting up lighting or adding in-app purchases. See the Unity plugin documentation for the full list.

    Agents without an official plugin still work in Unity through the CLI. So do scripts, test runners and CI jobs with no AI involved at all. To see it in action, watch the Automate with Unity CLI livestream.

    Agents and automation are also getting a supported place to run. The Build Server license now covers agents and automation, not only builds: one license per instance lets you run agents on a headless Editor or in a container, on any computer.

    Coming soon: the Linux containerized Editor, a supported headless Unity Editor in a Linux container, built for CI, build machines and agents.

    What’s next?

    We’ll keep shipping updates the way we did during the beta. Next, we’re bringing more of Unity to the terminal: commands for AI Generators, Live Games and Build Automation, and accounts built for agents.

    Get started

    If you're on the latest Unity Hub, you already have the CLI. Open a terminal and start with the Unity CLI documentation. New to the terminal? Try A beginner's guide to Unity CLI and the Pipeline package, or the Unity CLI introduction video.

    And keep telling us what you build: your feedback shaped 1.0, and it will shape what comes next.

item.title: Gamer：把感知、记忆、多步推理放进一个端到端 agent，同时应付 2D 界面与 3D 模拟世界 ｜ Gamer: A Generalist Vision-Language-Action Foundation Model for Long-Horizon Real-Time Game Agent
item.description:
一句话：同一套训练与部署管线，既能操作 2D 图形界面，也能在 3D 模拟世界里跑长时任务。

要点：

  • 定位：面向复杂交互环境中的**长时程任务**，端到端架构把感知、记忆管理与多步推理合在一起
  • 覆盖两类环境：既能处理传统 **2D 图形界面**，也能进入复杂 **3D 模拟世界**，共用同一套训练与部署管线
  • 训练上先在与游戏相关的构造数据上继续预训练，再做后续适配（论文以长时程任务为主线）

为什么值得看：「一个 agent 同时会点 UI 和会在 3D 世界里跑任务」是自动化测试与 AI NPC 的共同需求。共享管线意味着不用为每种环境重训一套——对需要批量做回归测试或 NPC 行为的团队，这是成本结构上的差别。

中文摘要：Gamer 是一个面向复杂交互环境中长时程任务的通用 agent 框架。它采用端到端架构，把感知、记忆管理与多步推理整合在一起，并用同一套训练与部署管线同时支持两类环境：传统的 2D 图形界面，以及复杂的 3D 模拟世界。训练上，它先在与游戏相关的构造数据集上继续预训练，再针对长时程任务做适配。这种「一套管线吃两类环境」的设计，对自动化测试与 AI NPC 都直接有用——不必为界面操作和 3D 世界行为各维护一套模型。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·cs.CV（English）

原文发布：2026-11-16

本期推送：2026-11-17

Gamer: A Generalist Vision-Language-Action Foundation Model for Long-Horizon Real-Time Game Agent

Abstract

We introduce Gamer, a generalist agent framework built for long-horizon tasks in complex interactive environments. Its end-to-end architecture combines perception, memory management, and multi-step reasoning. A shared training and deployment pipeline supports interaction with both conventional 2D graphical interfaces and complex 3D simulated worlds. We first continue pre-training on a dataset constructed from tens of thousands of hours of device-level keyboard and mouse interaction. These trajectories span simulated games and embodied environments, allowing the model to learn environmental dynamics across both physical and virtual domains. Sparse-thinking instruction tuning then substantially reduces redundant computation while preserving the reasoning needed for complex decisions. We train the policy for long-horizon interaction with a stable multi-turn reinforcement learning method that addresses finite context windows, accumulated rollout errors, and sparse rewards. For real-time interaction, a cloud–edge inference engine serves numerous simulated game environments concurrently, supports unbounded-context execution, and keeps online inference latency low. Across multiple challenging 3D open-world games, Gamer demonstrates solid generalization and operational efficiency comparable to skilled players. It also achieves competitive results on a range of conventional 2D game benchmarks. These results suggest that even repetitive keyboard and mouse trajectories can support substantial gains from scaling data and learning algorithms. Training on these trajectories helps Gamer learn complex skills more steadily in environments with both physical and digital properties. This approach offers a path toward generalist agents that can interact across digital and physical worlds.

1 Introduction

Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) [45, 2, 13, 7, 6, 25] are rapidly evolving from static input processors into interactive agents that can operate in digital and physical environments. In particular, vision-language-action (VLA) models [46, 28, 24, 58] offer a promising path toward embodied artificial general intelligence. However, high trial-and-error costs and the lack of environmental controllability significantly hinder both the evaluation and algorithm scaling of real-world physical agents.

Modern large-scale games [11, 4, 60, 47, 61, 59, 32] provide an ideal testbed for developing generalist VLA agents and studying their scaling behaviors because they combine realistic complexity with rigorous experimental control. Compared with traditional 2D games, web interfaces, and simplified simulators, contemporary games require agents to parse complex visual scenes, navigate intricate 3D layouts, and advance multi-stage quests. Agents must continually make strategic decisions and manage resources under partial observability and delayed feedback, all through fine-grained, low-level keyboard and mouse actions. Tasks may last hours or longer, requiring reliable memory, planning, and decision-making throughout. Such environments therefore serve as an uncompromising benchmark for coordinating perception, reasoning, memory, and control.

Honkai: Star Rail (HSR) exemplifies this setting by condensing these demands into a continuously evolving game environment. Its gameplay combines narrative-driven exploration across diverse regions with turn-based combat, squad management, resource allocation, and multi-level UI operation. This environment features nested objectives and long-term progression that challenge an agent’s cross-task generalization, long-term memory, and closed-loop execution. Developing agents in this system compels MLLMs to transition from passive visual understanding to sustained, proactive interaction. Mastering such challenges paves a concrete pathway toward generalist agents capable of operating across both complex digital worlds and embodied physical environments. As illustrated in Figure 1, Gamer is designed to operate across visually and mechanically diverse environments via a single screen-to-action interface.

Although games have long served as standard testbeds for AI, extending these successes to modern, complex games remains challenging. With domain-specific policy optimization, prior agents have matched or exceeded human performance in benchmarks such as Atari [27], Minecraft [11], and StarCraft [43]. However, these methods typically use privileged internal states, tailored action spaces, or dedicated APIs, which generalize poorly beyond their narrow training domains. As summarized in Table 1, existing game agents differ substantially in their training recipes, game coverage, and real-time execution capabilities. Because modern games rarely expose internal states or dedicated interaction APIs, a true generalist agent should operate like a human player [41, 51, 33]: perceiving the world through raw visual pixels and acting through standard keyboard-and-mouse interfaces. Unifying transferable control, long-horizon decision-making, and non-invasive execution within a single generalist model remains largely unaddressed.

Unlike static benchmarks, dynamic game environments evolve continuously while an agent observes, reasons, and acts. Therefore, real-time interaction introduces a critical system bottleneck. Conventional inference engines introduce high inference latency, causing actions to be executed after the observed game state has changed. Over long trajectories, these delays can lead to control errors, unnecessary interactions, and early failures. This latency penalty also affects online reinforcement learning (RL): delayed rollouts not only inflate wall-clock collection times but also dilute the quality of policy feedback. Consequently, real-time inference is not merely a deployment requirement, but an important part of effective online learning.

To address these challenges, we present Gamer, a scalable generalist agent framework for complex interactive games. Gamer observes raw screen pixels and executes native keyboard and mouse controls. This unified device-level interface enables non-invasive interaction across diverse environments, eliminating reliance on game-specific APIs or customized action spaces. We first conduct continued pre-training (CPT) on thousands of hours of multi-source gameplay trajectories and map heterogeneous control formats into a unified keyboard-and-mouse representation to establish a transferable control prior. A scalable data-construction pipeline is built to transform raw gameplay trajectories into multi-level instruction data. Using LLM-assisted annotation, the pipeline adds task instructions, reasoning at critical decisions, and memory summaries while preserving the original observation-action sequences. We produce over a thousand hours of instruction data covering local operations, intermediate subgoals, and complete tasks. We leverage this corpus for sparse-thinking instruction tuning, enabling the policy to organize executable behavior around long-horizon objectives while retaining task-relevant memory. Finally, we introduce Temporal-Aware Group Relative Policy Optimization (TA-GRPO) to further optimize the game policy through online environment feedback and address accumulated execution errors and sparse rewards over extended interactions.

We support large-scale training and real-time deployment through a unified training, evaluation, and inference infrastructure. We extend Verl [40] to support CPT, SFT, and online RL within a shared training framework, with self-developed Streaming-vLLM serving as the inference engine for interactive evaluation and rollout generation. Streaming-vLLM combines stateful KV-cache reuse, architecture-aware execution, FSM-guided speculative decoding with BF16 verification, and streaming action dispatch to reduce inference latency. Equipped with a sandbox supporting concurrent game instances and a data pipeline that collects trajectories and identifies failures, this system enables iterative policy improvement under real-time interaction constraints. Gamer demonstrates solid generalization and operational efficiency comparable to skilled human players on several challenging 3D game tasks and achieves competitive performance on a range of traditional 2D game benchmarks in real-time. These results demonstrate that a unified keyboard-and-mouse action space which is coupled with cross-domain trajectory scaling and real-time online learning can offer a viable pathway toward generalist interactive agents.

We make the following contributions:

  • •

    A generalist agent framework for complex games. Gamer interacts with complex game environments non-invasively, using screen images as input and standard keyboard and mouse operations as a unified action space. We demonstrate how learning in this shared action space generalizes across diverse game.

  • •

    A scalable pipeline for long-horizon instruction data construction. We develop a pipeline that transforms multi-source and multi-format gameplay trajectories into instruction data. Through LLM-assisted annotation and quality validation, the pipeline enriches recorded interactions with task instructions, reasoning at critical decisions, and persistent memory summaries. Applied to tens of thousands of hours of gameplay data, it produces over a thousand hours of high-quality instruction data spanning operations, subgoals, and complete quests, providing supervision for long-horizon reasoning and control.

  • •

    Stable and scalable training, evaluation, and real-time inference. We extend Verl into a unified training and evaluation framework spanning CPT, SFT, and TA-GRPO and introduce Streaming-vLLM to support efficient online rollouts and deployment. Our RL approach optimizes memory-linked trajectory segments using verifiable environment feedback at scale.

  • •

    Strong empirical results. Gamer demonstrates solid generalization and operational efficiency comparable to skilled human players on challenging 3D commercial game tasks, and achieves competitive performance on several traditional 2D game benchmarks. These results support its potential for industrial-scale deployment.

    • 2 Continued Pre-Training for Cross-Game Control

    Games differ in world, mechanics, and objectives, but most games share a unified device-level interface: screen observations and native keyboard and mouse inputs. As shown in Figure 2, CPT adapts a pretrained multimodal model to this interface and learns transferable control from trajectories collected across environments. We first unify action representations across games and reduce biases caused by key frequencies and repeated control states. We then summarize findings from GameScaling [58] on how model capacity, gameplay data, and game composition affect control learning and cross-game generalization.

    2.1 Unified Observation-Action Representation

    Training across games requires a common action format that preserves the meaning of each game’s controls. We represent each gameplay trajectory as interleaved screen observations and native keyboard-mouse actions. For each game, a control specification B maps physical inputs to their logical functions:

    B={(kᵢ,dᵢ)}ᵢ₌₁^|B|,

    where kᵢ is a keyboard key or mouse button and dᵢ describes its in-game function. We include this specification in the policy input so that the model can interpret the shared input vocabulary using the target game’s controls.

    Following previous works [41, 51], we decouple visual decision making from low-level action execution. Observations are sampled every 200 ms (5 Hz), and each observation interval is divided into six keyboard-mouse action blocks. Let 𝔼ₜ denote as the set of mouse movement events in interval t, where each event is represented by {(δxᵢ,δyᵢ,δzᵢ)}, corresponding to horizontal movement, vertical movement, and scrolling, respectively. We define the action for interval t as

    aₜ=(ΔPₜ;K_t,1,…,K_t,6), ΔPₜ=∑_𝔼ₜ(δxᵢ,δyᵢ,δzᵢ),

    		(1)

    where ΔPₜ is the accumulated mouse movement in the interval t, and K_t,j (j=1,…,6) is the set of keyboard keys and mouse buttons pressed in action block j. We show more details of the action format in Figure 3. Each block lasts approximately 33 ms, yielding a 30 Hz action rate. Keys and buttons shared by consecutive blocks remain pressed, while those absent from the next block are released. This representation supports held movement, brief taps, dragging, and simultaneous input combinations without increasing the visual observation rate. Actions are serialized using the pretrained language model’s output vocabulary, without an additional output head.

    Given B and a recent interaction history Hₜ containing the current observation and preceding observation-action pairs, the policy autoregressively generates an output sequence yₜ=[rₜ,aₜ]:

    π_θ(yₜ|B,Hₜ)=∏ⱼ₌₁^|yₜ|π_θ(y_t,j|B,Hₜ,y_t,

    		(2)

    where rₜ is an optional reasoning sequence preceding the executable action aₜ, and y_t,j is the j-th output token. For a small fraction of CPT turns, rₜ contains retrospective reasoning annotated from the observation and recorded action. These annotations preserve the backbone’s optional reason-then-act format without changing the action targets. The same executable action representation is retained during SFT, online RL, and deployment.

    2.2 Trajectory Debiasing and Temporal Reweighting

    Gameplay data exhibit two biases that can limit transferable control learning. Uneven key frequencies encourage the model to associate actions with specific inputs rather than their functions, while long runs of repeated actions can dominate the token-level supervision. We address these biases with random key remapping and repeat-aware loss decay, respectively.

    Random key remapping.

    For each trajectory, we sample a random bijection σ:K_bind→K_bind over rebindable keys. Inputs with fixed semantics remain unchanged. The same mapping is applied to the control specification and the actions:

    B^σ={(σ(kᵢ),dᵢ)}ᵢ₌₁^|B|, K_t,j^σ={σ(k)|k∈K_t,j}, aₜ^σ=(ΔPₜ;K_t,1^σ,…,K_t,6^σ).(3)

    Historical actions are remapped consistently to obtain Hₜ^σ, whereas visual observations and mouse displacements remain unchanged. The policy is trained to predict aₜ^σ∼π_θ(aₜ^σ|B^σ,Hₜ^σ). The mapping remains fixed within a trajectory, preserving its control semantics while reducing shortcuts based on frequent key identities.

    Repeat-aware loss decay.

    More than 85% of the action steps in our interaction data repeat the preceding action, which is common in gameplay since players often hold the same inputs across multiple time steps to perform sustained behaviors such as moving or waiting. These repetitions record how long such behaviors last, so we retain the full trajectories while reducing the contribution of prolonged repetitions. Following the decaying-loss formulation in Game-TARS [51], we down-weight consecutive repeated actions. Specifically, the action-token component of the CPT objective we used is

    L_action=-∑ₜ₌₁ᵀωₜ∑ⱼ₌₁^|aₜ|\logπ_θ(a_t,j|B,Hₜ,rₜ,a_t,(4)

    where nₜ counts consecutive repetitions of the current action and resets to 1 whenever the action changes. We use γ=0.9 and omit the remapping superscript for clarity. When present, retrospective reasoning tokens are additionally supervised as part of the same autoregressive response. Eq. (4) specifies the reweighting applied to action tokens, not the full mixed-token objective.

    A newly issued action receives full weight, while successive repetitions contribute progressively less. This preserves action duration while emphasizing behavior transitions, such as stopping, turning, and interacting. Random key remapping discourages reliance on key identity, while repeat-aware decay shifts supervision toward changes in behavior.

    The CPT objective combines the reweighted action-token loss with a standard autoregressive loss for the optional reasoning tokens:

    L_CPT=L_action+Lᵣₑₐₛₒₙ,(5)
    Lᵣₑₐₛₒₙ=-∑ₜ₌₁ᵀ∑ⱼ₌₁^|rₜ|\logπ_θ(r_t,j|B,Hₜ,r_t,

    Here, rₜ=∅ for turns without reasoning, so the corresponding reasoning loss is zero. The repeat-aware weight ωₜ is applied only to action tokens. For clarity, we omit the remapping superscript; when key remapping is applied, the control specification, interaction history, and action targets are remapped consistently.

    2.3 Scaling Laws and Cross-Game Generalization

    Although a shared control interface makes cross-game CPT possible, the benefits of additional gameplay data depend on how well the training data cover the target environment. GameScaling [58] examines this dependence by varying model size, gameplay budget, and game composition. We summarize its findings here to contextualize Gamer’s CPT stage.

    To characterize these effects, a composition-aware scaling relation based on D-CPT Law [35] is adopted. Let N be model size, D the gameplay budget in hours, and q∈[0,1] the proportion of gameplay relevant to a specified validation distribution. The validation loss is modeled as

    Lᵥₐₗ(N,D,q)=E+(C_N)/(Nᵃ)+(C_Dq^η)/(Dᵇ)+(C_q)/((q+ε)ᶜ),

    		(6)

    where E, C_N, C_D, C_q, a, b, c, and η are fitted variables. The small constant ε>0 keeps the expression finite when the target game’s share is zero. In view of the widespread use of Minecraft in prior work [51, 11], Gamescaling [58] varies its proportion in the gameplay mixture to study the effect of data composition. We use q=w_MC for Minecraft validation and q=1-w_MC for validation over the remaining training-game distribution, where w_MC is the Minecraft fraction of the gameplay mixture.

    The data term describes how validation loss changes with the gameplay budget, and the final term captures differences between data mixtures. The scaling relation fits the training-game distributions and supports held-out prediction within the measured range. However, distant unseen games do not exhibit sustained gains from additional CPT data. Sec. 8.2 provides the controlled study and its empirical limits. CPT thus provides transferable control, while more distant worlds and longer tasks motivate additional task-conditioned supervision and online interaction.

    3 Supervised Fine-Tuning for Sparse Reasoning and Cross-Context Memory

    CPT learns transferable action control from visual observations, while supervised fine-tuning (SFT) teaches the model to follow explicit task objectives. We train on tasks at different difficulty levels, from local operations and intermediate subgoals to complete objectives, with reasoning and memory summaries at key decision points. The need for reasoning is inherently sparse in long-horizon gameplay. Routine movement and repeated attacks favor direct action, while route failures, target switches, and resource decisions often require replanning. Gamer therefore uses a single autoregressive policy to alternate between direct control, sparse reasoning, and memory updates. Persistent summaries carry task state across context boundaries. Figure 4 illustrates how adaptive reasoning and memory compaction are integrated into an interaction sequence.

    3.1 Multi-level Task Conditioning and Sparse Reasoning

    SFT retains the control specification B and recent interaction history Hₜ introduced during CPT, and additionally conditions the policy on a task instruction I and long-term memory Mₜ. The resulting context is

    (B,I,Mₜ,Hₜ),

    where Hₜ contains the current observation together with recent observations, actions, and previously generated reasoning. To expose the policy to task structure at different temporal scales, the instruction I is instantiated at three difficulty levels:

    I∈{Iᵒᵖ,Iˢᵘᵇ,Iᵗᵃˢᵏ},

    in which Iᵒᵖ, Iˢᵘᵇ, and Iᵗᵃˢᵏ correspond to local operations, intermediate subgoals, and complete tasks, respectively. Training data at all three levels use the same observation–action interface and are used to train a single policy that produces executable keyboard and mouse actions.

    At each interaction step, the model first generates an optional reasoning sequence rₜ and then produces the executable action aₜ. Their joint distribution follows the autoregressive generation order:

    π_θ(rₜ,aₜ|B,I,Mₜ,Hₜ)=π_θ(rₜ|B,I,Mₜ,Hₜ)·π_θ(aₜ|B,I,Mₜ,Hₜ,rₜ).

    		(7)

    The reasoning sequence takes one of three forms:

    rₜ∈{∅,rₜᶜᵘʳ,rₜᵐᵉᵐ},

    		(8)

    when rₜ=∅, π_θ(aₜ|B,I,Mₜ,Hₜ,rₜ) naturally simplifies to π_θ(aₜ|B,I,Mₜ,Hₜ). rₜᶜᵘʳ denotes reasoning for the current decision and rₜᵐᵉᵐ denotes a memory summary for future contexts. At routine control steps, the model sets rₜ=∅ and generates an action directly. At decision-critical or memory-update steps, the model generates reasoning before the action. Current reasoning captures immediate judgment, next subgoal, or short-term plan, such as revising a route, selecting an interaction target, or switching combat strategy. Memory summaries, by contrast, retain information needed beyond the current context, including task progress, important locations, resource states, failed attempts, and remaining plans. The policy learns when to generate reasoning within the same autoregressive process, without a separate classifier or routing head. Here, rₜ refers only to the explicitly supervised reasoning text generated by the policy and does not characterize all latent computation within the model.

    SFT trains current reasoning, memory summaries, and executable actions within the same autoregressive output space. Let

    yₜ=[rₜ,aₜ]

    denote the complete output sequence at step t, and let y_t,

    L_SFT=-∑ₜ∑ⱼ₌₁^|yₜ|\logπ_θ(y_t,j|B,I,Mₜ,Hₜ,y_t,

    		(9)

    The objective uses the same token-level autoregressive formulation as CPT, with the target extended from the action aₜ to the reasoning-action sequence [rₜ,aₜ]. It also introduces the task instruction I and long-term memory Mₜ into the conditioning context.

    3.2 Summary-Based Cross-Context Memory

    Long-horizon tasks require the agent to retain relevant information after earlier observations and actions leave the active context. We update long-term memory Mₜ when the task changes stage, a subgoal is completed, or older interactions are about to leave the active context. Consider a memory-update step in which the short-term history Hₜ is partitioned as

    Hₜ=Hₜᵒˡᵈ⊕Hₜᵏᵉᵉᵖ,

    where Hₜᵒˡᵈ contains earlier interactions that will leave the active context, Hₜᵏᵉᵉᵖ contains recent interactions that remain directly accessible, and ⊕ denotes temporal concatenation.

    Before Hₜᵒˡᵈ is discarded, the model generates a memory summary from the complete information currently available. The long-term memory and short-term history are then updated as

    rₜᵐᵉᵐ∼π_θ(·|B,I,Mₜ,Hₜ), (Mₜ⁺,Hₜ⁺)=(Mₜ̄⊕rₜᵐᵉᵐ,Hₜᵏᵉᵉᵖ).

    		(10)

    Here, Mₜ⁺ and Hₜ⁺ denote the updated long-term memory and short-term history. Mₜ̄ denotes the portion of the previous memory retained after reserving space for the new summary. When the memory budget is exceeded, the oldest complete summaries are removed in temporal order.

    The update preserves overall task progress in memory and recent interaction details in the active history. Task-relevant information contained in Hₜᵒˡᵈ is carried forward through rₜᵐᵉᵐ, while fine-grained recent evidence remains directly accessible in Hₜᵏᵉᵉᵖ. When memory is updated at a task boundary without context eviction, we set Hₜᵒˡᵈ=∅ and Hₜᵏᵉᵉᵖ=Hₜ.

    A memory-update step remains an ordinary interaction step. After generating rₜᵐᵉᵐ, the policy still produces the corresponding executable action aₜ. Memory generation remains part of the reasoning–action process, allowing closed-loop control to continue without help from another memory model. During training, each step uses only the information that would be available at inference time. Each memory summary is generated only from interactions available at the corresponding update point.
