The model-facing interface is shared across Qwen3-VL [3] and Qwen3.5 [36], including dense and mixture-of-experts (MoE) backbones. Architecture-specific kernels and schedules support each backbone while preserving the same observation–action protocol. Appendix C reports representative Dense and MoE serving configurations on Ampere (NVIDIA A800) and Hopper (NVIDIA H200).

    5.1 Memory-Compacted Streaming Context

    At each interaction step, the model consumes the control specification, task instruction, long-term memory, and recent observation-action history (B,I,Mₜ,Hₜ). Re-encoding the visual and textual history at every turn would repeat the same prefill work. As shown in Figure 6, Streaming-vLLM instead preserves KV states of retained context and computes new states only for newly appended tokens, following stateful streaming inference [53, 54]. A short-term queue holds recent complete interaction rounds, while a long-term queue stores generated memory summaries. At a compaction boundary, the policy summarizes history before eviction. The discarded rounds release their KV pages, and recent rounds retain cached states. Each environment keeps its own logical-to-physical block table over the paged allocator [16], allowing requests with different history lengths to coexist.

    Compaction also changes the logical token positions of retained states. We update the rotary phase of the corresponding cached keys using the positional shift, without recomputing their projections or modifying the value cache. The retained cache preserves state across turns, so it need not be numerically equivalent to a full re-encoding of the shortened context. The precise RoPE refresh and its scope are detailed in Appendix C.2. The same bounded history and persistent summaries are used in SFT and to link TA-GRPO trajectory segments.

    5.2 Architecture-Aware Execution Across Backbones

    Frequent short requests incur costs beyond prefill, including decoder launches, inter-device communication, and architecture-specific operations. Streaming-vLLM separates a common serving interface from specialized execution paths. Dense and MoE variants share action serialization, context compaction, and client scheduling, while the compute backend accommodates their respective attention, expert, and recurrent or gated-delta-network operations. We combine operator fusion, tensor-parallel execution, communication overlap, and CUDA Graph replay to reduce serial overhead. We apply tensor parallelism selectively. It can reduce decoder compute time, but communication and synchronization may outweigh the savings for the smaller ViT workload. The measured tradeoff is analyzed in Table 9. On NVIDIA H200, a C++ and bare-PTX BF16 backend further reduces kernel and orchestration costs on the critical path. Optional W8A8 paths are evaluated independently because lower precision does not always improve latency at a given model size or tensor-parallel degree.

    We assess portability across model families and hardware configurations. We support Qwen3-VL [3] dense models at 2B, 4B, 8B, and 32B and its 30B-A3B MoE model, as well as Qwen3.5 [36] dense models at 0.8B, 2B, 9B, and 27B and its 35B-A3B MoE model. Our experiments and analysis cover representative Qwen3-VL Dense and Qwen3.5 MoE workloads across A800 and H200. The appendix compares numerical precision and tensor-parallel settings on each GPU.

    5.3 Verified FSM Decoding and Streaming Actions

    After execution overhead is reduced, autoregressive generation remains sequential. A fast finite-state-machine (FSM) drafter proposes predictable structural tokens in the reasoning–action output. The FSM tracks , , <|action_start|>, and <|action_end|> boundaries. It proposes closing an empty reasoning span or starting an action packet after reasoning ends. Within the action, it drafts whitespace after mouse-coordinate numbers, the separator following the Z coordinate, and predictable delimiters and empty-key patterns across the six keyboard-mouse groups. Mouse-coordinate values remain model-generated. The target model verifies FSM proposals using BF16 computation, and only accepted prefixes are committed. The policy retains control over action selection, while verification reduces the number of sequential decoding iterations. See Appendix C.1 for more details.

    Streaming-vLLM also reduces the time to the first executable action. Once the mouse fields and first verified key block are ready, the server sends that prefix to the client while the remaining blocks continue decoding. The client executes the six blocks in order, maintaining key press-hold-release semantics. Action execution can therefore begin while the remaining blocks are still being generated. The theoretical block-generation rate reported in the system ablation and the nominal 30 Hz client control protocol are distinct measurements, as clarified in Appendix C.4.

    5.4 Concurrent Serving for Online Rollouts

    Real-time rollouts require scheduling that accounts for both action deadlines and throughput. Each game environment maintains its own short-term history, long-term memory, KV pages, and timing deadlines. A shared scheduler batches context extension and decoding while limiting queueing delays that could make actions stale. This balances aggregate throughput against the progress rate of each active environment. Real-time evaluation and TA-GRPO training share the same serving path, so training rollouts are collected under the same execution protocol while the game continues to advance.

    Stateful cache reuse reduces the cost of long contexts, architecture-specific backends support different models and GPUs, and verified FSM drafting reduces action-generation cost. Combined with early action dispatch, these components enable responsive, high-frequency control and parallel RL rollouts linked by memory summaries. Section 8.6 reports latency and closed-loop evaluations, and Appendix C.4 provides representative GPU, precision, and parallelism settings.

    6 Data Construction for Cross-Game Learning

    Raw gameplay videos provide rich visual and control experience, but they rarely specify the player’s objective, the decisions that require reasoning, or the information that should be retained beyond the recent context. We develop a scalable annotation pipeline that turns heterogeneous recordings into supervision for long-horizon task following, as shown in Figure 7. Starting from tens of thousands of hours of raw gameplay collected across different sources, we filter invalid or misaligned recordings and balance coverage across gameplay scenarios. For SFT, we curate approximately 1K hours of gameplay trajectories. GPT-5.6-Luna [31] generates sparse action reasoning, task segments with instructions and scene descriptions, and task-state memories. We organize these annotations into three instruction levels: local operations, intermediate subgoals, and extended task stages.

    6.1 Trajectory Preparation and Temporal Alignment

    Data sources, filtering, and scenario balancing. We collect raw gameplay recordings with associated keyboard and mouse events from multiple sources. Within this collection, the HSR recording track contains roughly 68K sessions and 11K hours of video. Rather than annotating all available videos, we first select recordings with reliable visual and action supervision. We reject corrupted or duplicated sessions, missing or discontinuous frames, and trajectories whose video and action timestamps cannot be aligned consistently. We also remove invalid action traces, including mouse coordinates outside the valid screen or control bounds, malformed action states, and events that cross recording or interaction boundaries. Long inactive periods and recordings without meaningful interaction are filtered, while valid held inputs and task-related waiting periods are retained.

    Filtering alone would leave the instruction corpus dominated by frequently recorded activities. We therefore balance scenario coverage by limiting repeated behaviors and retaining less frequent interactions and longer task transitions. After these quality and coverage checks, we obtain approximately 3.2K sessions and 1K hours of video, which we use as the source for SFT annotation.

    Action-observation alignment. We retain the original ordering of keyboard and mouse events and associate each action block with its corresponding frame using corrected recording timestamps. Each device-level action interval spans approximately 200 ms and contains the six finer control blocks defined in Sec. 2.1. Source videos are sampled to obtain the visual observations used for annotation. When frame indices are discontinuous, or timestamps show a recording gap, an action window is not allowed to cross that boundary. Short button presses are kept as short pulses rather than being dropped by temporal aggregation. This preserves movement duration and interaction timing while producing the same executable action interface used by the policy.

    6.2 Sparse Reasoning and Visual Task Segmentation

    The annotation process separates local action reasoning from longer visual task understanding. Short video-action windows identify key decisions, while longer visual clips reveal task structure and progress. We use GPT-5.6-Luna for both annotation passes and align their outputs by the original frame IDs and recording timestamps.

    Decision-focused Thinking. We divide the action stream into windows of 50 device-level action intervals, corresponding to roughly 10 seconds of interaction. Each window contains 25 ordered game observations and the associated 50 action intervals. GPT-5.6-Luna identifies a sparse set of decision points, typically when the player selects or corrects a route, handles a new interaction prompt, changes objective, recovers from an unsuccessful attempt, or responds to a significant scene transition. Each Think annotation describes the observed outcome, the current decision, and an intended next action. Continuous movement, repeated controls, and minor camera corrections usually receive no separate reasoning target. Windows with neither meaningful input nor visual change can be skipped. This process yields approximately 1.2M timestamp-aligned Think annotations.

    Long-context instruction and scene annotation. We divide each session into the minimum number of equal-length visual clips of at most 288 seconds. Frames are selected at approximately one-second intervals and arranged into 3×2 timestamped mosaics, yielding at most 49 mosaic images per clip. This lets GPT-5.6-Luna inspect continuous visual context without exceeding the image-input budget. The model identifies contiguous task segments and assigns each a task instruction, a gameplay label, and a short scene description of the visible evidence. These task segments provide the temporal and semantic basis for the instruction hierarchy.

    We prompt the model to segment gameplay by the player’s current task. Brief movements and reward collection are grouped with the task they support, while an explicit challenge restart begins a new segment. Postprocessing adjusts adjacent segment boundaries to form a continuous timeline and converts clip-relative start and end times to timestamps in the original recording. This yields approximately 63K task segments, with a median duration of about 40 seconds. The activity labels cover seven gameplay categories: navigation, NPC dialogue, combat, minigames, system menus, Currency Wars, and other activities.

    6.3 Memory Annotation from Continuous Visual Context

    After task segmentation, we reuse the clip images and cleaned task segments in a second conversational turn to generate memory annotations. The model returns all summaries for the clip in one response, typically one per 16-second window. Each summary briefly describes, in the first person, the cumulative accomplishments and outcomes within the clip up to the window end. A final window shorter than 8 seconds is merged into the preceding window. Postprocessing associates each summary with the active task instruction and the latest image frame at or before the window end.

    The dataset contains approximately 223K memory annotations. At each training step, we condition the policy on the latest summary whose end timestamp is no later than the current observation. The annotation model receives the complete visual clip and is prompted to summarize only events up to each window end.

    6.4 Three-Level Instruction Construction

    Building on the first-pass task segments, we construct easy, medium, and hard instructions according to the scope of the objective and the number of annotated decisions it covers. These levels correspond to local operations, intermediate subgoals, and extended task stages, respectively. The same recorded interval can support instructions at multiple levels.

    Easy: local operations. Easy instructions cover one or two annotated decisions, such as approaching an NPC, selecting a menu option, or collecting an item. Medium: intermediate subgoals. Medium instructions combine related operations into a subgoal spanning three to five annotated decisions, such as navigating around an obstruction and completing the required interaction. Hard: extended task stages. Hard instructions connect multiple subgoals into a task stage spanning six or more annotated decisions, such as navigating through several areas and resolving intervening challenges.

    We construct the instruction hierarchy bottom-up from temporally aligned annotations. Task-segment instructions and scene descriptions establish the activity and its boundaries, Think annotations identify key decisions, and memories track task progress. We group adjacent operations that advance a common subgoal, then combine related subgoals into extended task stages. Human-annotated examples guide the wording and scope of the generated instructions. All three levels share the recorded actions and Think annotations, and each provides an instruction and memory context appropriate to its objective.

    Horizon-dependent training targets. For a selected supervision horizon h∈{op,sub,task}, an example is represented as

    xₜʰ=(B,Iʰ,Mₜʰ,Hₜ), yₜ=[rₜ,aₜ],

    		(15)

    where Iʰ denotes the task instruction at level h, Mₜʰ denotes its task memory, and Hₜ contains the current observation and recent interaction history. The reasoning text rₜ and action target aₜ are drawn from the same recorded trajectory and its annotations. Every step includes action supervision, including steps without Think annotations.

    7 Implementation Details

    7.1 Model and Training Configuration

    Gamer supports both dense and mixture-of-experts (MoE) architectures across Qwen3-VL and Qwen3.5 families. The trained models share the same autoregressive keyboard-mouse action interface without an additional output head. We first analyze CPT scaling across 120 controlled Qwen3.5 Dense configurations, referred to as GameScaling. Guided by these findings, we train Gamer from Qwen3-VL-8B with additional HSR gameplay data.

    Training follows three stages while preserving the model architecture and action representation. CPT learns transferable control with key remapping and repeat-aware loss decay. SFT introduces multi-level task supervision, sparse reasoning, and cross-context memory. TA-GRPO then improves long-horizon behavior through online interaction, using environment-verifiable rewards and temporal credit assignment. Gameplay trajectories are sampled at 5 Hz, with six action blocks per step providing approximately 30 Hz control and a local visual history of 20 frames.

    We extend Verl [40] into a unified training and evaluation framework, using Streaming-vLLM for interactive evaluation and online RL rollouts. A sharded inference service pool backed by 64 NVIDIA H200 GPUs serves 32 parallel game environments. Each RL iteration collects 128 rollouts in groups of 8, with environment-verifiable rewards and no learned process reward model. Updated policy weights are synchronized across the service pool before the next rollout collection, keeping policy versions aligned throughout online training. Streaming-vLLM also supports dense and MoE backbones on NVIDIA A800 and H200 GPUs. Further configuration details are provided in Table 15 and Appendix F.1.

    The controlled scaling study spans 120 CPT configurations and approximately 45K H200 GPU-hours. Shorter training budgets are derived from shared Warmup-Stable-Decay trajectories with separate final decay phases. For the subsequent Gamer training stages, CPT uses a distributed H200 cluster, SFT uses a distributed A800 cluster, and online RL uses Megatron/MCore with BF16 optimization. Real-time rollouts run in parallel game environments served by a sharded Streaming-vLLM pool backed by 64 H200 GPUs. The pool receives synchronized policy checkpoints between rollout iterations, enabling consistent interaction data collection as training progresses. More details of training configurations and stage-specific settings are summarized in Table 15.

    7.2 Data Composition and Sampling

    Our training data combines cross-game interaction trajectories, general multimodal data, multi-level task supervision, and online policy experience. Figure 8 summarizes how these sources are filtered and routed into the CPT, SFT, and RL stages, while Table 2 reports their corresponding usage and scale.

    In the CPT stage, we perform controlled scaling experiments (i.e., GameScaling) using a mixture of VPT [4], D2E [8], and OpenP2P [56] gameplay data while holding the token ratio at 85% gameplay and 15% general vision-language data (Appendix B.1). General multimodal data sources include LLaVA-OneVision [19], Zebra-CoT [18], GameQA [42], Embodied-Reasoner [62], and Cambrian-S [55]. Gamer’s CPT stage retains this data mixture ratio and adds additional HSR gameplay trajectories.

    In the SFT stage, we annotate approximately 1K hours of curated HSR gameplay trajectories. As described in Sec. 6.4, operation-level examples train local control and sparse reasoning. Subgoal-level examples add intermediate objectives and longer memory, while task-level examples cover complete long-horizon tasks. Examples at different annotation levels may come from the same trajectory and we count their derived samples and supervision tokens separately.

    To improve coverage across gameplay scenarios, we downsample overrepresented streams and excessively idle intervals while preserving meaningful movement, held controls, and waiting periods. In the HSR portion of the CPT corpus, filtering retains approximately 149K aligned clips, corresponding to around 332 hours of gameplay. Data splits are assigned at the recording or complete-task level before creating overlapping windows or multi-level examples, so derived samples from a source remain in the same split.

    7.3 Automated RL Environment

    A shared infrastructure for learning, evaluation, and testing. Many existing game-RL benchmarks run as lightweight, self-contained simulators that can be reset cheaply and queried directly for rewards. Modern commercial games present a substantially harder setting. In particular, Honkai: Star Rail depends on a full game client, supporting online services, GPU-accelerated rendering, and complex game-state dependencies. Reproducing its native mechanics in a lightweight simulator would change the interaction setting, while simply replicating game clients does not provide controlled initialization or objective verification. These challenges extend beyond online RL to large-scale automated evaluation and gameplay testing, where hundreds of executions must start from comparable states and be judged against consistent success criteria. We therefore build a dedicated, engine-instrumented sandbox that makes this resource-intensive game reproducible, verifiable, and scalable without changing the agent’s visual-control interface.

    Game-native rules as a unified source of feedback. We adapt the game engine to expose task-relevant state transitions and completion conditions to the environment backend. The resulting rule-based verifiers serve three complementary purposes. During online RL, they provide environment-verifiable rewards for TA-GRPO without a learned process reward model. During evaluation, they measure task completion objectively across models and policy checkpoints. For automated gameplay testing, the same checks provide reproducible pass/fail criteria for interactions and quest progression. This shared verification layer avoids relying on subjective assessments of generated text or inferring complex task outcomes from individual screenshots.

    GM-controlled initialization and reproducible execution. We integrate game-master (GM) commands to prepare predefined task states and restore the corresponding conditions before an episode. Each task pairs an initialization procedure with a target state, a completion check, and a termination rule. This allows the same objective to be executed repeatedly for policy optimization, fair comparison, and systematic testing of game behaviors. It also makes failed executions easier to reproduce and inspect. Crucially, all privileged engine access remains within the environment backend. The policy receives only screen observations and task context, and its actions are executed through the same keyboard–mouse interface used in real gameplay.

    Scalable execution across use cases. We construct verifiable environments spanning navigation, dialogue and interaction, and game-specific puzzle mechanics. For online RL, 32 parallel Windows game environments are served by a sharded Streaming-vLLM inference pool backed by 64 NVIDIA H200 GPUs. Each iteration collects 128 trajectories in groups of eight, with policy checkpoints synchronized before the next collection round. The same initialization, execution, and verification interfaces also support batched evaluation and automated regression tests without manually resetting or judging each attempt. Beyond enabling real-time policy optimization, this infrastructure provides a practical foundation for scalable assessment and testing in modern commercial games. Sec. 8.1 introduces the held-out side-quest and minigame evaluations.

    8 Experiments

    Our evaluation examines three complementary questions. First, we summarize the study in GameScaling, which evaluates 120 CPT configurations to characterize the effects of model scale, gameplay budget, and data composition. We then assess the executable cross-game performance of CPT policies built on Dense and MoE backbones. Next, we evaluate the separately trained HSR-augmented Gamer-CPT and its SFT and RL successors on HSR side quests and minigames, separating broad interaction skills from long-horizon task execution. Finally, we test whether real-time rollout collection supports online learning and whether Streaming-vLLM delivers the accuracy and latency needed for sustained interaction. All interactive evaluations use the shared keyboard-mouse interface.

    8.1 Evaluation Setup

    Public game benchmarks.

    We evaluate game-control policies on MCU [63], ViZDoom [52], OmniGameArena [23], and GameWorld [32]. These benchmarks vary in how far they differ from the gameplay data used for CPT. Specifically, MCU and ViZDoom evaluate game domains represented during CPT and primarily measure control learning within training-covered environments. OmniGameArena evaluates transfer to unseen three-dimensional games with related interaction semantics. GameWorld provides a more distant cross-game transfer setting with larger shifts in visual appearance, control mechanics, and task structure.

    We follow the task definitions, environment settings, and native scoring protocols of the corresponding benchmarks. Each benchmark retains its original evaluation metric. We distinguish idealized time-paused (TP) evaluation from real-time (RT) interaction. TP pauses the environment during model inference, whereas RT allows the game to continue advancing. In the public game comparison, we report the RT score as the main value and its signed difference from TP (RT-TP) in parentheses.

    Across game evaluations, we use the same set of strong multimodal baselines wherever they support the required visual-control interface. These include GPT-6.1-Sol [30], Gemini-3.8-Flash [12], GPT-5.6-Sol [31], GPT-5.6-Luna [31], Claude-Opus-5.0 [1], GLM-5.3-Flash [57], and DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Vision [9]. The same baseline pool is reused in the Honkai: Star Rail side-quest and minigame evaluations to provide a consistent comparison across control, instruction following, and gameplay generalization.

    Honkai: Star Rail evaluation suite.

    We construct two complementary evaluation sets in Honkai: Star Rail, comprising side quests and minigame tasks held out from training (Figure 9). Although the final CPT model has seen other gameplay from the same game, it has not been trained on these evaluation tasks or their target completions. This setting tests generalization to new tasks within a familiar game, rather than zero-shot transfer to an unseen game.

    The first set contains two long-horizon side quests that test sustained progress on complex instructions. Each quest may combine navigation, dialogue, combat, puzzles, and item interactions across several intermediate objectives. To finish a quest, the agent must remember quest information, track subgoal progress, and use that task state to guide low-level control.

    The two evaluated quests are Opportunity Makes the Thief (Part I) and Bestial Ferocity. They contain 30 and 55 evaluation milestones, grouped into 22 and 40 parent steps, respectively. The first quest combines navigation, dialogue, combat, and UI interaction. The second also includes three automaton-repair puzzles and repeated visits to earlier locations. The total time budgets across milestones are 30 minutes and 100 minutes, respectively.

    Each quest has a fixed initial state, task objective, milestone sequence, verifier, and termination condition. We report accuracy as the fraction of evaluated task executions that succeed, both overall and for each interaction type. The milestone inventory covers navigation, dialogue, combat, UI interaction, and, where applicable, puzzle solving. These rates measure verified progress across task executions rather than uninterrupted end-to-end quest completion. The complete milestones, types, and budgets are given in Appendix D.

    The second subset contains 40 instances across 7 minigame types, covering pattern composition, logical reasoning, spatial reasoning, temporal planning, and timing-sensitive control. Each type contains between one and sixteen evaluated instances. Figure 10 illustrates the minigame mechanics and instance distribution. We report the success rates for each type and compute overall accuracy as the unweighted mean of the seven type-level rates. Each type therefore contributes equally, regardless of its number of instances. Per-instance evaluation and taxonomy are described in Appendix D.

    8.2 Scaling Cross-Game Control with CPT

    8.2.1 Controlled Scaling Setup

    The controlled study in GameScaling [58] examines how model size, gameplay budget, and game composition affect CPT performance and cross-game generalization. These results guide further HSR-augmented Gamer-CPT recipes. We summarize its experimental setup here.

    As summarized in Table 3, the study comprises 4×6×5=120 configurations spanning Qwen3.5 backbone sizes, gameplay budgets, and data mixtures. All other training settings are held fixed. Across configurations, gameplay trajectories account for 85% of training tokens, while the remaining 15% come from a fixed pool of general multimodal data. The five mixtures, S1–S5, vary only the composition of the gameplay portion: Minecraft accounts for 100%, 51.4%, 27.1%, 2.8%, and 0%, respectively. The remaining gameplay data in S2–S5 are sampled from the same multi-game pool.

    Let w_MC denote the Minecraft fraction of the gameplay mixture. Consistent with Sec. 2.3, we use q=w_MC for Minecraft validation loss, and q=1-w_MC for validation over the multi-game training distribution. The latter denotes the non-Minecraft fraction of the gameplay experience.

    8.2.2 Interface Adaptation and Scaling Behavior

    We summarize the interface-adaptation and scaling results reported in GameScaling [58]. The corresponding plots are provided in Appendix B.2.

    Early CPT adapts the pretrained model to the shared control interface.

    Figure 12 shows that keyboard, mouse, and action-format losses decrease rapidly during the early stage of CPT, while directional prediction accuracy steadily improves. Checkpoints trained for only 50 gameplay hours already reduce validation loss on both training and unseen games relative to their corresponding base models. This early improvement across distinct action components suggests that a substantial part of initial CPT learning concerns the mechanics of executable control. It also explains why interface adaptation can precede the larger gameplay-specific gains that emerge with additional interaction experience.

    Later scaling gains increasingly depend on game composition.

    Figure 13 separates training fit from cross-game generalization. Minecraft-heavy mixtures S1-S3 continue to reduce Minecraft validation loss as the interaction budget increases, while the low-Minecraft mixtures S4 and S5 tend to saturate. On the remaining training games, multi-game mixtures continue to improve while Minecraft-only training eventually plateaus or degrades. Adding the same amount of gameplay data can therefore produce different gains, depending on its coverage of the target distribution.

    Larger models learn more efficiently early in training, but their gains still depend on data composition. Under single-game training, stronger adaptation to Minecraft can coincide with degraded performance on other games. Multi-game mixtures alleviate this effect. For distant unseen games, validation loss typically improves during early interface adaptation and then plateaus or increases even while training loss continues to decrease. These observations motivate considering model capacity, interaction budget, and target-game coverage jointly.

    Evaluation results on game benchmarks complement the validation-loss analysis with executable gameplay outcomes. As shown in Figure 14, additional CPT experience generally improves performance in training-covered and behaviorally related environments, particularly at smaller model scales. The comparison across S1-S5 also shows why the amount of gameplay alone is an incomplete description of the training signal. Mixtures that expose the model to multiple interaction patterns provide broader coverage than single-game training and support transfer to related environments. For Gamer, these findings motivate scaling game diversity alongside data volume rather than treating all recorded gameplay hours as equally informative for every target game.

    8.2.3 Scaling-Law Fit and Predictive Range

    GameScaling [58] fits the empirical relation summarized in Sec. 2.3,

    Lᵥₐₗ(N,D,q)=E+(C_N)/(Nᵃ)+(C_Dq^η)/(Dᵇ)+(C_q)/((q+ε)ᶜ),

    		(16)

    to characterize validation loss as a function of model size, gameplay budget, and target-dependent data composition.

    The study reports that the standard model-and-data scaling relation fits training loss with R²=0.980 and RMSE =0.0041. For Minecraft and the multi-game training distribution, the composition-aware relation achieves the fit accuracy reported in Table 4.

    Both validation distributions yield a positive fitted η. At a fixed model size, increasing the interaction budget therefore produces larger gains when the training mixture contains more experience relevant to the validation distribution. The fit captures the same interaction between data quantity and composition visible in the measured curves. In particular, it distinguishes a model that has seen more gameplay from one that has seen more gameplay relevant to the target environment. This provides a practical basis for choosing CPT mixtures when expanding the training corpus.

    GameScaling further performs block-wise holdout tests over model sizes, data budgets, and game mixtures. Capacity and budget holdouts support prediction within the measured range. Mixture prediction is more sensitive to the availability of nearby compositions. The fitted relation summarizes the observed scaling regime across the evaluated distributions. Fitting details and holdout results are provided in Appendix B.3.

    Distant unseen games provide a useful negative control. Their validation loss rises again after early adaptation. Fitting the same functional form yields a data exponent close to b=0. The nominal R²=0.855 is dominated by static differences across mixtures, while the within-mixture R² is only 0.079. A high overall fit score therefore does not imply continued improvement from additional interaction data.

    8.2.4 Cross-Game Performance of CPT Policies

    While the controlled GameScaling study reveals how model size and gameplay data affect CPT, an important question remains: whether CPT can translate general-purpose visual understanding into executable control across diverse games. Unlike static visual reasoning, gameplay requires the agent to continuously interpret observations, execute precise actions, and adapt to evolving environments. We therefore evaluate whether CPT-trained policies can achieve effective real-time control across different games and backbone architectures. Table 5 compares two CPT checkpoints, initialized from Qwen3-VL-8B Dense and Qwen3.5-35B-A3B MoE, with general-purpose multimodal baselines on four public game benchmarks. We report real-time (RT) scores as the primary results, together with their signed differences from time-paused (TP) evaluation.

    CPT supports effective cross-game control across Dense and MoE backbones. The Qwen3-VL-8B CPT policy achieves an average real-time score of 29.5, while the Qwen3.5-35B-A3B MoE CPT policy reaches 31.5. Both exceed the strongest listed general-purpose baseline. The difference is especially clear on MCU, where the two CPT policies score 47.7 and 65.3, respectively. Their results also show complementary strengths across games. The 8B Dense policy achieves 21.9 on OmniGameArena and 34.0 on GameWorld, while the MoE policy performs particularly strongly on MCU. These results extend the scaling analysis from action prediction and validation loss to executable gameplay, and show that the CPT approach is applicable to both Dense and MoE model architectures.

    Real-time evaluation provides a practical measure of control ability. The paired RT and TP results further highlight the importance of real-time inference for interactive game control. While most general-purpose models experience substantial performance degradation when the game continues advancing during inference, our 8B CPT policy shows only a modest decrease, demonstrating its ability to maintain effective control under real-time constraints. Notably, the MoE CPT policy achieves an average RT–TP improvement of +3.4 points. This positive gain is consistent with its faster inference, which enables more timely interaction with the evolving environment and reduces the accumulation of control errors. These results suggest that low-latency inference is important not only for preserving gameplay performance but also for fully realizing the capabilities learned through CPT. Further details and results of the 120-configuration GameScaling study are provided in [Zhang et al. [58]]. Table 5 complements the scaling analysis with direct evidence of executable cross-game control. We further investigate the inference optimizations enabling real-time interaction in Sec. 8.6.

    8.3 Long-Horizon Instruction Following in Side Quests

    The two side quests require the agent to carry out multi-stage tasks while retaining information from earlier interactions. Table 6 reports verified task-execution success rates on Gamer.

    SFT substantially improves long-horizon task execution. On Opportunity Makes the Thief (Part I), overall accuracy increases from 0.0% for Qwen3-VL-8B to 34.4% after HSR-augmented CPT and 72.2% after SFT. On Bestial Ferocity, the corresponding scores are 13.9%, 47.9%, and 69.1%. Thus, SFT adds 37.8 and 21.2 percentage points over the respective CPT checkpoints. The improvement is visible across distinct interaction types. For example, navigation rises from 14.3% to 47.6% on the first quest, while dialogue increases from 70.8% to 97.9% on the second. These outcomes are consistent with the objective of multi-level instruction tuning, which trains the same action policy to follow goals that span local operations, intermediate subgoals, and longer task sequences.

    Both quests involve repeated scene transitions, UI interactions, and changes in objectives. To make progress, the agent must retain relevant information from earlier interactions and use it to decide what to do next. SFT improves performance on held-out tasks, suggesting that task-conditioned reasoning and memory can support this behavior in a familiar game, even when the specific evaluation objectives were excluded from training.

    Online RL further strengthens long-horizon execution. We perform online RL on the basis of the SFT checkpoint. Relative to its SFT initialization, TA-GRPO improves overall task-execution accuracy from 72.2% to 80.0% on Opportunity Makes the Thief (Part I) and from 69.1% to 83.6% on Bestial Ferocity. These correspond to gains of 7.8 and 14.5 percentage points, respectively. Navigation accuracy rises from 47.6% to 69.1% on the first quest and from 55.2% to 80.2% on the second. On Bestial Ferocity, dialogue reaches 100% after RL. These results suggest that verified interaction feedback helps refine the policy’s ability to advance toward task goals over extended trajectories.

    The gains across both side quests highlight the complementary roles of instruction supervision and online policy optimization. SFT provides task-conditioned decisions and memory, while RL allows the policy to learn from the consequences of its own actions under game-native verification. Importantly, these improvements are obtained without changing the underlying action interface or model architecture. Appendix E provides representative training and held-out development rollouts that illustrate how navigation and final-target interactions evolve across checkpoints.

    8.4 Instruction Generalization across Diverse Minigames

    The minigame suite emphasizes instruction following across different gameplay mechanics. This broader coverage is important because the tasks require different combinations of spatial reasoning, rule interpretation, visual matching, and device-level interaction rather than a single repeated control routine. Table 7 reports success for each of the seven types and their unweighted macro-average.

    Instruction tuning broadens success across distinct minigame mechanics. The seven-type macro-average increases from 3.2% for the base Qwen3-VL-8B to 15.0% for Gamer-CPT and 39.2% for Gamer-SFT, a further gain of 24.2 percentage points after instruction tuning. SFT reaches 76.2% on Janus’s Hidden Passage, 52.4% on Janus’s Maze, and 50.0% on Navigation Compass. It also obtains non-zero mean success in all seven types, compared with three for the base model. The CPT checkpoint already improves the macro-average, providing a useful foundation for responding to gameplay observations and actions. SFT then connects these control capabilities to task-specific goals, which is reflected in improvements across puzzles with different interfaces and completion rules. The evaluation tasks are held out from training, so the comparison measures generalization to new instances and objectives within HSR.

    Online RL further improves performance across diverse mechanics. Following SFT, Gamer-RL raises the seven-type macro-average from 39.2% to 49.7%, an additional gain of 10.5 percentage points. The improvement is particularly pronounced on Navigation Compass, where accuracy increases from 50.0% to 95.8%. RL also improves Magflow Link from 40.0% to 53.3%, Hexanexus from 11.1% to 33.3% and Janus’s Hidden Passage from 76.2% to 81.0%, with additional gains on Abacus Circuitry and Golden Scapegoat. These results extend the benefits of online policy optimization beyond long-horizon quests to tasks involving diverse rules and interaction patterns. Together, the CPT, SFT, and RL stages progressively improve the model’s ability to interpret instructions and execute actions across different game mechanics.

    To prevent game types with more tasks from dominating the aggregate, the overall metric first averages attempts within each task and then gives each of the seven types equal weight. This makes the reported improvement a measure of breadth across mechanics rather than only the most frequent minigame.

    8.5 Impact of Real-Time Rollouts on Online RL

    Real-time interaction is critical for online RL in modern games. Unlike lightweight simulators, modern games involve continuously evolving environments, complex gameplay mechanics, and state-dependent interactions. In this setting, inference latency affects not only the responsiveness of the deployed agent but also the quality and efficiency of online policy learning. Delayed control can cause subsequent actions to operate on outdated observations, making it harder to obtain timely feedback from the environment. We therefore examine the effect of rollout frequency on RL training, comparing real-time Streaming-vLLM against standard vLLM rollouts. The game continues to advance under both settings.

item.title: 实时新视角合成别再「先优化再渲染」：DIRT 用深度补全 + 双带混合，做即拍即看的自由视角 ｜ DIRT: Depth-completed Image-based Rendering using Two-band Blending for Live Novel-view Synthesis
item.description:
一句话：主流 NVS 要逐场景优化才能渲染，而「实时/临时」场景要求采集时就能低延迟出画面。

要点：

  • 矛盾点明确：SOTA 新视角合成通常需要**逐场景优化**之后才能渲染，这限制了它在 live 场景中的可用性；而 live/ad-hoc NVS 要求采集过程中就能低延迟渲染，并泛化到新场景
  • 已有做法是把训练/优化类方法硬改成低延迟，代价是画质
  • DIRT 改用**深度补全**加**双带混合（two-band blending）**的基于图像的渲染路线，直接面向实时出图

为什么值得看：「采集时就能看」是手机空间视频、直播与远程协作的真实需求，而逐场景优化的路线天然不满足。用深度补全 + 分带混合绕开优化，是把 IBR 那套老手艺接回实时管线的做法。

中文摘要：当前主流的新视角合成（NVS）方法通常需要先做逐场景优化再渲染，这限制了它们在实时场景中的适用性；而实时或临时的 NVS（例如采集过程中就要看到结果）要求低延迟渲染，并且要对新场景有强泛化能力。已有工作尝试把训练与优化类方法改造成低延迟版本，但往往以画质为代价。DIRT 走的是基于图像的渲染路线：用深度补全补齐几何缺失，再用双带混合处理合成过程中的接缝与光影不一致，从而在不需要逐场景优化的前提下实现实时新视角合成。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·cs.GR（English）

本期推送：2026-11-17

DIRT: Depth-completed Image-based Rendering using Two-band Blending for Live Novel-view Synthesis

Abstract

State-of-the-art novel-view synthesis (NVS) methods commonly require per-scene optimization before rendering, limiting their applicability in live settings. Live or ad-hoc NVS, however, demands low-latency rendering during capture and strong generalization to new scenes. Some previous work tried to address this task by adapting training- and optimization-based methods, trading quality for low latency. We introduce a live NVS approach following traditional image-based rendering that operates on a posed set of depth sensor observations and images. Our method leverages explicit, sparse point-based geometry obtained from active sensors, resulting in a sparsely filled depth buffer that is completed in the (novel) target view’s screen-space. Using this proxy, a posed set of images is projected into the target frame before fusing the resulting observations through a frequency-aware two-band blending strategy. The pipeline is entirely non-neural and optimization-free, requiring no training data or scene-specific optimization. As a result, our approach reduces the delay between capture and novel-view rendering and does not rely on favorable network generalization. We validate the method’s applicability to heterogeneous sensor setups — including handheld RGB-D cameras, automotive LiDAR, and thermal cameras — as well as challenging scenarios, such as low light captures. Our experiments demonstrate that the approach outperforms prior methods in live reconstruction scenarios, while maintaining competitive performance in conventional NVS benchmarks.

1 Introduction

Recent advances in novel-view synthesis (NVS) have demonstrated stunning visual quality, enabling photorealistic rendering of scenes from previously unseen viewpoints [FRFS24, BMV*22, KKLD23]. These approaches typically utilize a dataset comprising multiple images as input to optimize a detailed intermediate scene representation that is subsequently leveraged to render the scene from novel viewpoints. High visual quality, however, is often achieved at the expense of lengthy scene-specific optimization procedures, significantly extending the time between scene capture and re-rendering. To overcome this constraint, generalizable neural rendering networks are explored which amortize per-scene optimization, enabling immediate, high-quality view synthesis [HFF*23, RK21, SESM22]. These networks, however, are contingent on favorable generalization to new datasets. Recently, 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) [KKLD23] has been applied in an on-the-fly manner by [MSL*25]: 3D Gaussians are predicted online and optimized concurrently while rendering novel views. Given the real-time constraints, their initial rendering starts out commendable, but the ongoing optimization process is still noticeable, and image quality and optimization duration remain tightly linked. In contrast, our work omits iterative optimization as well as neural components within the NVS pipeline, thereby enabling more efficient resource allocation. We target scenarios involving simultaneous acquisition and re-rendering, a process that enables an observer to commence exploration of a scene while capture is still ongoing. Instead of solely focusing on RGB-only camera setups, we demonstrate how multi-sensor configurations enhance visual fidelity by leveraging data from different modalities. Therefore, we specifically target scenarios where multiple cameras, in addition to depth sensors (e.g., LiDAR sensors) are operating simultaneously.

Our framework maintains an updating scene state that holds a posed set of images and an accumulated point cloud fused from depth sensor observations. For rendering, the point cloud is projected to a target view and completed into a dense depth map, refining sparse data via a hierarchical filling strategy anchored to real-world measurements. By using the resulting dense depth as proxy geometry for multi-view two-band blending [BL*03], we facilitate accurate NVS.

We evaluate our method qualitatively and quantitatively across these challenging settings and via conventional NVS benchmarks, measuring the suitability for live settings by the latency between the arrival of sensor data and view synthesis completion. We further illustrate its versatility across diverse datasets: handheld RGB-D captures, night-time driving scenarios, LiDAR-augmented multi-camera rigs, and thermal imagery. Our results show that a fully non-neural image-based rendering (IBR) pipeline remains competitive with state-of-the-art NVS methods amid dominant per-scene optimization and feed-forward learned approaches, attaining superior image quality and faster rendering in live settings, and competitive results on established offline benchmarks.

In summary, we propose a computation-efficient approach for live-synthesis of high-quality, novel views from sparse spatial data. Distinctive characteristics and contributions are

  • •

    the ability to transform sparse point clouds into a high-quality dense depth map through a measurement-anchored hierarchical depth completion;

  • •

    the seamless integration of established two-band blending in a NVS context;

  • •

    the inherent architectural flexibility to support heterogeneous sensor inputs and various data modalities without relying on optimization or neural network training.

    • 2 Related Work

    Many NVS methods assume that sufficiently complete observations are available before rendering begins [FRF*23]. In live settings, novel views must be synthesized while acquiring observations, with computational resources shared among tracking, generation of scene representation, and rendering itself. Accordingly, we review related work by its suitability for online operation, distinguishing optimization-based, scene-agnostic, and sensor-assisted approaches, as well as methods tailored to challenging domains such as driving.

    Methods such as NeRFs [MST*21, BMT*21, BMV*23], 3D Gaussian Splatting [KKLD23, HFEM26, WYZ*24], or other neural rendering approaches [RFS22, ASK*20, TZN19, FRFS24] achieve high-quality NVS by optimizing a scene-specific representation before rendering. While this is highly effective when observations can be processed offline, the optimization phase often requires minutes to hours, making it poorly suited to live operation. Several works consequently accelerate per-scene reconstruction in order to produce useful renderings as early as possible [MESK22, MSL*25, TZG*26]. [MSL*25] encapsulate feed-forward prediction and optimization of gaussian primitives on-the-fly, to enable live NVS. Despite these advances, accelerated optimization-based methods still require computational effort to build and continually update a scene-specific representation. In a live system, this computation competes with rendering, camera tracking, and the processing of newly arriving observations.

    This motivates a complementary direction in NVS, rooted in image-based rendering [SCK08], that seeks to synthesize novel views without per-scene optimization. Recently, such methods have increasingly been augmented with neural methodologies by incorporating learned components [HPP*18, HXR*25, RK21, RALB22, HFF*23, FRF*23], often relying on sensor-based depth observations such as RGB-D or point cloud input. In foundational work by [HPP*18] blending weights are predicted by a CNN to perform image synthesis. [HXR*25] extend this idea for dynamic scenes captured by multi-view video in controlled studio settings. Similar to our approach, they use per-view proxy geometry by fusing a temporal consistent TSDF [CL96] which guides the image blending network. [FRF*23] fuse depths from a live RGB-D stream, before projecting neural features into a target-view feature map, subsequently decoding into a novel view by a generalizable CNN. [HFF*23] do so similarly, but leverage a point-based representation.

    Others adopt target-view-aligned multi-plane images (MPI) [MSO*19, FBM*24], building upon two-plane light fields [GGSC96]. [MSO*19] show that MPI parameters can be predicted in a generalizable way. Further, [FBM*24] enable real-time NVS through an iterative render-and-refine architecture with tailored attention operations, at the cost of extensive multi-GPU training.

    Recent advances in transformer-based architectures have enabled feed-forward prediction of explicit 3D geometry that can be readily used for NVS. Several directly regress per-pixel Gaussians [JMX*25, ZBT*24, LCL*25, ZTZ*25, KNY*26, ICH*25, ZTW*25, TTXM25] or surface representations [WZB*24, FFK*26]. A related line of work instead casts image synthesis as a decoding task, rendering views from ray-based queries and encoded image features [WWG*21, SESM22, JJT*24, SCW*26, JTW*25]. All of these approaches have substantial training demands and access to large-scale multi-view datasets.

    Our method retains explicit geometry to deliver scene-agnostic, high-quality NVS, without relying on learned components. Rather than reconstructing geometry from image evidence alone, we exploit data from sensors such as LiDAR or depth cameras. This design enables interactive rendering during capture while retaining quality that is competitive with optimization-based and neural methods alike.

    Natural applications of NVS under our set of constraints are automotive settings or high-quality previews for handheld RGB-D capturing. Driving scenarios pose a particularly challenging setting for offline and online NVS [TTXM25, ZLS*24, YPY*25, HLF*25]. Building a sufficiently complete representation requires fusing heterogeneous observations from multiple cameras and, often, additional sensors such as LiDAR [CBL*20, SKD*20, LXG22]. Moreover, data are acquired in uncontrolled outdoor environments containing occlusions, moving objects, and substantial appearance variation [ZLW*25, SKD*20, CBL*20]. Finally, the capture trajectory is dictated by vehicle motion and the road network, resulting in predominantly street-level viewpoints and incomplete coverage of the scene [CBL*20, SKD*20, WQA*21], making view extrapolation specifically challenging [ZLW*25, YPY*25]. Due to these challenges, existing methods get specifically tailored to automotive settings, hindering their use in broader NVS scenarios. In case of handheld capture systems, live previews are central, communicating coverage, progress, and potential failures to users [FRF*23, MSL*25]. However, for capture guidance, visually plausible learned synthesis [HFF*23, FRF*23] is not necessarily desirable: prior-driven predictions may hide missing observations or acquisition artifacts. Conversely, our approach offers a visually appealing, yet deterministic rendering that unveils the current state of capture.

    3 Depth-completed Image-based Rendering

    Inspired by preceding IBR pipelines [BBM*01, DYB98], our approach comprises three main steps to perform view synthesis: initially, we construct a target view aligned geometric depth proxy (Sec. 3.1). This proxy enables projection of auxiliary images to the target view during the subsequent warping step (Sec. 3.2). Finally, data from multiple, projected auxiliary images is blended to create a novel view (Sec. 3.3). An overview of our method is presented in Fig. 1.

    Our method assumes posed images {I} combined with an unstructured point cloud ℙ as input. We denote the target space as T and the auxiliary images as {I_A}ᵏ_i=1...k⊆{I}. While our approach allows the number of auxiliary images, k, to be freely chosen, we generally set k=4 as practical trade-off between coverage and overall performance, see supp. material (S5). Note that the approach neither assumes {I} are captured by a single camera or modality, nor do they require uniform aspect ratio or resolution.

    3.1 Geometric Proxy

    Sparse Depth Reconstruction. The input point cloud ℙ can be provided as a complete cloud for the entire scene, or accumulated from a continuous stream of consecutive depth observations, like single depth images or LiDAR sweeps. In the latter case, our accumulation is inspired by [KLL*13], filtering out transient or dynamic objects. We extend [KLL*13] by a spherical camera model for LiDAR sensors and condense the point cloud structure, omitting normals and radii. When rendering a target view I_T, this accumulated point cloud ℙ is combined with the most recent partial observation to form ℙᵗ, allowing to roughly approximate scene dynamics. ℙᵗ is rendered to the target frame’s image space. This yields a sparse 2D depth map S of the target frame with unresolved point visibility. In order to increase coverage and avoid artifacts in background regions, additional points are generated within these areas at a maximum depth value. We resolve visibility based on ℙᵗ’s projection in 2D image space, as it focuses processing on the potentially visible point set rather than costly computation over the whole, large-scale point cloud in 3D.

    Depth Completion. In order to resolve holes and faulty point visibility present in S, we apply a recursive image-space depth completion inspired by [GD98]. Unlike learned depth completion methods, which densify sparse measurements via models trained on domain-specific benchmarks [USS*17, PJH*20] and may hallucinate geometry where observations are absent, our completion remains classical and measurement-anchored, requiring no training and transferring across sensors unadapted. To construct the dense depth map D, we face two main challenges: first, missing data has to be predicted based on the surrounding samples; and second, determining whether depth samples belong to visible geometry or should be occluded. Alg. 1 outlines our approach to address these challenges. The two following paragraphs detail its subcomponents.

    Depth Completion: Hierarchical Filling. To predict missing data from the available samples, we repeatedly filter occluded points and downsample S , whereby each downsampled depth map level Sˡ will contain less holes than the previous. To do so, we first filter out occluded points (next paragraph) and then downsample by averaging valid samples in a 2×2 neighborhood. Thus, we acquire the next lower resolution of the depth map Sˡ⁺¹ (Alg. 1:6). We repeat the occlusion filtering and downsampling steps interleaved until we reach the highest possible level l. This extracts low frequency but dense information from the sparse input data. The resulting depth map hierarchy is fused back together by progressively upsampling, executing the following procedure at every level: firstly, a bilateral smoothing is applied to Sˡ⁺¹ yielding Dˡ⁺¹, which prevents staircasing, following work by [Jim14]; secondly, the image is bilinearly upsampled to acquire a dense depth map Dˡ; and thirdly, Dˡ is fused with high frequency detail from Sˡ. Thus, low-frequency information from coarser resolution levels fills missing data in higher resolutions (Alg. 1:7).

    Depth Completion: Occluded Point Filtering. Due to the sparsity of point clouds, the depth map Sˡ on any level may display points of occluded scene content. We filter such occluded samples by estimating the depth of each pixels local neighborhood ℕˡ and discard samples that are significantly more distant. This is done by applying a zero-centered high-pass kernel K (see supp. material (S1.1) for details) to Sˡ at each level l (Alg. 1:4). For brevity, we omit the level in the following descriptions of the filtering step whenever feasible. The neighborhood ℕ is given by:

    ℕ=(K∗S)/(K∗M),withM(x,y)=\begincases1&ifS(x,y)is set 0&else , \endcases

    where M represents the mask of valid points. The result of the high-pass filtering is normalized using M to ensure that only values contribute where the corresponding pixel (x,y) in S has a valid depth value. This effectively measures the local neighborhoods depth, thereby allowing for filtering of points that demonstrate a high degree of deviation. If the neighborhood ℕ is found to be significantly closer to the camera than the current point, the point is considered to be occluded and gets discarded by setting its value to 0.

    S(x,y)=\begincasesS(x,y)&ifS(x,y)≤ℕ(x,y)·τˡ 0&else\hskip9.24994pt\hskip9.24994pt\hskip9.24994pt\hskip9.24994pt\hskip9.24994pt\hskip9.24994pt\hskip9.24994pt\hskip9.24994pt\hskip9.24994pt\hskip9.24994pt. \endcases(2)

    The parameter τˡ≥1 controls the sensitivity for sample rejection. (In our experiments, we found τˡ=1+5ˡ·0.02 strikes a good balance between the preservation of detail and the avoidance of occlusion based geometric inaccuracies.) Note that while the methodology is mathematically defined in linear depth parametrization for clarity, the implementation uses inverse depth for correct interpolation.

    3.2 Warping and Disocclusion Detection

    After constructing the geometric proxy in the form of the dense depth map D, a subset of k auxiliary images {I_A} is projected onto the recovered geometry. Conventionally, this is achieved through one of two methods. In a forward approach, auxiliary pixels are warped to the proxy geometry, effectively splatting information to the target view T. Hence, depth data for each auxiliary image is required. Conversely, in a backward approach, target pixels are warped to auxiliary images, from which information is retrieved. Given that acquiring depth data for each view entails a high computational cost, the latter is better suited to real-time constraints. However, backward warping is susceptible to disocclusion artifacts, whereby target pixels may be mapped to areas occluded in the auxiliary view I_A. Therefore, these pixels require explicit handling to prevent misprojections. We unproject the depth map D for each pixel position (x,y), yielding a point set p∈ℙ_T . This point set is used in two ways: we first construct a continuous scaffold in the form of a triangle mesh from ℙ_T by connecting points of neighboring pixels to form triangles. By rendering this scaffold from the perspective of each I_A, we get a new approximate dense depth map D_A. Then, we use the per-pixel points ℙ_T a second time, projecting them to the auxiliary views as well. This yields the depths dₚ of the projected points in the perspective of each auxiliary image I_A. The subset ℙ_Ã, visible in I_A, is then determined by

    ℙ_Ã={p∈ℙ_T:dₚ-D_A(xₚ,yₚ)<ε}.(3)

    (xₚ,yₚ) are p’s pixel positions in I_A, and ε is a depth and normal dependent interval to account for numerical errors. Finally, we get the warped image I_T in the target view space by fetching the color of I_A at (x_p̃,y_p̃) of p̃∈ℙ_Ã and write it to the pixel position (x,y). Because colors are only fetched for pixels that belong to visible points, disocclusions show as holes in the warped image (Fig. 2). We track the position of these holes to get the occlusion mask O_T, yielding a set of k warped images {I_T} and occlusion masks {O_T}. Disocclusion handling and depth test are illustrated in Fig. 2.

    3.3 Blending

    The final step in the pipeline is the blending of the warped auxiliary images {I_T} to create the novel view.

    Blending Weights. Following conventional IBR approaches [BBM*01, DYB98], a weight image W is assigned to each candidate I_T. Our weights build upon the occlusion mask O_T exclusively. This occlusion aspect is prioritized, as depth-completed geometry and scene content may be misaligned, resulting in foreground image content projected onto background geometry, or vice versa, particularly at border regions, visible as seams. As these artifacts occur in the neighborhood of outlines of occlusion masks, they are hereafter denoted as occlusion edges. To minimize these, we employ an approximate, smoothed Euclidean distance transform (softEDT; see supp. material (S1.2)) to estimate a distance function D to the occlusion edges. D stays faithful near the foreground and smooths increasingly with distance, eliminating the ridges and banding characteristics of a Euclidean distance transform. The resultant value is then used as blending weights W, see Fig. 3. Consequently, pixels near occlusion edges are assigned a reduced weight, while more distant ones are assigned a higher weight. This process facilitates the elimination of seam artifacts while focusing on regions where the information is likely to be reliable.

    Two-band Blending. Blending images naively with per-pixel weights {W}, may compromise high frequency detail and result in ghosting. Such artifacts can be attributed to imperfect pose calibration or deviation of the synthesized geometry from ground truth. Our proposed blending strategy draws on related work by [BL*03]. Based on foundational work by [BA83a], they develop a two-band blending approach for stitching panoramas from multiple images mitigating the loss of high-frequencies. This blending strategy is well suited to the challenges inherent in our scenario, including varying aperture or exposure time and vignetting. The idea is the seamless blending of low-frequency information of all images within a broader spatial area, simultaneously focusing on blending high-frequency detail only in a small spatial neighborhood. The separation in two frequency bands is achieved through the use of a Laplacian Pyramid [BA83], leading to fast frequency-aware blending. We propose the application of two-band blending to image-based rendering. The low-frequency band L for a frame I_T is obtained by applying a low-pass filter using a gaussian function G_σ, where σ=0.95. The high-frequency detail for each frame is recovered by subtracting this low-frequency band from the warped input image, yielding

    L=G_σ∗I_TH=I_T-L .(4)

    The synthesis of the final image I^⊗_T is then achieved per pixel, whereby the set of low frequencies {L} are blended with the corresponding weights {W}. The high frequencies are selected from the candidate view of maximum weight.

    I^⊗_T(x,y)=H_Wₘₐₓ(x,y)+∑ᵢᵏ{L}ᵢ(x,y)*{W}ᵢ(x,y) .

    		(5)

    As demonstrated in Fig. 3, low frequencies are seamlessly blended, thereby reducing the visibility of image borders, while high-frequency detail is retained. Finally, non-covered image regions are filled with a simple PushPull[GGSC96] algorithm, coloring such regions by interpolating nearby data.

    4 Results

    4.1 Experimental Setup

    All methods are evaluated on the same machine (Intel i9-12900 CPU, NVIDIA A5000 GPU 24 GB VRAM, 64 GB RAM). To evaluate image quality, we report PSNR and LPIPS [ZIE*18] (with AlexNet [KSH12] backbone). Given our focus on live NVS, we define the primary performance metric capture-to-image as the interval between the arrival of the last input view’s sensor data and the subsequent synthesis of the test view. We benchmark competing methods as faithful as possible. All evaluations are conducted with the previously described set of hyperparameters, e.g., τˡ, σ, and k.

    Baselines. Unless stated otherwise, we evaluate generalizable approaches using their released checkpoints without fine-tuning [HFF*23, FRF*23, LCL*25, ZTZ*25, TTXM25]. Further details on the setup of baselines is provided in the supp. material (S2).

    We identify On-the-fly NVS[MSL*25], which targets live NVS from unposed RGB streams, as our closest baseline with publicly available code. To isolate NVS performance, we replace its pose-estimation with ground-truth poses. We further evaluate the neural IBR methods LiveNVS[FRF*23] and Inovis[HFF*23]. We compare to LiveNVS exclusively on RGB-D data as it requires dense depth maps. As general feed-forward Gaussian reconstruction baselines, we include Depth Anything 3[LCL*25] and Long-LRM[ZTZ*25], as well as DrivingForward[TTXM25], which is specifically tailored to driving scenarios. For offline evaluation, we remove runtime constraints and allow On-the-fly NVS[MSL*25] to process all images before re-rendering. We additionally compare with Faster-GS[HFEM26], which accelerates reconstruction while mirroring the quality of 3DGS[KKLD23], also with default optimization time.

    Datasets. For live evaluation, we simulate an evolving capture process using timestamped observations. Adopting the protocol of [TTXM25], methods receive only observations within the preceding temporal window to render a test view, evaluating extrapolation to the next viewpoint rather than interpolation between observed views. We select automotive scenes from nuScenes[CBL*20], Waymo[SKD*20], and Argoverse 2[WQA*21] with limited dynamic content, as all evaluated methods assume predominantly static scenarios. For each test frame, methods receive observations from the preceding 5 seconds. While all datasets feature multi-camera rigs, we evaluate on front cameras only, as some competing methods do not support multiple camera streams [HFF*23, MSL*25, FRF*23]. In contrast, DrivingForward receives all camera streams, as it is designed for such scenarios. We evaluate handheld RGB-D capture on the keyframed LiveNVS dataset [FRF*23], with sequences at roughly one frame per second; methods receive data from the preceding 15 seconds to render a test view.

    For conventional offline NVS, we evaluate on seven MipNeRF 360[BMV*22] and four Tanks and Temples scenes [KPZK17]. To assess cross-modal robustness, we further evaluate on thermal imagery from RGBT-Scenes[LCZ*24]. Extensive details on dataset preprocessing can be found in the supp. material (S3).

    4.2 Evaluation

    Live. Quantitative live-reconstruction results are reported in Tab. 1. Our method achieves the best LPIPS across all datasets, competitive PSNR, and substantially lower capture-to-image time than baselines with comparable fidelity. Although Long-LRM, DrivingForward, and On-the-fly NVS achieve higher PSNR on individual nuScenes and Waymo evaluations, ours obtains lower LPIPS in all comparisons. Fig. 4 shows representative live automotive and handheld RGB-D results. Our method produces sharper textured details than On-the-fly NVS. Though ours can exhibit local artifacts at depth discontinuities, the latter’s time-constrained optimization may fail to converge, particularly for small capture baselines. Long-LRM suffers from blurry textures, missing high-frequency detail. Compared to DrivingForward, our method recovers finer detail but can smear in regions poorly covered by depth observations, while they better preserve dynamic objects. Under a lane shift setting, our method yields substantially more plausible views than both On-the-fly NVS and DrivingForward.

    Offline.

    Qualitative and quantitative offline results are shown in Fig. 5 and Tab. 2. Our method is competitive with Faster-GS and consistently outperforms On-the-fly NVS. Runtime includes full-scene optimization time before rendering. On-the-fly NVS struggles with sharp geometry and planar regions, while ours mainly exhibits seam-like artifacts near depth discontinuities. This demonstrates our method’s flexibility beyond the primary scenario of live NVS. Further live and offline qualitative results, plus discussion of the differing metric trends, are provided in the supp. material (S4).

    Multimodal and Challenging Scenarios. Fig. 6 evaluates night-time automotive scenes and thermal imagery from RGBT-Scenes, while Tab. 2 reports corresponding thermal metrics. Our method remains robust under low-light conditions, where the optimization-based baselines often fail to converge to a consistent scene representation. On thermal data, our method outperforms Faster-GS and On-the-fly NVS, demonstrating robustness across sensing modalities.

    Ablation: Depth Source. To emulate RGB-D data, we compare different sources of depth (monocular [LCL*25], transformer-based multi-view stereo (MVS) [CF24]) against captured RGB-D stereo [Ste23]. We also evaluate our depth processing against TSDF [CL96, MOW*24] ablating our methods’ effectiveness to acquire target view depth from input data (Tab. 3). See supp. material (S5) for more details, a qualitative comparison, and further ablations on number of input views, point cloud density, depth completion, and blending.

    5 Discussion and Conclusion

    Dynamic Scenes. Our point accumulation splits scenes into static and dynamic components. Likewise, extending the IBR pipeline could enable handling of dynamic scenes.

    Accumulation Performance. The point cloud accumulations’ performance depends on size and frequency of depth observations. In our experiments accumulation time was negligible compared to the other parts of the pipeline, hence we consider efficient handling of larger scenes future work.

    Edge Artifacts. Our approach tends to produce artifacts at occlusion edges. As these stem from misalignment of reconstructed depth maps to ground truth, this invites further research regarding refinement of the depth completion.

    Occlusion Resolution. Our conservative disocclusion resolution allows false negatives. Improving depth maps or the warping process could yield higher image quality.

    Data Dependency. Insufficient sensor coverage results in degradation of image features. The exploration of additional assumptions or heuristics could be considered.

    Temporal Stability. Our weights may cause temporal instability under movement. To reduce these artifacts, we employ temporal anti-aliasing, following [LRSF25]. We demonstrate the efficacy in the supp. video (S6).

    In summary, we present a live novel-view synthesis approach based on image-based rendering, combining measurement-anchored depth completion with frequency-aware two-band blending. We demonstrate its effectiveness across diverse capture settings and heterogeneous sensor modalities. Visually (LPIPS), our method consistently outperforms all baselines. On PSNR, which is forgiving with low-frequency reconstructions, performance is scene-dependent; still, we improve PSNR by up to 11 % relative to the second-best state-of-the-art method for handheld RGB-D captures, and by up to 6 % for driving scenarios, while reducing capture-to-render time by at least a factor of two. Despite requiring neither scene-specific optimization nor training, our approach remains competitive on established benchmarks and outperforms prior methods in challenging settings, including night-time and thermal capture, paving the way toward reliable live novel-view synthesis for robust, real-world capture workflows.

    Supplementary Material

    This supplementary material provides supporting methodological information (Sec. S1), further details on baseline (Sec. S2) and dataset setup (Sec. S3), additional results (Sec. S4) and ablations (Sec. S5) complementing the main paper, and a description of the accompanying video (Sec. S6).

    S1 Method

    S1.1 Depth Completion

    For the high-pass kernel K, introduced in the main paper for computing a representative depth value of a pixel’s neighborhood, we use the zero-centered 5×5 kernel:

    K=\beginbmatrix1&4&6&4&1 4&16&24&16&4 6&24&0&24&6 4&16&24&16&4 1&4&6&4&1\endbmatrix(1)

    This kernel is applied to Dˡ at each level l (Algorithm 1:4).

    S1.2 SoftEDT

    Our softEDT algorithm (Algorithm 2)

    computes an approximate, smoothed Euclidean distance transform (EDT) D that stays faithful near the foreground and becomes increasingly smoothed away from it. A squared distance field D² (foreground →0, background →+∞), is refined in a multi-resolution approach. At each scale, squared distances propagate by a single min-plus convolution (D²\boxplusΔ)(p)=\min_qD²(q)+Δ(p-q) over a 3×3 paraboloid, Δ=\tiny[\beginsmallmatrix2&1&2 1&0&1 2&1&2\endsmallmatrix] of squared distances to its eight neighbors. Since one pass propagates the distance field by a pixel, longer ranges stem from recursion: the field is 2×2 min-pooled, biased by a conservative offset of ((√1/2)/(2))²=1/8, and rescaled into the respective coarser distance units, and then further transformed recursively, before bilinear upsampling that coarser with current levels by pointwise minimum. Linearized approximate distances are finally determined as D=√D².

    S2 Baselines

    In the following, we give further detail on the employed baselines and our experimental setup of their methods.

    For On-the-fly NVS[MSL*25], we report performance by measuring the average processing time of a single frame in a sequence, including Gaussian sampling and optimization. As this quantifies the time interval between the last train view detected and the rendering of the test view, we argue that this is the most analogous to capture-to-image time. Although we pass ground truth poses to the method, they still perform their pose initialization, which needs eight keyframes by default. They select keyframes based on similarity to previous keyframes to choose sufficiently differing frames. In some scenes, this led to their approach not being capable of operating under the experiments’ constraints, as a camera stream from a front facing automotive camera does not change significantly between frames. We modified their pipeline such that every frame is accepted as a keyframe to enable fair comparison. Notably, their results improved with our modifications in place, compared to their standard keyframe selection for our datasets.

    Image-based rendering approaches, like Inovis by [HFF*23] and LiveNVS by [FRF*23], are compared as follows. We compare to Inovis on all live reconstruction datasets. For all comparisons, we use the checkpoint published with their codebase that has been trained on their custom office dataset and finetuned on Kitti 360 data [LXG22]. As their method assumes point data to be colored, we color input data using the input images. LiveNVS is evaluated exclusively on their own dataset, as other datasets do not provide dense depth images, which the method depends on. Another relevant approach is Quark presented by [FBM*24], who report high rendering quality and efficiency. However, a direct comparison is not feasible due to the closed-source nature of their approach.

    As representatives for feed-forward Gaussian reconstruction approaches, we compare to DepthAnythingV3 by [LCL*25] and Long-LRM by [ZTZ*25]. Due to VRAM demands, we keep DepthAnythingV3’s default processing resolution, which sets the width to 504 and scales the height according to the input aspect ratio (processing in native dataset resolution imposed VRAM requirements >24 GB). When passing ground truth poses into the model, predicted and ground truth poses are aligned by a least squares estimation [Ume91]. We found this to cause severe misalignments and simplified the alignment strategy to only apply the scale transformation between the closest input view (i.e the pose captured right before the test view) and the test view. This significantly improved metrics for the NVS use case. For Long-LRM, we utilized the author’s Self-Reimplemented Version. The provided checkpoint requires images of height 544 and aspect ratio ≤ 1. Hence, input images are rescaled to match the desired height. For input images with aspect ratio < 1 (Argoverse 2 dataset), we utilize their option to rescale images to the max input resolution of 960×544. While images are downscaled for reconstruction, the feed-forward predicted 3D gaussians are rendered in the target frame’s resolution.
item.content:encoded:
一句话：主流 NVS 要逐场景优化才能渲染，而「实时/临时」场景要求采集时就能低延迟出画面。

要点：

  • 矛盾点明确：SOTA 新视角合成通常需要**逐场景优化**之后才能渲染，这限制了它在 live 场景中的可用性；而 live/ad-hoc NVS 要求采集过程中就能低延迟渲染，并泛化到新场景
  • 已有做法是把训练/优化类方法硬改成低延迟，代价是画质
  • DIRT 改用**深度补全**加**双带混合（two-band blending）**的基于图像的渲染路线，直接面向实时出图

为什么值得看：「采集时就能看」是手机空间视频、直播与远程协作的真实需求，而逐场景优化的路线天然不满足。用深度补全 + 分带混合绕开优化，是把 IBR 那套老手艺接回实时管线的做法。

中文摘要：当前主流的新视角合成（NVS）方法通常需要先做逐场景优化再渲染，这限制了它们在实时场景中的适用性；而实时或临时的 NVS（例如采集过程中就要看到结果）要求低延迟渲染，并且要对新场景有强泛化能力。已有工作尝试把训练与优化类方法改造成低延迟版本，但往往以画质为代价。DIRT 走的是基于图像的渲染路线：用深度补全补齐几何缺失，再用双带混合处理合成过程中的接缝与光影不一致，从而在不需要逐场景优化的前提下实现实时新视角合成。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·cs.GR（English）

原文发布：2026-11-16

本期推送：2026-11-17

DIRT: Depth-completed Image-based Rendering using Two-band Blending for Live Novel-view Synthesis

Abstract

State-of-the-art novel-view synthesis (NVS) methods commonly require per-scene optimization before rendering, limiting their applicability in live settings. Live or ad-hoc NVS, however, demands low-latency rendering during capture and strong generalization to new scenes. Some previous work tried to address this task by adapting training- and optimization-based methods, trading quality for low latency. We introduce a live NVS approach following traditional image-based rendering that operates on a posed set of depth sensor observations and images. Our method leverages explicit, sparse point-based geometry obtained from active sensors, resulting in a sparsely filled depth buffer that is completed in the (novel) target view’s screen-space. Using this proxy, a posed set of images is projected into the target frame before fusing the resulting observations through a frequency-aware two-band blending strategy.
