The pipeline is entirely non-neural and optimization-free, requiring no training data or scene-specific optimization. As a result, our approach reduces the delay between capture and novel-view rendering and does not rely on favorable network generalization. We validate the method’s applicability to heterogeneous sensor setups — including handheld RGB-D cameras, automotive LiDAR, and thermal cameras — as well as challenging scenarios, such as low light captures. Our experiments demonstrate that the approach outperforms prior methods in live reconstruction scenarios, while maintaining competitive performance in conventional NVS benchmarks.

1 Introduction

Recent advances in novel-view synthesis (NVS) have demonstrated stunning visual quality, enabling photorealistic rendering of scenes from previously unseen viewpoints [FRFS24, BMV*22, KKLD23]. These approaches typically utilize a dataset comprising multiple images as input to optimize a detailed intermediate scene representation that is subsequently leveraged to render the scene from novel viewpoints. High visual quality, however, is often achieved at the expense of lengthy scene-specific optimization procedures, significantly extending the time between scene capture and re-rendering. To overcome this constraint, generalizable neural rendering networks are explored which amortize per-scene optimization, enabling immediate, high-quality view synthesis [HFF*23, RK21, SESM22]. These networks, however, are contingent on favorable generalization to new datasets. Recently, 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) [KKLD23] has been applied in an on-the-fly manner by [MSL*25]: 3D Gaussians are predicted online and optimized concurrently while rendering novel views. Given the real-time constraints, their initial rendering starts out commendable, but the ongoing optimization process is still noticeable, and image quality and optimization duration remain tightly linked. In contrast, our work omits iterative optimization as well as neural components within the NVS pipeline, thereby enabling more efficient resource allocation. We target scenarios involving simultaneous acquisition and re-rendering, a process that enables an observer to commence exploration of a scene while capture is still ongoing. Instead of solely focusing on RGB-only camera setups, we demonstrate how multi-sensor configurations enhance visual fidelity by leveraging data from different modalities. Therefore, we specifically target scenarios where multiple cameras, in addition to depth sensors (e.g., LiDAR sensors) are operating simultaneously.

Our framework maintains an updating scene state that holds a posed set of images and an accumulated point cloud fused from depth sensor observations. For rendering, the point cloud is projected to a target view and completed into a dense depth map, refining sparse data via a hierarchical filling strategy anchored to real-world measurements. By using the resulting dense depth as proxy geometry for multi-view two-band blending [BL*03], we facilitate accurate NVS.

We evaluate our method qualitatively and quantitatively across these challenging settings and via conventional NVS benchmarks, measuring the suitability for live settings by the latency between the arrival of sensor data and view synthesis completion. We further illustrate its versatility across diverse datasets: handheld RGB-D captures, night-time driving scenarios, LiDAR-augmented multi-camera rigs, and thermal imagery. Our results show that a fully non-neural image-based rendering (IBR) pipeline remains competitive with state-of-the-art NVS methods amid dominant per-scene optimization and feed-forward learned approaches, attaining superior image quality and faster rendering in live settings, and competitive results on established offline benchmarks.

In summary, we propose a computation-efficient approach for live-synthesis of high-quality, novel views from sparse spatial data. Distinctive characteristics and contributions are

  • •

    the ability to transform sparse point clouds into a high-quality dense depth map through a measurement-anchored hierarchical depth completion;

  • •

    the seamless integration of established two-band blending in a NVS context;

  • •

    the inherent architectural flexibility to support heterogeneous sensor inputs and various data modalities without relying on optimization or neural network training.

    • 2 Related Work

    Many NVS methods assume that sufficiently complete observations are available before rendering begins [FRF*23]. In live settings, novel views must be synthesized while acquiring observations, with computational resources shared among tracking, generation of scene representation, and rendering itself. Accordingly, we review related work by its suitability for online operation, distinguishing optimization-based, scene-agnostic, and sensor-assisted approaches, as well as methods tailored to challenging domains such as driving.

    Methods such as NeRFs [MST*21, BMT*21, BMV*23], 3D Gaussian Splatting [KKLD23, HFEM26, WYZ*24], or other neural rendering approaches [RFS22, ASK*20, TZN19, FRFS24] achieve high-quality NVS by optimizing a scene-specific representation before rendering. While this is highly effective when observations can be processed offline, the optimization phase often requires minutes to hours, making it poorly suited to live operation. Several works consequently accelerate per-scene reconstruction in order to produce useful renderings as early as possible [MESK22, MSL*25, TZG*26]. [MSL*25] encapsulate feed-forward prediction and optimization of gaussian primitives on-the-fly, to enable live NVS. Despite these advances, accelerated optimization-based methods still require computational effort to build and continually update a scene-specific representation. In a live system, this computation competes with rendering, camera tracking, and the processing of newly arriving observations.

    This motivates a complementary direction in NVS, rooted in image-based rendering [SCK08], that seeks to synthesize novel views without per-scene optimization. Recently, such methods have increasingly been augmented with neural methodologies by incorporating learned components [HPP*18, HXR*25, RK21, RALB22, HFF*23, FRF*23], often relying on sensor-based depth observations such as RGB-D or point cloud input. In foundational work by [HPP*18] blending weights are predicted by a CNN to perform image synthesis. [HXR*25] extend this idea for dynamic scenes captured by multi-view video in controlled studio settings. Similar to our approach, they use per-view proxy geometry by fusing a temporal consistent TSDF [CL96] which guides the image blending network. [FRF*23] fuse depths from a live RGB-D stream, before projecting neural features into a target-view feature map, subsequently decoding into a novel view by a generalizable CNN. [HFF*23] do so similarly, but leverage a point-based representation.

    Others adopt target-view-aligned multi-plane images (MPI) [MSO*19, FBM*24], building upon two-plane light fields [GGSC96]. [MSO*19] show that MPI parameters can be predicted in a generalizable way. Further, [FBM*24] enable real-time NVS through an iterative render-and-refine architecture with tailored attention operations, at the cost of extensive multi-GPU training.

    Recent advances in transformer-based architectures have enabled feed-forward prediction of explicit 3D geometry that can be readily used for NVS. Several directly regress per-pixel Gaussians [JMX*25, ZBT*24, LCL*25, ZTZ*25, KNY*26, ICH*25, ZTW*25, TTXM25] or surface representations [WZB*24, FFK*26]. A related line of work instead casts image synthesis as a decoding task, rendering views from ray-based queries and encoded image features [WWG*21, SESM22, JJT*24, SCW*26, JTW*25]. All of these approaches have substantial training demands and access to large-scale multi-view datasets.

    Our method retains explicit geometry to deliver scene-agnostic, high-quality NVS, without relying on learned components. Rather than reconstructing geometry from image evidence alone, we exploit data from sensors such as LiDAR or depth cameras. This design enables interactive rendering during capture while retaining quality that is competitive with optimization-based and neural methods alike.

    Natural applications of NVS under our set of constraints are automotive settings or high-quality previews for handheld RGB-D capturing. Driving scenarios pose a particularly challenging setting for offline and online NVS [TTXM25, ZLS*24, YPY*25, HLF*25]. Building a sufficiently complete representation requires fusing heterogeneous observations from multiple cameras and, often, additional sensors such as LiDAR [CBL*20, SKD*20, LXG22]. Moreover, data are acquired in uncontrolled outdoor environments containing occlusions, moving objects, and substantial appearance variation [ZLW*25, SKD*20, CBL*20]. Finally, the capture trajectory is dictated by vehicle motion and the road network, resulting in predominantly street-level viewpoints and incomplete coverage of the scene [CBL*20, SKD*20, WQA*21], making view extrapolation specifically challenging [ZLW*25, YPY*25]. Due to these challenges, existing methods get specifically tailored to automotive settings, hindering their use in broader NVS scenarios. In case of handheld capture systems, live previews are central, communicating coverage, progress, and potential failures to users [FRF*23, MSL*25]. However, for capture guidance, visually plausible learned synthesis [HFF*23, FRF*23] is not necessarily desirable: prior-driven predictions may hide missing observations or acquisition artifacts. Conversely, our approach offers a visually appealing, yet deterministic rendering that unveils the current state of capture.

    3 Depth-completed Image-based Rendering

    Inspired by preceding IBR pipelines [BBM*01, DYB98], our approach comprises three main steps to perform view synthesis: initially, we construct a target view aligned geometric depth proxy (Sec. 3.1). This proxy enables projection of auxiliary images to the target view during the subsequent warping step (Sec. 3.2). Finally, data from multiple, projected auxiliary images is blended to create a novel view (Sec. 3.3). An overview of our method is presented in Fig. 1.

    Our method assumes posed images {I} combined with an unstructured point cloud ℙ as input. We denote the target space as T and the auxiliary images as {I_A}ᵏ_i=1...k⊆{I}. While our approach allows the number of auxiliary images, k, to be freely chosen, we generally set k=4 as practical trade-off between coverage and overall performance, see supp. material (S5). Note that the approach neither assumes {I} are captured by a single camera or modality, nor do they require uniform aspect ratio or resolution.

    3.1 Geometric Proxy

    Sparse Depth Reconstruction. The input point cloud ℙ can be provided as a complete cloud for the entire scene, or accumulated from a continuous stream of consecutive depth observations, like single depth images or LiDAR sweeps. In the latter case, our accumulation is inspired by [KLL*13], filtering out transient or dynamic objects. We extend [KLL*13] by a spherical camera model for LiDAR sensors and condense the point cloud structure, omitting normals and radii. When rendering a target view I_T, this accumulated point cloud ℙ is combined with the most recent partial observation to form ℙᵗ, allowing to roughly approximate scene dynamics. ℙᵗ is rendered to the target frame’s image space. This yields a sparse 2D depth map S of the target frame with unresolved point visibility. In order to increase coverage and avoid artifacts in background regions, additional points are generated within these areas at a maximum depth value. We resolve visibility based on ℙᵗ’s projection in 2D image space, as it focuses processing on the potentially visible point set rather than costly computation over the whole, large-scale point cloud in 3D.

    Depth Completion. In order to resolve holes and faulty point visibility present in S, we apply a recursive image-space depth completion inspired by [GD98]. Unlike learned depth completion methods, which densify sparse measurements via models trained on domain-specific benchmarks [USS*17, PJH*20] and may hallucinate geometry where observations are absent, our completion remains classical and measurement-anchored, requiring no training and transferring across sensors unadapted. To construct the dense depth map D, we face two main challenges: first, missing data has to be predicted based on the surrounding samples; and second, determining whether depth samples belong to visible geometry or should be occluded. Alg. 1 outlines our approach to address these challenges. The two following paragraphs detail its subcomponents.

    Depth Completion: Hierarchical Filling. To predict missing data from the available samples, we repeatedly filter occluded points and downsample S , whereby each downsampled depth map level Sˡ will contain less holes than the previous. To do so, we first filter out occluded points (next paragraph) and then downsample by averaging valid samples in a 2×2 neighborhood. Thus, we acquire the next lower resolution of the depth map Sˡ⁺¹ (Alg. 1:6). We repeat the occlusion filtering and downsampling steps interleaved until we reach the highest possible level l. This extracts low frequency but dense information from the sparse input data. The resulting depth map hierarchy is fused back together by progressively upsampling, executing the following procedure at every level: firstly, a bilateral smoothing is applied to Sˡ⁺¹ yielding Dˡ⁺¹, which prevents staircasing, following work by [Jim14]; secondly, the image is bilinearly upsampled to acquire a dense depth map Dˡ; and thirdly, Dˡ is fused with high frequency detail from Sˡ. Thus, low-frequency information from coarser resolution levels fills missing data in higher resolutions (Alg. 1:7).

    Depth Completion: Occluded Point Filtering. Due to the sparsity of point clouds, the depth map Sˡ on any level may display points of occluded scene content. We filter such occluded samples by estimating the depth of each pixels local neighborhood ℕˡ and discard samples that are significantly more distant. This is done by applying a zero-centered high-pass kernel K (see supp. material (S1.1) for details) to Sˡ at each level l (Alg. 1:4). For brevity, we omit the level in the following descriptions of the filtering step whenever feasible. The neighborhood ℕ is given by:

    ℕ=(K∗S)/(K∗M),withM(x,y)=\begincases1&ifS(x,y)is set 0&else , \endcases

    where M represents the mask of valid points. The result of the high-pass filtering is normalized using M to ensure that only values contribute where the corresponding pixel (x,y) in S has a valid depth value. This effectively measures the local neighborhoods depth, thereby allowing for filtering of points that demonstrate a high degree of deviation. If the neighborhood ℕ is found to be significantly closer to the camera than the current point, the point is considered to be occluded and gets discarded by setting its value to 0.

    S(x,y)=\begincasesS(x,y)&ifS(x,y)≤ℕ(x,y)·τˡ 0&else\hskip9.24994pt\hskip9.24994pt\hskip9.24994pt\hskip9.24994pt\hskip9.24994pt\hskip9.24994pt\hskip9.24994pt\hskip9.24994pt\hskip9.24994pt\hskip9.24994pt. \endcases(2)

    The parameter τˡ≥1 controls the sensitivity for sample rejection. (In our experiments, we found τˡ=1+5ˡ·0.02 strikes a good balance between the preservation of detail and the avoidance of occlusion based geometric inaccuracies.) Note that while the methodology is mathematically defined in linear depth parametrization for clarity, the implementation uses inverse depth for correct interpolation.

    3.2 Warping and Disocclusion Detection

    After constructing the geometric proxy in the form of the dense depth map D, a subset of k auxiliary images {I_A} is projected onto the recovered geometry. Conventionally, this is achieved through one of two methods. In a forward approach, auxiliary pixels are warped to the proxy geometry, effectively splatting information to the target view T. Hence, depth data for each auxiliary image is required. Conversely, in a backward approach, target pixels are warped to auxiliary images, from which information is retrieved. Given that acquiring depth data for each view entails a high computational cost, the latter is better suited to real-time constraints. However, backward warping is susceptible to disocclusion artifacts, whereby target pixels may be mapped to areas occluded in the auxiliary view I_A. Therefore, these pixels require explicit handling to prevent misprojections. We unproject the depth map D for each pixel position (x,y), yielding a point set p∈ℙ_T . This point set is used in two ways: we first construct a continuous scaffold in the form of a triangle mesh from ℙ_T by connecting points of neighboring pixels to form triangles. By rendering this scaffold from the perspective of each I_A, we get a new approximate dense depth map D_A. Then, we use the per-pixel points ℙ_T a second time, projecting them to the auxiliary views as well. This yields the depths dₚ of the projected points in the perspective of each auxiliary image I_A. The subset ℙ_Ã, visible in I_A, is then determined by

    ℙ_Ã={p∈ℙ_T:dₚ-D_A(xₚ,yₚ)<ε}.(3)

    (xₚ,yₚ) are p’s pixel positions in I_A, and ε is a depth and normal dependent interval to account for numerical errors. Finally, we get the warped image I_T in the target view space by fetching the color of I_A at (x_p̃,y_p̃) of p̃∈ℙ_Ã and write it to the pixel position (x,y). Because colors are only fetched for pixels that belong to visible points, disocclusions show as holes in the warped image (Fig. 2). We track the position of these holes to get the occlusion mask O_T, yielding a set of k warped images {I_T} and occlusion masks {O_T}. Disocclusion handling and depth test are illustrated in Fig. 2.

    3.3 Blending

    The final step in the pipeline is the blending of the warped auxiliary images {I_T} to create the novel view.

    Blending Weights. Following conventional IBR approaches [BBM*01, DYB98], a weight image W is assigned to each candidate I_T. Our weights build upon the occlusion mask O_T exclusively. This occlusion aspect is prioritized, as depth-completed geometry and scene content may be misaligned, resulting in foreground image content projected onto background geometry, or vice versa, particularly at border regions, visible as seams. As these artifacts occur in the neighborhood of outlines of occlusion masks, they are hereafter denoted as occlusion edges. To minimize these, we employ an approximate, smoothed Euclidean distance transform (softEDT; see supp. material (S1.2)) to estimate a distance function D to the occlusion edges. D stays faithful near the foreground and smooths increasingly with distance, eliminating the ridges and banding characteristics of a Euclidean distance transform. The resultant value is then used as blending weights W, see Fig. 3. Consequently, pixels near occlusion edges are assigned a reduced weight, while more distant ones are assigned a higher weight. This process facilitates the elimination of seam artifacts while focusing on regions where the information is likely to be reliable.

    Two-band Blending. Blending images naively with per-pixel weights {W}, may compromise high frequency detail and result in ghosting. Such artifacts can be attributed to imperfect pose calibration or deviation of the synthesized geometry from ground truth. Our proposed blending strategy draws on related work by [BL*03]. Based on foundational work by [BA83a], they develop a two-band blending approach for stitching panoramas from multiple images mitigating the loss of high-frequencies. This blending strategy is well suited to the challenges inherent in our scenario, including varying aperture or exposure time and vignetting. The idea is the seamless blending of low-frequency information of all images within a broader spatial area, simultaneously focusing on blending high-frequency detail only in a small spatial neighborhood. The separation in two frequency bands is achieved through the use of a Laplacian Pyramid [BA83], leading to fast frequency-aware blending. We propose the application of two-band blending to image-based rendering. The low-frequency band L for a frame I_T is obtained by applying a low-pass filter using a gaussian function G_σ, where σ=0.95. The high-frequency detail for each frame is recovered by subtracting this low-frequency band from the warped input image, yielding

    L=G_σ∗I_TH=I_T-L .(4)

    The synthesis of the final image I^⊗_T is then achieved per pixel, whereby the set of low frequencies {L} are blended with the corresponding weights {W}. The high frequencies are selected from the candidate view of maximum weight.

    I^⊗_T(x,y)=H_Wₘₐₓ(x,y)+∑ᵢᵏ{L}ᵢ(x,y)*{W}ᵢ(x,y) .

    		(5)

    As demonstrated in Fig. 3, low frequencies are seamlessly blended, thereby reducing the visibility of image borders, while high-frequency detail is retained. Finally, non-covered image regions are filled with a simple PushPull[GGSC96] algorithm, coloring such regions by interpolating nearby data.

    4 Results

    4.1 Experimental Setup

    All methods are evaluated on the same machine (Intel i9-12900 CPU, NVIDIA A5000 GPU 24 GB VRAM, 64 GB RAM). To evaluate image quality, we report PSNR and LPIPS [ZIE*18] (with AlexNet [KSH12] backbone). Given our focus on live NVS, we define the primary performance metric capture-to-image as the interval between the arrival of the last input view’s sensor data and the subsequent synthesis of the test view. We benchmark competing methods as faithful as possible. All evaluations are conducted with the previously described set of hyperparameters, e.g., τˡ, σ, and k.

    Baselines. Unless stated otherwise, we evaluate generalizable approaches using their released checkpoints without fine-tuning [HFF*23, FRF*23, LCL*25, ZTZ*25, TTXM25]. Further details on the setup of baselines is provided in the supp. material (S2).

    We identify On-the-fly NVS[MSL*25], which targets live NVS from unposed RGB streams, as our closest baseline with publicly available code. To isolate NVS performance, we replace its pose-estimation with ground-truth poses. We further evaluate the neural IBR methods LiveNVS[FRF*23] and Inovis[HFF*23]. We compare to LiveNVS exclusively on RGB-D data as it requires dense depth maps. As general feed-forward Gaussian reconstruction baselines, we include Depth Anything 3[LCL*25] and Long-LRM[ZTZ*25], as well as DrivingForward[TTXM25], which is specifically tailored to driving scenarios. For offline evaluation, we remove runtime constraints and allow On-the-fly NVS[MSL*25] to process all images before re-rendering. We additionally compare with Faster-GS[HFEM26], which accelerates reconstruction while mirroring the quality of 3DGS[KKLD23], also with default optimization time.

    Datasets. For live evaluation, we simulate an evolving capture process using timestamped observations. Adopting the protocol of [TTXM25], methods receive only observations within the preceding temporal window to render a test view, evaluating extrapolation to the next viewpoint rather than interpolation between observed views. We select automotive scenes from nuScenes[CBL*20], Waymo[SKD*20], and Argoverse 2[WQA*21] with limited dynamic content, as all evaluated methods assume predominantly static scenarios. For each test frame, methods receive observations from the preceding 5 seconds. While all datasets feature multi-camera rigs, we evaluate on front cameras only, as some competing methods do not support multiple camera streams [HFF*23, MSL*25, FRF*23]. In contrast, DrivingForward receives all camera streams, as it is designed for such scenarios. We evaluate handheld RGB-D capture on the keyframed LiveNVS dataset [FRF*23], with sequences at roughly one frame per second; methods receive data from the preceding 15 seconds to render a test view.

    For conventional offline NVS, we evaluate on seven MipNeRF 360[BMV*22] and four Tanks and Temples scenes [KPZK17]. To assess cross-modal robustness, we further evaluate on thermal imagery from RGBT-Scenes[LCZ*24]. Extensive details on dataset preprocessing can be found in the supp. material (S3).

    4.2 Evaluation

    Live. Quantitative live-reconstruction results are reported in Tab. 1. Our method achieves the best LPIPS across all datasets, competitive PSNR, and substantially lower capture-to-image time than baselines with comparable fidelity. Although Long-LRM, DrivingForward, and On-the-fly NVS achieve higher PSNR on individual nuScenes and Waymo evaluations, ours obtains lower LPIPS in all comparisons. Fig. 4 shows representative live automotive and handheld RGB-D results. Our method produces sharper textured details than On-the-fly NVS. Though ours can exhibit local artifacts at depth discontinuities, the latter’s time-constrained optimization may fail to converge, particularly for small capture baselines. Long-LRM suffers from blurry textures, missing high-frequency detail. Compared to DrivingForward, our method recovers finer detail but can smear in regions poorly covered by depth observations, while they better preserve dynamic objects. Under a lane shift setting, our method yields substantially more plausible views than both On-the-fly NVS and DrivingForward.

    Offline.

    Qualitative and quantitative offline results are shown in Fig. 5 and Tab. 2. Our method is competitive with Faster-GS and consistently outperforms On-the-fly NVS. Runtime includes full-scene optimization time before rendering. On-the-fly NVS struggles with sharp geometry and planar regions, while ours mainly exhibits seam-like artifacts near depth discontinuities. This demonstrates our method’s flexibility beyond the primary scenario of live NVS. Further live and offline qualitative results, plus discussion of the differing metric trends, are provided in the supp. material (S4).

    Multimodal and Challenging Scenarios. Fig. 6 evaluates night-time automotive scenes and thermal imagery from RGBT-Scenes, while Tab. 2 reports corresponding thermal metrics. Our method remains robust under low-light conditions, where the optimization-based baselines often fail to converge to a consistent scene representation. On thermal data, our method outperforms Faster-GS and On-the-fly NVS, demonstrating robustness across sensing modalities.

    Ablation: Depth Source. To emulate RGB-D data, we compare different sources of depth (monocular [LCL*25], transformer-based multi-view stereo (MVS) [CF24]) against captured RGB-D stereo [Ste23]. We also evaluate our depth processing against TSDF [CL96, MOW*24] ablating our methods’ effectiveness to acquire target view depth from input data (Tab. 3). See supp. material (S5) for more details, a qualitative comparison, and further ablations on number of input views, point cloud density, depth completion, and blending.

    5 Discussion and Conclusion

    Dynamic Scenes. Our point accumulation splits scenes into static and dynamic components. Likewise, extending the IBR pipeline could enable handling of dynamic scenes.

    Accumulation Performance. The point cloud accumulations’ performance depends on size and frequency of depth observations. In our experiments accumulation time was negligible compared to the other parts of the pipeline, hence we consider efficient handling of larger scenes future work.

    Edge Artifacts. Our approach tends to produce artifacts at occlusion edges. As these stem from misalignment of reconstructed depth maps to ground truth, this invites further research regarding refinement of the depth completion.

    Occlusion Resolution. Our conservative disocclusion resolution allows false negatives. Improving depth maps or the warping process could yield higher image quality.

    Data Dependency. Insufficient sensor coverage results in degradation of image features. The exploration of additional assumptions or heuristics could be considered.

    Temporal Stability. Our weights may cause temporal instability under movement. To reduce these artifacts, we employ temporal anti-aliasing, following [LRSF25]. We demonstrate the efficacy in the supp. video (S6).

    In summary, we present a live novel-view synthesis approach based on image-based rendering, combining measurement-anchored depth completion with frequency-aware two-band blending. We demonstrate its effectiveness across diverse capture settings and heterogeneous sensor modalities. Visually (LPIPS), our method consistently outperforms all baselines. On PSNR, which is forgiving with low-frequency reconstructions, performance is scene-dependent; still, we improve PSNR by up to 11 % relative to the second-best state-of-the-art method for handheld RGB-D captures, and by up to 6 % for driving scenarios, while reducing capture-to-render time by at least a factor of two. Despite requiring neither scene-specific optimization nor training, our approach remains competitive on established benchmarks and outperforms prior methods in challenging settings, including night-time and thermal capture, paving the way toward reliable live novel-view synthesis for robust, real-world capture workflows.

    Acknowledgments

    We sincerely thank e.solutions GmbH for supporting this work. Thanks to Linus Franke for his guidance during early stages of the project. The authors gratefully acknowledge the scientific support and HPC resources provided by the Erlangen National High Performance Computing Center (NHR@FAU) of the Friedrich-Alexander-Universität Erlangen-Nürnberg (FAU). The hardware is partially funded by the German Research Foundation (DFG). Noah Lewis was supported by the Bavarian Transformation and Research Foundation AZ-1626-24.

    （参考文献见原文。）


    Supplementary Material

    This supplementary material provides supporting methodological information (Sec. S1), further details on baseline (Sec. S2) and dataset setup (Sec. S3), additional results (Sec. S4) and ablations (Sec. S5) complementing the main paper, and a description of the accompanying video (Sec. S6).

    S1 Method

    S1.1 Depth Completion

    For the high-pass kernel K, introduced in the main paper for computing a representative depth value of a pixel’s neighborhood, we use the zero-centered 5×5 kernel:

    K=\beginbmatrix1&4&6&4&1 4&16&24&16&4 6&24&0&24&6 4&16&24&16&4 1&4&6&4&1\endbmatrix(1)

    This kernel is applied to Dˡ at each level l (Algorithm 1:4).

    S1.2 SoftEDT

    Our softEDT algorithm (Algorithm 2)

    computes an approximate, smoothed Euclidean distance transform (EDT) D that stays faithful near the foreground and becomes increasingly smoothed away from it. A squared distance field D² (foreground →0, background →+∞), is refined in a multi-resolution approach. At each scale, squared distances propagate by a single min-plus convolution (D²\boxplusΔ)(p)=\min_qD²(q)+Δ(p-q) over a 3×3 paraboloid, Δ=\tiny[\beginsmallmatrix2&1&2 1&0&1 2&1&2\endsmallmatrix] of squared distances to its eight neighbors. Since one pass propagates the distance field by a pixel, longer ranges stem from recursion: the field is 2×2 min-pooled, biased by a conservative offset of ((√1/2)/(2))²=1/8, and rescaled into the respective coarser distance units, and then further transformed recursively, before bilinear upsampling that coarser with current levels by pointwise minimum. Linearized approximate distances are finally determined as D=√D².

    S2 Baselines

    In the following, we give further detail on the employed baselines and our experimental setup of their methods.

    For On-the-fly NVS[MSL*25], we report performance by measuring the average processing time of a single frame in a sequence, including Gaussian sampling and optimization. As this quantifies the time interval between the last train view detected and the rendering of the test view, we argue that this is the most analogous to capture-to-image time. Although we pass ground truth poses to the method, they still perform their pose initialization, which needs eight keyframes by default. They select keyframes based on similarity to previous keyframes to choose sufficiently differing frames. In some scenes, this led to their approach not being capable of operating under the experiments’ constraints, as a camera stream from a front facing automotive camera does not change significantly between frames. We modified their pipeline such that every frame is accepted as a keyframe to enable fair comparison. Notably, their results improved with our modifications in place, compared to their standard keyframe selection for our datasets.

    Image-based rendering approaches, like Inovis by [HFF*23] and LiveNVS by [FRF*23], are compared as follows. We compare to Inovis on all live reconstruction datasets. For all comparisons, we use the checkpoint published with their codebase that has been trained on their custom office dataset and finetuned on Kitti 360 data [LXG22]. As their method assumes point data to be colored, we color input data using the input images. LiveNVS is evaluated exclusively on their own dataset, as other datasets do not provide dense depth images, which the method depends on. Another relevant approach is Quark presented by [FBM*24], who report high rendering quality and efficiency. However, a direct comparison is not feasible due to the closed-source nature of their approach.

    As representatives for feed-forward Gaussian reconstruction approaches, we compare to DepthAnythingV3 by [LCL*25] and Long-LRM by [ZTZ*25]. Due to VRAM demands, we keep DepthAnythingV3’s default processing resolution, which sets the width to 504 and scales the height according to the input aspect ratio (processing in native dataset resolution imposed VRAM requirements >24 GB). When passing ground truth poses into the model, predicted and ground truth poses are aligned by a least squares estimation [Ume91]. We found this to cause severe misalignments and simplified the alignment strategy to only apply the scale transformation between the closest input view (i.e the pose captured right before the test view) and the test view. This significantly improved metrics for the NVS use case. For Long-LRM, we utilized the author’s Self-Reimplemented Version. The provided checkpoint requires images of height 544 and aspect ratio ≤ 1. Hence, input images are rescaled to match the desired height. For input images with aspect ratio < 1 (Argoverse 2 dataset), we utilize their option to rescale images to the max input resolution of 960×544. While images are downscaled for reconstruction, the feed-forward predicted 3D gaussians are rendered in the target frame’s resolution.

item.title: 角色布料的模拟太慢、参数太烦：Pose-based Neural Clothing 用姿态直接出形变，推理是实时的 ｜ Pose-based Neural Clothing for Animated Characters
item.description:
一句话：数据驱动能学出高质量形变，轻量网络设计才能做到实时推理。

要点：

  • 痛点来自传统管线：给动画角色做服装仿真是美术的时间黑洞——**模拟慢、参数调整琐碎**
  • 近期数据驱动方法提供了替代方案：从仿真数据集中学习，直接生成高质量形变
  • 关键在于**轻量网络设计**——只有足够轻，数据驱动系统才能达到实时推理速度，从而真正替掉逐帧模拟

为什么值得看：布料是角色管线里最后一个还在靠离线仿真 + 手工调的环节。用姿态驱动、轻量网络实时出形变，等于把它变成「渲染时的一步」，而不是「生产时的一道工序」。

中文摘要：给动画角色做传统服装仿真是美术环节的时间黑洞：模拟很慢，参数调整又极其琐碎。近期的数据驱动方法提供了有力替代——从仿真数据集里学习，直接生成高质量的布料形变，而不必每次重新跑物理。真正让它在生产中可行的关键，是轻量的网络设计：只有网络足够小，数据驱动系统才能达到实时推理速度，从而把「逐帧仿真」替换成「按姿态直接推断形变」。这类方法的工程价值就在于它落在实时预算内，能进引擎而不是留在离线工具链里。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·cs.GR（English）

原文发布：2026-11-16

本期推送：2026-11-17

Pose-based Neural Clothing for Animated Characters

Abstract

Traditional garment simulation for animated characters is a time-consuming bottleneck for artists due to slow simulations and tedious parameter tunings. Recent data-driven methods offer a powerful alternative, capable of learning from a dataset of simulated data to generate high-quality deformations. A lightweight network design allows data-driven systems to achieve a real-time inference speed. This significantly improves the artist workflow, as they can interactively pose a character and see high-quality folds and wrinkles at animation time, thereby allowing to make creative decisions ahead of time. However, existing neural clothing methods have presented appealing results on datasets based on realistic human models (e.g., SMPL), but when trained on animated character datasets, they struggle to generalize to unseen poses. In this paper, we aim at designing neural networks and training strategies to generalize better to unseen poses in real-time to enable the interactive posing applications. We focus on a production-oriented setting where the model is trained for a single garment in a quasi-static setup. Technically, we leverage a smooth, expressive latent space by first training a Variational Auto-Encoder (VAE). We then progressively train the VAE encoder to transition from reconstruction to pose-driven prediction. To guide this prediction, we condition the network on both low-dimensional pose parameters and character body surface displacements. Finally, we introduce a novel local gradient histogram loss that mitigates the over-smoothing effect of reconstruction losses. Extensive evaluations on production-level assets and public datasets demonstrate that our method produces sharp, realistic wrinkles, smooth large-scale drape, and temporal coherence in real-time, offering a robust and easily integrable solution for interactive posing workflows.

1 Introduction

Cloth deformation plays a central role in conveying both realism and style in digital characters. In production settings such as film, interactive media, virtual try-on, and web-based character customization, interactive posing is essential in artistic decisions: artists expect immediate visual feedback when posing a character, including how garments fold and wrinkle. Standard physically-based cloth simulation is therefore often unsuitable for interactive use, due to its dynamic formulation and computational cost, even though it produces highly realistic results. Moreover, production cloth is rarely “off-the-shelf”: studios rely on highly specialized solvers and carefully tuned pipelines refined over the years of show-specific expertise. It is not uncommon for artists to perform manual interventions on certain frames to resolve difficult cases: persistent body inter-penetrations, unstable contacts causing popping or jitter, loss of volume in layered folds, or solver artifacts such as cloth snagging and sticking in extreme poses are some examples. As a result, even though deploying a faster GPU-based simulator [WWYW20, WWW22, GWL∗25] can potentially reach interactive rates, they are often insufficient to reproduce the final production-approved look. These constraints motivate a data-driven alternative: a supervised neural deformer trained directly on production-generated targets, capturing both the solver’s tuned behavior and the artist-approved outcomes.

A vast literature [PLPM20, SOC22, STOC21, BME22, GBH23, ZL24, BME21] has explored learning-based approaches to improve the performance–realism trade-off of cloth simulation, typically by approximating full simulations using neural networks that operate over time or leverage simplified dynamics. While these learning-based methods present appealing results on datasets featuring realistic human models (e.g., SMPL [LMR∗15]), our experiments in Section 4 reveal that they struggle when trained on animated characters, often producing inaccurate details and visual artifacts. Furthermore, these approaches often assume access to simulation states or poses in previous frames, which are typically unavailable during interactive character posing. Additionally, while many existing methods train their models to generalize across multiple body shapes and garment materials [PLPM20, GBH23], we intentionally focus on a single-mesh paradigm. This targeted approach allows us to train a lightweight network that faithfully preserves the unique style avoiding the loss of detail often caused by generic priors and guarantees real-time inference. Finally, although some works incorporate physically-based unsupervised [BME21, BME22, SOC22, LKL23, GBH23, GBB∗24] terms to improve visual quality, production-level garment deformations are hard to reproduce with simple energy terms, compelling us to adhere to a strictly supervised setting to ensure our results faithfully replicate targeted artistic intent.

We aim to train real-time neural deformers that predict cloth deformations from character poses. Additionally, we target a single garment simulated using a quasi-static setup for a single character. The design space, the input representations, and training strategies of our network are extensively explored in the paper. We start with a popular architecture, employing spiral convolutions for mesh-aware computations [CMM∗20], which outperforms simpler options such as variants of global and local MLPs [BODO18, PLPM20]. Our first insight decouples the task of predicting pose-dependent deformations from the generation of plausible, high-frequency wrinkle patterns: before training the deformer, we first train a Variational Auto-Encoder (VAE) to reconstruct a modest set of deformations to create a smooth, concise, and expressive latent space. Our second insight is to progressively train the VAE encoder to transition from reconstruction to deformation prediction from body poses, thus simplifying the task. We find that this progressive strategy significantly improves the visual quality while maintaining architectural complexity and keeping inference times at interactive rate. In addition to conditioning the re-purposed encoder on low-dimensional pose parameters, we splat body surface displacements onto the garment mesh using linear blend skinning weights to provide deformation guidance on the mesh level. Finally, we leverage a novel local gradient histogram loss over surface neighborhoods to preserve high-frequency wrinkles and mitigate the over-smoothing that is commonly associated with reconstruction-based losses.

We evaluate our approach against state-of-the-art methods from both academia [BODO18, PLPM20, CMM∗20, STOC21] and production pipelines [Aut25, Epi25] on production-level shirt and pants assets, as well as previously published virtual try-on datasets. Across datasets, our method produces sharp, realistic wrinkles while maintaining smooth large-scale drape at interactive rates, and exhibits temporally coherent behavior as a byproduct of the structured latent space despite operating per-frame. Extensive ablations further justify each stage of our pipeline and its design choices. Overall, our experiments demonstrate a production-ready approach that is easy to integrate into existing workflows, giving artists a robust and high-quality preview in real-time.

2 Related Work

2.1 Numerical Simulation of Cloth

Cloth simulation is a long-standing and widely researched topic in computer animation. Since the debut of the seminal Baraff–Witkin model [BW98], many improvements have been proposed to simulate fabrics with higher fidelity [BMF05, CK05, TPS09, LB15, Kim20]. For a detailed analysis regarding production implementation practicalities, we refer to Kim et al. [KE20]. Recent efforts have greatly boosted the efficiency of cloth solvers on both CPUs and GPUs [WWYW20, WWW22, GWL∗25, LLL∗24, LLL∗25, CHL∗25]. However, implementing these efficient solvers in production settings often poses practical challenges. Production solvers must handle broken animations, non-physical setups, self-intersections, solver-specific heuristics, and artist-authored corrections. Neural networks, such as our method, are not only efficient, but also easily portable to different digital content creation software.

One well-researched area within numerical simulation is sub-space solvers [KJ09, JF03, TLP06, HSL∗06, PBH15, YLX∗15, MWW16, BEH18, LSW∗18, WKS20], thus reducing the excessive degrees of freedom for a given application. Many learning-based cloth deformation methods [STOC21, SYWL22, DLLG∗23] reflect this idea by training Auto-Encoders to reduce the garments into smooth and expressive latent space. We similarly reduce the dimensionality of the problem by training a VAE on deformation deltas.

Collision handling [BMF05, Sta09, FTP16, TWL∗18, WWYW20] also plays an important role in cloth simulations. Most neural clothing methods either perform simple repulsion-based post-processing at inference time to resolve collisions [SOC19, PLPM20, SOC22, CGY∗23, LSK23], or formulate a loss term based on interpenetration distance [STOC21, GCP∗20, BME21, BME22]. We utilize the post-processing approach in our method as we find it sufficiently robust and efficient.

2.2 Learning-based Methods

Cloth regression.

Many prior works regress garment deformations directly from character poses or refine a coarse simulation to create more realistic wrinkles. Data-driven methods were first explored to predict cloth deformations without relying on neural networks [KV08, FYK10, WHRO10, KGBS11, GRH∗12, WCC∗21]. TailorNet [PLPM20] trains MLPs in two stages to separate low- and high-frequency deformations. [LTY∗24] extends the two-stream idea and trained Graph Transformer to obtain high-frequency wrinkles. Bertiche et al. [BME20] solve the same problem by training a Conditional VAE. Santesteban et al. [SOC19] extend this work with RNNs to capture dynamic cloth motion from time-varying animation. Chentanez et al. [CMM∗20] proposed a new spiral convolution operation for regressing garment deformations. Our work is in these lines: we regress deformations directly from character poses with a single feed-forward pass.

The above works all create or reuse a cloth deformation dataset through physically-based simulations and perform supervised trainings. Another option is to employ a set of physically-based unsupervised losses [BME21, BME22, SOC22, LKL23, GBH23, GBB∗24]. Using unsupervised losses relieves the burden of dataset creation while providing high-quality wrinkle configurations. However, it is difficult, if not impossible, to replicate production simulation setups in this manner due to their complexities. We thus train our models in fully supervised settings.

Instead of directly regressing 3D deformations, some methods represent deformations via 2D displacement maps and use convolutional neural networks [LCT18, JZGF20, SYWL22, GYS∗25]. Though leveraging well-studied 2D network architectures, handling seams and distortions in texture maps is often challenging. Other methods train an upsampler of low-resolution cloth to obtain fine details [CYZ21, ZWCM21, CGY∗23, ZL24]. However, these works usually use coarse simulations as input, which is not always available in production settings.

Neural simulations.

Another type of approach to learn cloth deformations is to replace the physically-based simulator with a neural network. A Graph Network-based Simulator (GNS) based on message passing is leveraged to learn particle-based [SGGP∗20] and mesh-based [PFSGB21] simulations. HOOD [GBH23] proposes a hierarchical message passing scheme to enhance the simulation quality. Subsequent works of HOOD handle multi-layered garments [GBB∗24] and address self-collisions [LWK24b, BHN∗25]. Transformer-based architectures have also been explored in the context of neural cloth simulation [SLD23, LWK∗24a]. Although demonstrating generalization capabilities to unseen meshes, GNS and transformers are usually expensive to evaluate due to their iterative or global nature. Most of these works also rely on physically-based unsupervised losses. As our focus is on real-time inference speed for production settings, we do not adopt this category of approach.

3 Method

The target of our neural cloth deformer is to efficiently regress a high-quality wrinkled garment mesh given input character joint transforms θ and a single baseline garment rest shape x_R for quasi-static scenarios. Similar to previous approaches [LMR∗15, BODO18, ZB24, PLPM20], our predictor outputs rest-pose deformations that are subsequently skinned to obtain the final garment positions x_G for a single frame as

x_G=W(x_R+ℕ_Φ(θ), θ),

(1)

where W is a skinning function, e.g., linear blend skinning (LBS), extended for the garment mesh and ℕ_Φ(θ) predicts per-vertex rest-space displacements. Assuming the skinning function is invertible, the ground-truth rest-space deformations can be computed as:

Δx=W⁻¹(x_G,θ)-x_R.

(2)

Training on Δx factors out world transforms and facilitates normalization. A general pose-to-mesh neural network predictor can then be trained with the following objective:

\argmin_Φ∑ᵢwᵢLᵢ(F(ℕ_Φ(θ)),F(Δx)),

(3)

where Φ are the trainable network weights, F is a user-specified feature extractor (e.g., computing vertex normals), and Lᵢ is a weighted (wᵢ) loss function that can represent distance metrics such as L², cosine similarity or a local norm distribution loss (Section 3.4); or even physically-inspired energy-based formulations [BME21, BME22]. Our work focuses on supervised losses, since the goal is to preserve the artistic intent for a particular setting, as captured by carefully tuned cloth simulations and occasional artist-authored frame edits.

Previous methods differ mainly in how they couple pose information to mesh deformations. A straightforward option is a global MLP that maps joint transforms directly to rest-space deformations. However, fully connected architectures scale poorly with mesh resolution; to keep parameter counts tractable, previous approaches predict a reduced set of scalar weights coupled with learned linear basis (e.g., blendshape-style subspaces)  [SOC19, BMTE21]. One issue is that these learned linear basis are oblivious to the mesh structure, which hinders the capacity of the network to efficiently learn non-linear local features that can improve generalization. A more structured alternative is the per-joint MLP formulation of [BODO18], which leverages the spatial locality implied by skinning. In this setting, each joint j has its own MLP ℕʲ_Φ(θⱼ) that takes the joint transform θⱼ as input and predicts rest-space displacements only for vertices influenced by that joint, implemented via a vertex mask M(·) derived from skinning weights. The posed garment is then obtained by aggregating the per-joint contributions:

x_G=W(x_R+∑ⱼMʲ(ℕʲ_Φ(θⱼ)),θ).

(4)

This formulation is highly effective for learning pose-dependent body corrections that bridge the gap between a simple LBS and high-quality rig deformations. Naively extending such an approach to neural garments, however, has its issues. For character rigs, rest-space corrections are typically smooth and localized around the driving joints; in contrast, cloth wrinkles are inherently non-local, and small changes in a shoulder or elbow can induce folds that propagate across the entire garment surface. Figure 7(a) shows a per-joint MLP baseline. The predicted deformations exhibit over-smoothed wrinkles, indicating that the per-joint locality assumption is insufficient to reproduce the production-quality wrinkling patterns required in our setting. In the next sections we will discuss how our proposed training pipeline can effectively capture long-range dependencies with a novel mesh-aware architecture that is tailored to efficiently condition pose information.

3.1 Latent Garment Prior via VAE Pre-Training

A recurring failure mode of direct pose-to-mesh regression is that the network must simultaneously infer global deformations and synthesize high-frequency wrinkle geometry in the correct spatial configuration. This end-to-end mapping remains high-dimensional and under-constrained: many mesh deformations are locally consistent with the pose descriptor but implausible as garments. To improve generalization, we therefore factor the problem into two steps: we first learn a pose-agnostic prior over rest-pose garment deformations using a Variational Auto-Encoder (VAE), and then learn a pose-conditioned encoder that predicts latent codes inside the learned space (Section 3.3).

The VAE consists of an encoder 𝔼_ψ(z|Δx) and a decoder D_θ(Δx|z), where z is a low-dimensional latent code. The decoder D_θ(z) is also implemented as a mesh-aware Convolutional Neural Network that outputs a displacement field on the original mesh resolution. We optimize the standard evidence lower bound:

\beginsplit\min_ψ,θ 𝔼_Δx[𝔼_z∼𝔼_ψ(z|Δx)[ L_rec(D_θ(Δx|z),Δx) ] + w_KL KL (𝔼_ψ(z|Δx) ∥ ℕ(0,I))],\endsplit

(5)

where the supervised reconstruction loss (e.g., vertex L² and normal terms) L_rec forces the decoder to represent high-frequency wrinkles while the Kullback–Leibler (KL) term shapes the latent space into a smooth, well-filled distribution aligned with an isotropic Gaussian prior. Note that Eq. (5) is trained on rest-space deformation residuals rather than absolute vertex positions. At inference time, obtaining these residuals requires inverse skinning, so the pose is implicitly involved through the skinning operation.

During VAE training, the decoder learns a strong deformation prior that captures the multiscale statistics of plausible rest-pose cloth shapes, while the KL term encourages a smooth, well-conditioned latent space in which nearby codes decode to coherent, nearby deformations. In practice, this leads to more stable wrinkle patterns under pose distribution shift and improved generalization across motions and characters, while preserving the deterministic behavior required for production inference. As shown in Figure 2, encoding ground-truth rest-pose deformations along an animated pose sequence produces a latent trajectory that varies smoothly over time. This supports our motivating assumption that the space of plausible deformations is locally low-dimensional and well-behaved: continuous changes in pose induce continuous changes in latent deformation, making it feasible to learn a pose-to-latent mapping that generalizes beyond the training distribution.

3.2 Progressive Transition to Pose Conditioning

The VAE pre-training in the previous section yields a garment-valid decoder that maps a compact latent code to detailed rest-pose displacements. An immediate next step could be to freeze the decoder and replace the VAE encoder with a pose-conditioned encoder operating on mesh-aligned pose features. In practice, we found this direct replacement to be too abrupt: the decoder has only been exposed to latent codes produced from geometric inputs, whereas a pose-conditioned encoder would initially produce latents from a markedly different input distribution. This mismatch leads to unstable optimization and weaker generalization, often manifesting as overfitting to the pose distribution seen during training or as high-frequency artifacts under pose variation.

To smooth out this transition, we introduce a progressive curriculum that gradually morphs the auto-encoding task into an “upsampling-from-coarse” task before training with pose features. Concretely, after training the VAE in the standard fine-to-fine setting, we continue training while progressively coarsening the encoder input through a Laplacian smoothing operator. The progressively smoothed inputs are defined by

Δx⁽⁰⁾=Δx, Δx⁽ˡ⁾=(I-λL)⁻¹Δx⁽ˡ⁻¹⁾, l=1,…,L,

(6)

where L is the cotangent Laplacian and λ controls the smoothing strength. Increasing l progressively removes high-frequency content (wrinkles and fine folds), producing a sequence of increasingly low-detail inputs that remain defined on the original mesh connectivity. A visualization of our smoothing operator, showing progressive removal of geometric detail, is shown in Figure 3 (top row).

During this refinement phase, we optimize the reconstruction term of Eq. (5) with the encoder conditioned on Δx⁽ˡ⁾ and the decoder supervised against the full-detail displacement field Δx. We disable the KL term by setting w_KL=0, ensuring a deterministic refinement that avoids imposing additional constraints on the latent distribution. In the meanwhile, the smoothing level l is increased according to a fixed curriculum (Section 4).

As illustrated in Figure 3, recovering wrinkle details from Laplacian-smoothed inputs is comparatively well-conditioned: the VAE consistently reconstructs high-frequency structures that closely matches the ground truth. This observation motivates our subsequent pose-conditioning strategy: if the decoder can reliably synthesize fine details from weak geometric cues, it can also be finetuned to predict deformations from mesh-aligned pose features.

3.3 Mesh-Aware Deformation Model

Once the autoencoder has been trained to decode detailed deformations from increasingly weaker geometric inputs, we replace its pose-agnostic encoder with a pose-conditioned encoder while keeping the decoder fixed. This curriculum substantially stabilizes the handoff: the pose-conditioned encoder can rely on the well-behaved decoder space already used for reconstruction, rather than learning the entire deformation synthesis process end-to-end. We implement pose conditioning through three complementary mechanisms: joint-to-mesh splatted pose features, fine-scale pose injection via FiLM modulation, and a coarse-level cross-attention block between pose embeddings and mesh latent features.

Joint-to-mesh splatted transforms.

Prior mesh-based deformer models often compress joint transforms into a global latent vector and inject it into the mesh decoder via fully connected layers  [CMM∗20]. This coupling can create a bottleneck for pose information to get through. Instead, we construct a mesh-aligned pose field by splatting joint information directly onto garment vertices using skinning weights. Each joint transform is embedded into a feature vector, and vertex-level pose features are obtained by smoothly blending the joint features according to their LBS influences. Additionally, the rest body deformations from the ground-truth data are also splatted to the cloth mesh, and concatenated to the splatted joint transforms as the input of the network. This produces a continuous per-vertex conditioning signal over the garment surface, enabling subsequent mesh convolutions to process pose information locally while still propagating effects globally through the multi-resolution hierarchy.

Improving pose parameters conditioning.

To further condition the network on pose parameters, we adopt two complementary mechanisms. For the finer-resolution encoder blocks, we apply FiLM modulation [PSV∗17], where pose information is pooled across joints using an attention mechanism and then used to generate per-channel scaling and shifting parameters that modulate the outputs of each SpiralConv layer. For the coarsest mesh level, we additionally employ cross-attention [VSP∗23], where the encoded pose parameters serve as keys and values and the current feature map serves as the query. This enables global feature interactions with the pose embeddings.

3.4 Local Normal Distribution Loss

Pointwise reconstruction losses (e.g., vertex L²) penalize small spatial misalignments of wrinkles and folds, even they exhibit visually plausible high-frequency details. To reduce sensitivity to such phase shifts while still supervising fine-scale appearance, we introduce a distributional loss that matches local surface orientation statistics between prediction and ground truth. Given predicted and ground-truth meshes, we compute per-vertex unit normals and represent each normal by spherical angles (φ,ω), with φ∈[0,π] and ω∈[0,2π). For each vertex i, we define a local neighborhood Ωₖ(i) using k-nearest neighbors in the bind-pose geometry; we optionally evaluate multiple neighborhood sizes k∈K to capture statistics at different spatial scales. Within each neighborhood, we differentiably construct a two-dimensional histogram over (φ,ω) using Gaussian kernel accumulation around fixed bin centers in angular space. The resulting histogram is normalized to sum to one, yielding a local probability distribution over surface orientations. We use 8 bins for φ and 16 bins for ω, with a fixed kernel bandwidth.

Let Ĥ_i,k and H_i,k denote the predicted and ground-truth normalized orientation histograms for vertex i and neighborhood size k, respectively. We define the local normal distribution loss as the mean squared error between corresponding histograms, averaged over vertices and neighborhood scales:

Lₕᵢₛₜ=(1)/(|K|)∑_k∈K(1)/(|V|)∑_i∈V\lVertĤ_i,k-H_i,k\rVert₂²,

(7)

where V is the set of vertices. This loss provides an alternative to pointwise supervision by encouraging realistic local wrinkle energy and directional variability.

4 Experiments and Results

Architecture details.

Our VAE architecture operates on mesh vertex features using a mesh-aware residual SpiralConv [GCBZ19] backbone. Each resolution level consists of an encoder block followed by a symmetric decoder block. The encoder applies a residual SpiralConv stack (GELU + SpiralConv + LayerNorm) to provide a strong locality bias directly on the surface while remaining more structure-aware than MLPs and transformers [CZG∗22]. We then reduce resolution using Quadric Error Metric (QEM) pooling; the decoder mirrors this structure with the corresponding unpooling operator. To mitigate resampling artifacts, we apply a Laplacian smoothing operator before each QEM pooling and unpooling. In all experiments we use a hierarchy with 3 levels of mesh resolutions and QEM pooling matrices. The channel widths increase from 64 at the finest level to 512 at the coarsest. Within each block, we use 5 residual sub-layers per level and pose conditioning is injected through the mechanisms described in Section 3.3, while the rest-space displacement field is decoded at full resolution.

Training.

We train all models with AdamW [LH19] with β₁=0.9, β₂=0.999 and batch size 16. The VAE pre-training is run for 400,000 optimization steps, and each progressive curriculum stage is trained for 100,000 steps, followed by the pose deformer training for another 100,000 steps. We use a cosine annealing schedule that decays the learning rate from 1×10⁻⁴ to 1×10⁻⁵ over each training horizon. Poses θ are represented as 4×4 homogeneous transformation matrices of each joint, including rotation, scaling and translation which are often all animated in the production setting. In addition to the local normal distribution loss, we use a weak latent supervision term (wₗₐₜ=0.1), computing MAE between predicted latent codes and the ground-truth ones from the pre-trained VAE. Additional architectural and training details are provided in Appendix A.

4.1 Datasets

Our dataset consists of a rigged human female character Jen, with three types of motions: (i) long artist-authored dancing animations; (ii) short motion clips sampled from a larger animation library; (iii) randomly sampled poses [BODO18]. Partition (i) consists of 1,264 frames over 6 sequences, and is used for validation. Partition (ii) has 9,090 frames and captures common actions such as walking, turning, or falling. To improve coverage of poses encountered at inference time, we extensively sample random joint transforms in Partition (iii), comprising 12,230 frames. This sampling is designed to cover a wide range of poses with large joint transforms. Partitions (ii) and (iii) are used for training.

Partition (iii) and the majority of Partition (ii) consist of discontinuous poses, generated with quasi-static simulation. While susceptible to temporal inconsistencies and reduced secondary dynamics, this often remains the only practical option, as dynamic simulation between poses frequently triggers self-intersections that cause the simulator to fail. We also evaluate our method on the VTO dataset [SOC19], a simulated virtual try-on benchmark with a T-shirt and a long dress modeled on SMPL [LMR∗15] human body models. A single body shape from the dataset was used. Various motion captured sequences of talking, walking, jumping sum up to 6,665 frames of training and 452 frames for validation.

4.2 Quantitative and Qualitative Evaluations

Figure  and Figure 4 show our model on representative validation frames from the Jen dataset. Despite complex motions and challenging wrinkling patterns, our model generates physically plausible garment deformations in real-time. We further compare against state-of-the-art baselines from both academia and available commercial software. Figure 5 summarizes qualitative comparisons using our internal dataset with the ML Deformers in Autodesk Maya 2025 [Aut25] and Unreal Engine 5.6 [Epi25], a per-joint MLP baseline adapted to garments [BODO18], a two-stage MLP model that predicts coarse and fine details [PLPM20], and a mesh-convolutional model [CMM∗20]. Across all above methods, our approach produces the most realistic fine-scale wrinkles and the best temporal coherence. Figure 6 shows the same comparisons on the VTO datasets. In some examples in Figure 6, both our model and several baselines exhibit minor high-frequency artifacts or reduced smoothness relative to the simulation ground truth, suggesting that these artifacts are not specific to a single loss formulation or architecture. We report Mean Absolute Error (MAE) of all methods in Table 1. We also report the measurements from training our method with the traditional reconstruction losses (Ours w/o NormDist). Our approach outperforms the other methods in terms of MAE across different datasets. Inference runtimes on Jen’s Shirt dataset are also reported in Table 2. Our method can run inference with 212.2 FPS. We demonstrate its real-time capability through a posing application in Figure  (left) and in the supplemental video.

Additional metrics.

Pointwise distances often fail to reflect perceptual deformation quality: small spatial shifts of wrinkles can inflate MAE despite visually plausible results. Additionally, low MAE does not guarantee a correct silhouette and physical plausibility. We therefore report complementary metrics that target specific failure modes. The Contour metric evaluates global shape by computing a symmetric Chamfer distance between boundary vertex sets of the predicted and ground-truth garments. The Collision quantifies garment-body interpenetration: we measure the minimum displacement required to move garment vertices outside the body surface and report the mean. LPIPS[ZIE∗18] is also reported by rendering garment images because perceptual metrics correlate more closely with human judgments than pixel-level errors. Finally, to assess wrinkle qualities invariant to small phase shifts, we compare distributions of surface detail using mean curvature (Curv): we form soft histograms over mean curvature magnitude of the vertices using 64 logarithmically spaced bins, and report the MAE between predicted and ground-truth histograms.

Table 2 summarizes evaluations of additional metrics on Jen’s Shirt dataset. Our method not only improves MAE over previous approaches, but also exhibits fewer collisions, better contour agreement, and higher perceptual similarity to the ground truth. The local normal distribution loss exhibits a slight increase in MAE. This reflects a deliberate trade-off: by supervising local deformation statistics rather than exact positions, we encourage richer wrinkle structures and high-frequency details, even when deformations are not perfectly phase-aligned with the reference. However, this can occasionally over-emphasize sharp normal variations in ambiguous fold regions, which may appear as localized crease-like wrinkles that are less smooth than the physics-based ground truth. Additional results are provided in Appendix C.

User study.

We conducted user study with 28 participants and collected 1096 votes. Participants were shown side-by-side comparisons of rendered frames of our method and baselines. They were asked to indicate their preference in terms of visual quality without knowing the source of images. The results are shown in Figure 8. In total, 96.3% of the votes are in favor of our method.

4.3 Ablation Studies

Table 3 analyzes the contributions of the main design choices in our pipeline on Jen’s Shirt dataset. We first study the effect of the VAE latent dimensionality by varying bottleneck sizes, measured in MAE (right column). Starting from Jen’s Shirt mesh with 4820 vertices (4820×3 degrees of freedom), we evaluate three bottlenecks: 624×3 (∼7.8× compression), 229×1 (∼64× compression), and 86×1 (∼228× compression). Size 229×1 provides the best trade-off between compression and reconstruction quality. This setting is used in all subsequent experiments. Then, we ablate the pose-conditioning components and training strategies (middle rows). Incorporating joint-to-mesh splatted pose features, body displacement cues, and VAE pre-training each improves performance. The best result is obtained with all three together (in green). Finally, progressive training consistently reduces MAE, indicating more stable optimization and improved generalization. As noted in Section 4.2, the histogram loss slightly increases MAE but yields sharper, more perceptually convincing high-frequency details. Figure 7 visually provides evidence on how each stage progressively improves wrinkle sharpness and perceptual details.

5 Conclusions

We presented a learning-based pipeline for quasi-static garment deformation tailored to production settings, where future usage requires reasonable predictions in large pose ranges and the target appearance demands high-quality, plausible wrinkles rather than merely low MAE metrics. To our knowledge, this is the first approach to explicitly address core production constraints in a unified system: generating a production-driven dataset that combines artist-authored motion snippets with carefully filtered random poses, and emphasizing perceptual wrinkle realism alongside physical plausibility. Our method combines mesh-aware pose conditioning with VAE pre-training and a staged training strategy that progressively transitions from the pre-training to pose-driven prediction, enabling robust generalization. Across multiple datasets, we show that each stage contributes measurably to performance, and that these improvements persist under a stricter validation protocol using held-out motion trajectories rather than near-duplicate training frames. In contrast to prior work where generalization is often assessed on samples closely related to the training distribution, our evaluation highlights the importance of validation on genuinely unseen sequences when targeting production deployment.

Limitations and future work.

Despite the encouraging results, several limitations remain. First, cloth deformation behavior is inherently history-dependent: similar poses with different inertia and history can correspond to different wrinkle configurations. This temporal ambiguity renders the regression problem ill-posed and encourages deterministic predictors to average over multiple plausible outcomes, especially under highly dynamic motions (Figure 9). Incorporating temporal information and/or modeling latent trajectories is a natural next step. Closely related, a deterministic formulation cannot represent the multi-modality of cloth at a fixed pose; probabilistic predictors with stochastic latent variables or diffusion models may better capture this variability and reduce over-smoothing. Second, our pose conditioning relies on skinning-derived correspondences to project joint transformations or body cues onto the garment. While effective for fitted clothing, garment–body sliding (common in loose garments and large motions) diverges from this correspondence and lead to systematic artifacts. Dynamic correspondences or motion fields that account for sliding are interesting future avenues. Third, our local normal distribution supervision illustrates a broader trade-off in deformation learning: matching local orientation statistics encourages expressive high-frequency detail and tolerates small spatial shifts, but can occasionally yield overly pronounced wrinkles or sharp creases in ambiguous regions, as well as globally inconsistent fold organization (Figure 9). Hybrid objectives that preserve distributional robustness while adding lightweight global or continuity constraints may alleviate these cases. Finally, evaluation remains challenging: no single metric reliably captures perceptual quality and physical plausibility across modeling choices. Though user studies help alleviate this situation, developing better quantitative criteria for wrinkle coherence, plausible material behavior, and perceptual realism remains an open problem.

（参考文献见原文。）

Appendix A Model Implementation Details

A.1 Mesh Auto-Encoder Architecture

Our VAE is implemented as a mesh-aware convolutional network based on spiral convolutions and a fixed multi-resolution mesh hierarchy. Spiral convolutions operate on ordered one-ring neighborhoods, enabling convolutions directly on irregular mesh surfaces while preserving geometric locality. This formulation provides a strong inductive bias for surface-based deformation modeling.

We construct a hierarchy of three mesh resolutions using Quadric Error Metrics (QEM) simplification, yielding a set of fixed pooling and unpooling operators. Coarser levels capture global shape variation, while finer levels model localized wrinkle detail. Both the encoder and decoder operate on this hierarchy, with feature dimensionality increasing towards coarser levels and decreasing symmetrically during decoding.

Residual spiral convolution blocks.

Each encoder level consists of a residual spiral convolution block, followed by optional Laplacian smoothing and QEM-based downsampling. The decoder mirrors this structure, applying unpooling, smoothing, and residual spiral convolution blocks to reconstruct higher-resolution features. The final decoder output is a per-vertex displacement field defined on the original mesh resolution. Each residual block processes vertex features through two parallel paths: a residual path and a skip path. The residual path consists of L stacked sublayers, each composed of a GELU activation, a spiral convolution, and Layer Normalization. Formally, a single sublayer is defined as (see Figure 12)

f(x)=LayerNorm(SpiralConv(GELU(x))) .

(8)

The residual path applies this function L times in sequence. In parallel, the skip path applies a single spiral convolution to the input features. The two paths are combined and normalized to produce the block output. To mitigate aliasing artifacts introduced by mesh resolution changes, we apply a lightweight Laplacian smoothing operator to the feature maps after pooling or unpooling. This promotes smooth feature variation across the surface while preserving high-frequency detail through the residual connections.
item.content:encoded:
一句话：数据驱动能学出高质量形变，轻量网络设计才能做到实时推理。

要点：

  • 痛点来自传统管线：给动画角色做服装仿真是美术的时间黑洞——**模拟慢、参数调整琐碎**
  • 近期数据驱动方法提供了替代方案：从仿真数据集中学习，直接生成高质量形变
  • 关键在于**轻量网络设计**——只有足够轻，数据驱动系统才能达到实时推理速度，从而真正替掉逐帧模拟

为什么值得看：布料是角色管线里最后一个还在靠离线仿真 + 手工调的环节。用姿态驱动、轻量网络实时出形变，等于把它变成「渲染时的一步」，而不是「生产时的一道工序」。

中文摘要：给动画角色做传统服装仿真是美术环节的时间黑洞：模拟很慢，参数调整又极其琐碎。近期的数据驱动方法提供了有力替代——从仿真数据集里学习，直接生成高质量的布料形变，而不必每次重新跑物理。真正让它在生产中可行的关键，是轻量的网络设计：只有网络足够小，数据驱动系统才能达到实时推理速度，从而把「逐帧仿真」替换成「按姿态直接推断形变」。这类方法的工程价值就在于它落在实时预算内，能进引擎而不是留在离线工具链里。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·cs.GR（English）

原文发布：2026-11-16

本期推送：2026-11-17

Pose-based Neural Clothing for Animated Characters

Abstract

Traditional garment simulation for animated characters is a time-consuming bottleneck for artists due to slow simulations and tedious parameter tunings. Recent data-driven methods offer a powerful alternative, capable of learning from a dataset of simulated data to generate high-quality deformations. A lightweight network design allows data-driven systems to achieve a real-time inference speed. This significantly improves the artist workflow, as they can interactively pose a character and see high-quality folds and wrinkles at animation time, thereby allowing to make creative decisions ahead of time. However, existing neural clothing methods have presented appealing results on datasets based on realistic human models (e.g., SMPL), but when trained on animated character datasets, they struggle to generalize to unseen poses. In this paper, we aim at designing neural networks and training strategies to generalize better to unseen poses in real-time to enable the interactive posing applications. We focus on a production-oriented setting where the model is trained for a single garment in a quasi-static setup. Technically, we leverage a smooth, expressive latent space by first training a Variational Auto-Encoder (VAE). We then progressively train the VAE encoder to transition from reconstruction to pose-driven prediction. To guide this prediction, we condition the network on both low-dimensional pose parameters and character body surface displacements. Finally, we introduce a novel local gradient histogram loss that mitigates the over-smoothing effect of reconstruction losses. Extensive evaluations on production-level assets and public datasets demonstrate that our method produces sharp, realistic wrinkles, smooth large-scale drape, and temporal coherence in real-time, offering a robust and easily integrable solution for interactive posing workflows.

1 Introduction

Cloth deformation plays a central role in conveying both realism and style in digital characters. In production settings such as film, interactive media, virtual try-on, and web-based character customization, interactive posing is essential in artistic decisions: artists expect immediate visual feedback when posing a character, including how garments fold and wrinkle. Standard physically-based cloth simulation is therefore often unsuitable for interactive use, due to its dynamic formulation and computational cost, even though it produces highly realistic results. Moreover, production cloth is rarely “off-the-shelf”: studios rely on highly specialized solvers and carefully tuned pipelines refined over the years of show-specific expertise. It is not uncommon for artists to perform manual interventions on certain frames to resolve difficult cases: persistent body inter-penetrations, unstable contacts causing popping or jitter, loss of volume in layered folds, or solver artifacts such as cloth snagging and sticking in extreme poses are some examples. As a result, even though deploying a faster GPU-based simulator [WWYW20, WWW22, GWL∗25] can potentially reach interactive rates, they are often insufficient to reproduce the final production-approved look. These constraints motivate a data-driven alternative: a supervised neural deformer trained directly on production-generated targets, capturing both the solver’s tuned behavior and the artist-approved outcomes.

A vast literature [PLPM20, SOC22, STOC21, BME22, GBH23, ZL24, BME21] has explored learning-based approaches to improve the performance–realism trade-off of cloth simulation, typically by approximating full simulations using neural networks that operate over time or leverage simplified dynamics. While these learning-based methods present appealing results on datasets featuring realistic human models (e.g., SMPL [LMR∗15]), our experiments in Section 4 reveal that they struggle when trained on animated characters, often producing inaccurate details and visual artifacts. Furthermore, these approaches often assume access to simulation states or poses in previous frames, which are typically unavailable during interactive character posing. Additionally, while many existing methods train their models to generalize across multiple body shapes and garment materials [PLPM20, GBH23], we intentionally focus on a single-mesh paradigm.
