This targeted approach allows us to train a lightweight network that faithfully preserves the unique style avoiding the loss of detail often caused by generic priors and guarantees real-time inference. Finally, although some works incorporate physically-based unsupervised [BME21, BME22, SOC22, LKL23, GBH23, GBB∗24] terms to improve visual quality, production-level garment deformations are hard to reproduce with simple energy terms, compelling us to adhere to a strictly supervised setting to ensure our results faithfully replicate targeted artistic intent.

We aim to train real-time neural deformers that predict cloth deformations from character poses. Additionally, we target a single garment simulated using a quasi-static setup for a single character. The design space, the input representations, and training strategies of our network are extensively explored in the paper. We start with a popular architecture, employing spiral convolutions for mesh-aware computations [CMM∗20], which outperforms simpler options such as variants of global and local MLPs [BODO18, PLPM20]. Our first insight decouples the task of predicting pose-dependent deformations from the generation of plausible, high-frequency wrinkle patterns: before training the deformer, we first train a Variational Auto-Encoder (VAE) to reconstruct a modest set of deformations to create a smooth, concise, and expressive latent space. Our second insight is to progressively train the VAE encoder to transition from reconstruction to deformation prediction from body poses, thus simplifying the task. We find that this progressive strategy significantly improves the visual quality while maintaining architectural complexity and keeping inference times at interactive rate. In addition to conditioning the re-purposed encoder on low-dimensional pose parameters, we splat body surface displacements onto the garment mesh using linear blend skinning weights to provide deformation guidance on the mesh level. Finally, we leverage a novel local gradient histogram loss over surface neighborhoods to preserve high-frequency wrinkles and mitigate the over-smoothing that is commonly associated with reconstruction-based losses.

We evaluate our approach against state-of-the-art methods from both academia [BODO18, PLPM20, CMM∗20, STOC21] and production pipelines [Aut25, Epi25] on production-level shirt and pants assets, as well as previously published virtual try-on datasets. Across datasets, our method produces sharp, realistic wrinkles while maintaining smooth large-scale drape at interactive rates, and exhibits temporally coherent behavior as a byproduct of the structured latent space despite operating per-frame. Extensive ablations further justify each stage of our pipeline and its design choices. Overall, our experiments demonstrate a production-ready approach that is easy to integrate into existing workflows, giving artists a robust and high-quality preview in real-time.

2 Related Work

2.1 Numerical Simulation of Cloth

Cloth simulation is a long-standing and widely researched topic in computer animation. Since the debut of the seminal Baraff–Witkin model [BW98], many improvements have been proposed to simulate fabrics with higher fidelity [BMF05, CK05, TPS09, LB15, Kim20]. For a detailed analysis regarding production implementation practicalities, we refer to Kim et al. [KE20]. Recent efforts have greatly boosted the efficiency of cloth solvers on both CPUs and GPUs [WWYW20, WWW22, GWL∗25, LLL∗24, LLL∗25, CHL∗25]. However, implementing these efficient solvers in production settings often poses practical challenges. Production solvers must handle broken animations, non-physical setups, self-intersections, solver-specific heuristics, and artist-authored corrections. Neural networks, such as our method, are not only efficient, but also easily portable to different digital content creation software.

One well-researched area within numerical simulation is sub-space solvers [KJ09, JF03, TLP06, HSL∗06, PBH15, YLX∗15, MWW16, BEH18, LSW∗18, WKS20], thus reducing the excessive degrees of freedom for a given application. Many learning-based cloth deformation methods [STOC21, SYWL22, DLLG∗23] reflect this idea by training Auto-Encoders to reduce the garments into smooth and expressive latent space. We similarly reduce the dimensionality of the problem by training a VAE on deformation deltas.

Collision handling [BMF05, Sta09, FTP16, TWL∗18, WWYW20] also plays an important role in cloth simulations. Most neural clothing methods either perform simple repulsion-based post-processing at inference time to resolve collisions [SOC19, PLPM20, SOC22, CGY∗23, LSK23], or formulate a loss term based on interpenetration distance [STOC21, GCP∗20, BME21, BME22]. We utilize the post-processing approach in our method as we find it sufficiently robust and efficient.

2.2 Learning-based Methods

Cloth regression.

Many prior works regress garment deformations directly from character poses or refine a coarse simulation to create more realistic wrinkles. Data-driven methods were first explored to predict cloth deformations without relying on neural networks [KV08, FYK10, WHRO10, KGBS11, GRH∗12, WCC∗21]. TailorNet [PLPM20] trains MLPs in two stages to separate low- and high-frequency deformations. [LTY∗24] extends the two-stream idea and trained Graph Transformer to obtain high-frequency wrinkles. Bertiche et al. [BME20] solve the same problem by training a Conditional VAE. Santesteban et al. [SOC19] extend this work with RNNs to capture dynamic cloth motion from time-varying animation. Chentanez et al. [CMM∗20] proposed a new spiral convolution operation for regressing garment deformations. Our work is in these lines: we regress deformations directly from character poses with a single feed-forward pass.

The above works all create or reuse a cloth deformation dataset through physically-based simulations and perform supervised trainings. Another option is to employ a set of physically-based unsupervised losses [BME21, BME22, SOC22, LKL23, GBH23, GBB∗24]. Using unsupervised losses relieves the burden of dataset creation while providing high-quality wrinkle configurations. However, it is difficult, if not impossible, to replicate production simulation setups in this manner due to their complexities. We thus train our models in fully supervised settings.

Instead of directly regressing 3D deformations, some methods represent deformations via 2D displacement maps and use convolutional neural networks [LCT18, JZGF20, SYWL22, GYS∗25]. Though leveraging well-studied 2D network architectures, handling seams and distortions in texture maps is often challenging. Other methods train an upsampler of low-resolution cloth to obtain fine details [CYZ21, ZWCM21, CGY∗23, ZL24]. However, these works usually use coarse simulations as input, which is not always available in production settings.

Neural simulations.

Another type of approach to learn cloth deformations is to replace the physically-based simulator with a neural network. A Graph Network-based Simulator (GNS) based on message passing is leveraged to learn particle-based [SGGP∗20] and mesh-based [PFSGB21] simulations. HOOD [GBH23] proposes a hierarchical message passing scheme to enhance the simulation quality. Subsequent works of HOOD handle multi-layered garments [GBB∗24] and address self-collisions [LWK24b, BHN∗25]. Transformer-based architectures have also been explored in the context of neural cloth simulation [SLD23, LWK∗24a]. Although demonstrating generalization capabilities to unseen meshes, GNS and transformers are usually expensive to evaluate due to their iterative or global nature. Most of these works also rely on physically-based unsupervised losses. As our focus is on real-time inference speed for production settings, we do not adopt this category of approach.

3 Method

The target of our neural cloth deformer is to efficiently regress a high-quality wrinkled garment mesh given input character joint transforms θ and a single baseline garment rest shape x_R for quasi-static scenarios. Similar to previous approaches [LMR∗15, BODO18, ZB24, PLPM20], our predictor outputs rest-pose deformations that are subsequently skinned to obtain the final garment positions x_G for a single frame as

x_G=W(x_R+ℕ_Φ(θ), θ),

(1)

where W is a skinning function, e.g., linear blend skinning (LBS), extended for the garment mesh and ℕ_Φ(θ) predicts per-vertex rest-space displacements. Assuming the skinning function is invertible, the ground-truth rest-space deformations can be computed as:

Δx=W⁻¹(x_G,θ)-x_R.

(2)

Training on Δx factors out world transforms and facilitates normalization. A general pose-to-mesh neural network predictor can then be trained with the following objective:

\argmin_Φ∑ᵢwᵢLᵢ(F(ℕ_Φ(θ)),F(Δx)),

(3)

where Φ are the trainable network weights, F is a user-specified feature extractor (e.g., computing vertex normals), and Lᵢ is a weighted (wᵢ) loss function that can represent distance metrics such as L², cosine similarity or a local norm distribution loss (Section 3.4); or even physically-inspired energy-based formulations [BME21, BME22]. Our work focuses on supervised losses, since the goal is to preserve the artistic intent for a particular setting, as captured by carefully tuned cloth simulations and occasional artist-authored frame edits.

Previous methods differ mainly in how they couple pose information to mesh deformations. A straightforward option is a global MLP that maps joint transforms directly to rest-space deformations. However, fully connected architectures scale poorly with mesh resolution; to keep parameter counts tractable, previous approaches predict a reduced set of scalar weights coupled with learned linear basis (e.g., blendshape-style subspaces)  [SOC19, BMTE21]. One issue is that these learned linear basis are oblivious to the mesh structure, which hinders the capacity of the network to efficiently learn non-linear local features that can improve generalization. A more structured alternative is the per-joint MLP formulation of [BODO18], which leverages the spatial locality implied by skinning. In this setting, each joint j has its own MLP ℕʲ_Φ(θⱼ) that takes the joint transform θⱼ as input and predicts rest-space displacements only for vertices influenced by that joint, implemented via a vertex mask M(·) derived from skinning weights. The posed garment is then obtained by aggregating the per-joint contributions:

x_G=W(x_R+∑ⱼMʲ(ℕʲ_Φ(θⱼ)),θ).

(4)

This formulation is highly effective for learning pose-dependent body corrections that bridge the gap between a simple LBS and high-quality rig deformations. Naively extending such an approach to neural garments, however, has its issues. For character rigs, rest-space corrections are typically smooth and localized around the driving joints; in contrast, cloth wrinkles are inherently non-local, and small changes in a shoulder or elbow can induce folds that propagate across the entire garment surface. Figure 7(a) shows a per-joint MLP baseline. The predicted deformations exhibit over-smoothed wrinkles, indicating that the per-joint locality assumption is insufficient to reproduce the production-quality wrinkling patterns required in our setting. In the next sections we will discuss how our proposed training pipeline can effectively capture long-range dependencies with a novel mesh-aware architecture that is tailored to efficiently condition pose information.

3.1 Latent Garment Prior via VAE Pre-Training

A recurring failure mode of direct pose-to-mesh regression is that the network must simultaneously infer global deformations and synthesize high-frequency wrinkle geometry in the correct spatial configuration. This end-to-end mapping remains high-dimensional and under-constrained: many mesh deformations are locally consistent with the pose descriptor but implausible as garments. To improve generalization, we therefore factor the problem into two steps: we first learn a pose-agnostic prior over rest-pose garment deformations using a Variational Auto-Encoder (VAE), and then learn a pose-conditioned encoder that predicts latent codes inside the learned space (Section 3.3).

The VAE consists of an encoder 𝔼_ψ(z|Δx) and a decoder D_θ(Δx|z), where z is a low-dimensional latent code. The decoder D_θ(z) is also implemented as a mesh-aware Convolutional Neural Network that outputs a displacement field on the original mesh resolution. We optimize the standard evidence lower bound:

\beginsplit\min_ψ,θ 𝔼_Δx[𝔼_z∼𝔼_ψ(z|Δx)[ L_rec(D_θ(Δx|z),Δx) ] + w_KL KL (𝔼_ψ(z|Δx) ∥ ℕ(0,I))],\endsplit

(5)

where the supervised reconstruction loss (e.g., vertex L² and normal terms) L_rec forces the decoder to represent high-frequency wrinkles while the Kullback–Leibler (KL) term shapes the latent space into a smooth, well-filled distribution aligned with an isotropic Gaussian prior. Note that Eq. (5) is trained on rest-space deformation residuals rather than absolute vertex positions. At inference time, obtaining these residuals requires inverse skinning, so the pose is implicitly involved through the skinning operation.

During VAE training, the decoder learns a strong deformation prior that captures the multiscale statistics of plausible rest-pose cloth shapes, while the KL term encourages a smooth, well-conditioned latent space in which nearby codes decode to coherent, nearby deformations. In practice, this leads to more stable wrinkle patterns under pose distribution shift and improved generalization across motions and characters, while preserving the deterministic behavior required for production inference. As shown in Figure 2, encoding ground-truth rest-pose deformations along an animated pose sequence produces a latent trajectory that varies smoothly over time. This supports our motivating assumption that the space of plausible deformations is locally low-dimensional and well-behaved: continuous changes in pose induce continuous changes in latent deformation, making it feasible to learn a pose-to-latent mapping that generalizes beyond the training distribution.

3.2 Progressive Transition to Pose Conditioning

The VAE pre-training in the previous section yields a garment-valid decoder that maps a compact latent code to detailed rest-pose displacements. An immediate next step could be to freeze the decoder and replace the VAE encoder with a pose-conditioned encoder operating on mesh-aligned pose features. In practice, we found this direct replacement to be too abrupt: the decoder has only been exposed to latent codes produced from geometric inputs, whereas a pose-conditioned encoder would initially produce latents from a markedly different input distribution. This mismatch leads to unstable optimization and weaker generalization, often manifesting as overfitting to the pose distribution seen during training or as high-frequency artifacts under pose variation.

To smooth out this transition, we introduce a progressive curriculum that gradually morphs the auto-encoding task into an “upsampling-from-coarse” task before training with pose features. Concretely, after training the VAE in the standard fine-to-fine setting, we continue training while progressively coarsening the encoder input through a Laplacian smoothing operator. The progressively smoothed inputs are defined by

Δx⁽⁰⁾=Δx, Δx⁽ˡ⁾=(I-λL)⁻¹Δx⁽ˡ⁻¹⁾, l=1,…,L,

(6)

where L is the cotangent Laplacian and λ controls the smoothing strength. Increasing l progressively removes high-frequency content (wrinkles and fine folds), producing a sequence of increasingly low-detail inputs that remain defined on the original mesh connectivity. A visualization of our smoothing operator, showing progressive removal of geometric detail, is shown in Figure 3 (top row).

During this refinement phase, we optimize the reconstruction term of Eq. (5) with the encoder conditioned on Δx⁽ˡ⁾ and the decoder supervised against the full-detail displacement field Δx. We disable the KL term by setting w_KL=0, ensuring a deterministic refinement that avoids imposing additional constraints on the latent distribution. In the meanwhile, the smoothing level l is increased according to a fixed curriculum (Section 4).

As illustrated in Figure 3, recovering wrinkle details from Laplacian-smoothed inputs is comparatively well-conditioned: the VAE consistently reconstructs high-frequency structures that closely matches the ground truth. This observation motivates our subsequent pose-conditioning strategy: if the decoder can reliably synthesize fine details from weak geometric cues, it can also be finetuned to predict deformations from mesh-aligned pose features.

3.3 Mesh-Aware Deformation Model

Once the autoencoder has been trained to decode detailed deformations from increasingly weaker geometric inputs, we replace its pose-agnostic encoder with a pose-conditioned encoder while keeping the decoder fixed. This curriculum substantially stabilizes the handoff: the pose-conditioned encoder can rely on the well-behaved decoder space already used for reconstruction, rather than learning the entire deformation synthesis process end-to-end. We implement pose conditioning through three complementary mechanisms: joint-to-mesh splatted pose features, fine-scale pose injection via FiLM modulation, and a coarse-level cross-attention block between pose embeddings and mesh latent features.

Joint-to-mesh splatted transforms.

Prior mesh-based deformer models often compress joint transforms into a global latent vector and inject it into the mesh decoder via fully connected layers  [CMM∗20]. This coupling can create a bottleneck for pose information to get through. Instead, we construct a mesh-aligned pose field by splatting joint information directly onto garment vertices using skinning weights. Each joint transform is embedded into a feature vector, and vertex-level pose features are obtained by smoothly blending the joint features according to their LBS influences. Additionally, the rest body deformations from the ground-truth data are also splatted to the cloth mesh, and concatenated to the splatted joint transforms as the input of the network. This produces a continuous per-vertex conditioning signal over the garment surface, enabling subsequent mesh convolutions to process pose information locally while still propagating effects globally through the multi-resolution hierarchy.

Improving pose parameters conditioning.

To further condition the network on pose parameters, we adopt two complementary mechanisms. For the finer-resolution encoder blocks, we apply FiLM modulation [PSV∗17], where pose information is pooled across joints using an attention mechanism and then used to generate per-channel scaling and shifting parameters that modulate the outputs of each SpiralConv layer. For the coarsest mesh level, we additionally employ cross-attention [VSP∗23], where the encoded pose parameters serve as keys and values and the current feature map serves as the query. This enables global feature interactions with the pose embeddings.

3.4 Local Normal Distribution Loss

Pointwise reconstruction losses (e.g., vertex L²) penalize small spatial misalignments of wrinkles and folds, even they exhibit visually plausible high-frequency details. To reduce sensitivity to such phase shifts while still supervising fine-scale appearance, we introduce a distributional loss that matches local surface orientation statistics between prediction and ground truth. Given predicted and ground-truth meshes, we compute per-vertex unit normals and represent each normal by spherical angles (φ,ω), with φ∈[0,π] and ω∈[0,2π). For each vertex i, we define a local neighborhood Ωₖ(i) using k-nearest neighbors in the bind-pose geometry; we optionally evaluate multiple neighborhood sizes k∈K to capture statistics at different spatial scales. Within each neighborhood, we differentiably construct a two-dimensional histogram over (φ,ω) using Gaussian kernel accumulation around fixed bin centers in angular space. The resulting histogram is normalized to sum to one, yielding a local probability distribution over surface orientations. We use 8 bins for φ and 16 bins for ω, with a fixed kernel bandwidth.

Let Ĥ_i,k and H_i,k denote the predicted and ground-truth normalized orientation histograms for vertex i and neighborhood size k, respectively. We define the local normal distribution loss as the mean squared error between corresponding histograms, averaged over vertices and neighborhood scales:

Lₕᵢₛₜ=(1)/(|K|)∑_k∈K(1)/(|V|)∑_i∈V\lVertĤ_i,k-H_i,k\rVert₂²,

(7)

where V is the set of vertices. This loss provides an alternative to pointwise supervision by encouraging realistic local wrinkle energy and directional variability.

4 Experiments and Results

Architecture details.

Our VAE architecture operates on mesh vertex features using a mesh-aware residual SpiralConv [GCBZ19] backbone. Each resolution level consists of an encoder block followed by a symmetric decoder block. The encoder applies a residual SpiralConv stack (GELU + SpiralConv + LayerNorm) to provide a strong locality bias directly on the surface while remaining more structure-aware than MLPs and transformers [CZG∗22]. We then reduce resolution using Quadric Error Metric (QEM) pooling; the decoder mirrors this structure with the corresponding unpooling operator. To mitigate resampling artifacts, we apply a Laplacian smoothing operator before each QEM pooling and unpooling. In all experiments we use a hierarchy with 3 levels of mesh resolutions and QEM pooling matrices. The channel widths increase from 64 at the finest level to 512 at the coarsest. Within each block, we use 5 residual sub-layers per level and pose conditioning is injected through the mechanisms described in Section 3.3, while the rest-space displacement field is decoded at full resolution.

Training.

We train all models with AdamW [LH19] with β₁=0.9, β₂=0.999 and batch size 16. The VAE pre-training is run for 400,000 optimization steps, and each progressive curriculum stage is trained for 100,000 steps, followed by the pose deformer training for another 100,000 steps. We use a cosine annealing schedule that decays the learning rate from 1×10⁻⁴ to 1×10⁻⁵ over each training horizon. Poses θ are represented as 4×4 homogeneous transformation matrices of each joint, including rotation, scaling and translation which are often all animated in the production setting. In addition to the local normal distribution loss, we use a weak latent supervision term (wₗₐₜ=0.1), computing MAE between predicted latent codes and the ground-truth ones from the pre-trained VAE. Additional architectural and training details are provided in Appendix A.

4.1 Datasets

Our dataset consists of a rigged human female character Jen, with three types of motions: (i) long artist-authored dancing animations; (ii) short motion clips sampled from a larger animation library; (iii) randomly sampled poses [BODO18]. Partition (i) consists of 1,264 frames over 6 sequences, and is used for validation. Partition (ii) has 9,090 frames and captures common actions such as walking, turning, or falling. To improve coverage of poses encountered at inference time, we extensively sample random joint transforms in Partition (iii), comprising 12,230 frames. This sampling is designed to cover a wide range of poses with large joint transforms. Partitions (ii) and (iii) are used for training.

Partition (iii) and the majority of Partition (ii) consist of discontinuous poses, generated with quasi-static simulation. While susceptible to temporal inconsistencies and reduced secondary dynamics, this often remains the only practical option, as dynamic simulation between poses frequently triggers self-intersections that cause the simulator to fail. We also evaluate our method on the VTO dataset [SOC19], a simulated virtual try-on benchmark with a T-shirt and a long dress modeled on SMPL [LMR∗15] human body models. A single body shape from the dataset was used. Various motion captured sequences of talking, walking, jumping sum up to 6,665 frames of training and 452 frames for validation.

4.2 Quantitative and Qualitative Evaluations

Figure  and Figure 4 show our model on representative validation frames from the Jen dataset. Despite complex motions and challenging wrinkling patterns, our model generates physically plausible garment deformations in real-time. We further compare against state-of-the-art baselines from both academia and available commercial software. Figure 5 summarizes qualitative comparisons using our internal dataset with the ML Deformers in Autodesk Maya 2025 [Aut25] and Unreal Engine 5.6 [Epi25], a per-joint MLP baseline adapted to garments [BODO18], a two-stage MLP model that predicts coarse and fine details [PLPM20], and a mesh-convolutional model [CMM∗20]. Across all above methods, our approach produces the most realistic fine-scale wrinkles and the best temporal coherence. Figure 6 shows the same comparisons on the VTO datasets. In some examples in Figure 6, both our model and several baselines exhibit minor high-frequency artifacts or reduced smoothness relative to the simulation ground truth, suggesting that these artifacts are not specific to a single loss formulation or architecture. We report Mean Absolute Error (MAE) of all methods in Table 1. We also report the measurements from training our method with the traditional reconstruction losses (Ours w/o NormDist). Our approach outperforms the other methods in terms of MAE across different datasets. Inference runtimes on Jen’s Shirt dataset are also reported in Table 2. Our method can run inference with 212.2 FPS. We demonstrate its real-time capability through a posing application in Figure  (left) and in the supplemental video.

Additional metrics.

Pointwise distances often fail to reflect perceptual deformation quality: small spatial shifts of wrinkles can inflate MAE despite visually plausible results. Additionally, low MAE does not guarantee a correct silhouette and physical plausibility. We therefore report complementary metrics that target specific failure modes. The Contour metric evaluates global shape by computing a symmetric Chamfer distance between boundary vertex sets of the predicted and ground-truth garments. The Collision quantifies garment-body interpenetration: we measure the minimum displacement required to move garment vertices outside the body surface and report the mean. LPIPS[ZIE∗18] is also reported by rendering garment images because perceptual metrics correlate more closely with human judgments than pixel-level errors. Finally, to assess wrinkle qualities invariant to small phase shifts, we compare distributions of surface detail using mean curvature (Curv): we form soft histograms over mean curvature magnitude of the vertices using 64 logarithmically spaced bins, and report the MAE between predicted and ground-truth histograms.

Table 2 summarizes evaluations of additional metrics on Jen’s Shirt dataset. Our method not only improves MAE over previous approaches, but also exhibits fewer collisions, better contour agreement, and higher perceptual similarity to the ground truth. The local normal distribution loss exhibits a slight increase in MAE. This reflects a deliberate trade-off: by supervising local deformation statistics rather than exact positions, we encourage richer wrinkle structures and high-frequency details, even when deformations are not perfectly phase-aligned with the reference. However, this can occasionally over-emphasize sharp normal variations in ambiguous fold regions, which may appear as localized crease-like wrinkles that are less smooth than the physics-based ground truth. Additional results are provided in Appendix C.

User study.

We conducted user study with 28 participants and collected 1096 votes. Participants were shown side-by-side comparisons of rendered frames of our method and baselines. They were asked to indicate their preference in terms of visual quality without knowing the source of images. The results are shown in Figure 8. In total, 96.3% of the votes are in favor of our method.

4.3 Ablation Studies

Table 3 analyzes the contributions of the main design choices in our pipeline on Jen’s Shirt dataset. We first study the effect of the VAE latent dimensionality by varying bottleneck sizes, measured in MAE (right column). Starting from Jen’s Shirt mesh with 4820 vertices (4820×3 degrees of freedom), we evaluate three bottlenecks: 624×3 (∼7.8× compression), 229×1 (∼64× compression), and 86×1 (∼228× compression). Size 229×1 provides the best trade-off between compression and reconstruction quality. This setting is used in all subsequent experiments. Then, we ablate the pose-conditioning components and training strategies (middle rows). Incorporating joint-to-mesh splatted pose features, body displacement cues, and VAE pre-training each improves performance. The best result is obtained with all three together (in green). Finally, progressive training consistently reduces MAE, indicating more stable optimization and improved generalization. As noted in Section 4.2, the histogram loss slightly increases MAE but yields sharper, more perceptually convincing high-frequency details. Figure 7 visually provides evidence on how each stage progressively improves wrinkle sharpness and perceptual details.

5 Conclusions

We presented a learning-based pipeline for quasi-static garment deformation tailored to production settings, where future usage requires reasonable predictions in large pose ranges and the target appearance demands high-quality, plausible wrinkles rather than merely low MAE metrics. To our knowledge, this is the first approach to explicitly address core production constraints in a unified system: generating a production-driven dataset that combines artist-authored motion snippets with carefully filtered random poses, and emphasizing perceptual wrinkle realism alongside physical plausibility. Our method combines mesh-aware pose conditioning with VAE pre-training and a staged training strategy that progressively transitions from the pre-training to pose-driven prediction, enabling robust generalization. Across multiple datasets, we show that each stage contributes measurably to performance, and that these improvements persist under a stricter validation protocol using held-out motion trajectories rather than near-duplicate training frames. In contrast to prior work where generalization is often assessed on samples closely related to the training distribution, our evaluation highlights the importance of validation on genuinely unseen sequences when targeting production deployment.

Limitations and future work.

Despite the encouraging results, several limitations remain. First, cloth deformation behavior is inherently history-dependent: similar poses with different inertia and history can correspond to different wrinkle configurations. This temporal ambiguity renders the regression problem ill-posed and encourages deterministic predictors to average over multiple plausible outcomes, especially under highly dynamic motions (Figure 9). Incorporating temporal information and/or modeling latent trajectories is a natural next step. Closely related, a deterministic formulation cannot represent the multi-modality of cloth at a fixed pose; probabilistic predictors with stochastic latent variables or diffusion models may better capture this variability and reduce over-smoothing. Second, our pose conditioning relies on skinning-derived correspondences to project joint transformations or body cues onto the garment. While effective for fitted clothing, garment–body sliding (common in loose garments and large motions) diverges from this correspondence and lead to systematic artifacts. Dynamic correspondences or motion fields that account for sliding are interesting future avenues. Third, our local normal distribution supervision illustrates a broader trade-off in deformation learning: matching local orientation statistics encourages expressive high-frequency detail and tolerates small spatial shifts, but can occasionally yield overly pronounced wrinkles or sharp creases in ambiguous regions, as well as globally inconsistent fold organization (Figure 9). Hybrid objectives that preserve distributional robustness while adding lightweight global or continuity constraints may alleviate these cases. Finally, evaluation remains challenging: no single metric reliably captures perceptual quality and physical plausibility across modeling choices. Though user studies help alleviate this situation, developing better quantitative criteria for wrinkle coherence, plausible material behavior, and perceptual realism remains an open problem.

（参考文献见原文。）

Appendix A Model Implementation Details

A.1 Mesh Auto-Encoder Architecture

Our VAE is implemented as a mesh-aware convolutional network based on spiral convolutions and a fixed multi-resolution mesh hierarchy. Spiral convolutions operate on ordered one-ring neighborhoods, enabling convolutions directly on irregular mesh surfaces while preserving geometric locality. This formulation provides a strong inductive bias for surface-based deformation modeling.

We construct a hierarchy of three mesh resolutions using Quadric Error Metrics (QEM) simplification, yielding a set of fixed pooling and unpooling operators. Coarser levels capture global shape variation, while finer levels model localized wrinkle detail. Both the encoder and decoder operate on this hierarchy, with feature dimensionality increasing towards coarser levels and decreasing symmetrically during decoding.

Residual spiral convolution blocks.

Each encoder level consists of a residual spiral convolution block, followed by optional Laplacian smoothing and QEM-based downsampling. The decoder mirrors this structure, applying unpooling, smoothing, and residual spiral convolution blocks to reconstruct higher-resolution features. The final decoder output is a per-vertex displacement field defined on the original mesh resolution. Each residual block processes vertex features through two parallel paths: a residual path and a skip path. The residual path consists of L stacked sublayers, each composed of a GELU activation, a spiral convolution, and Layer Normalization. Formally, a single sublayer is defined as (see Figure 12)

f(x)=LayerNorm(SpiralConv(GELU(x))) .

(8)

The residual path applies this function L times in sequence. In parallel, the skip path applies a single spiral convolution to the input features. The two paths are combined and normalized to produce the block output. To mitigate aliasing artifacts introduced by mesh resolution changes, we apply a lightweight Laplacian smoothing operator to the feature maps after pooling or unpooling. This promotes smooth feature variation across the surface while preserving high-frequency detail through the residual connections.

item.title: 长视频重建的注意力别再看全部帧：EcoVGGT 假设「关键 key 不看内容也能选」，做可流式的前馈重建 ｜ EcoVGGT: Pinned-Key Inference for Efficient and Streamable Feed-Forward 3D Reconstruction from Long Videos
item.description:
一句话：VGGT 这类前馈模型一次恢复相机与几何，但跨帧注意力随帧数平方增长、长视频精度还掉。

要点：

  • 现状：VGGT 之类的前馈多视图 transformer 能一次前向恢复视频的相机与几何，但**跨帧注意力成本随帧数平方增长**，且长视频上精度会下降
  • 常见补救是在预算内近似全帧注意力，或按内容挑选少量 key
  • EcoVGGT 的假设更激进：长视频的 key 可以**不看内容就选**（pinned-key），于是推理可以做成流式

为什么值得看：「流式」是这条能不能进实时管线的分水岭：如果必须拿到整段视频才能重建，就只能离线用。把 key 选择从「看内容」变成「预置」，等于把重建变成可以边录边算的过程。

中文摘要：VGGT 这类前馈多视图 transformer 能一次前向恢复整段视频的相机与几何，但它们的跨帧注意力开销随帧数呈平方增长，长视频上的精度也会下降。现有补救大致两类：在给定预算内近似全帧注意力，或依据内容挑出少量 key。EcoVGGT 提出的假设更激进——长视频的 key 可以不看内容就预先固定（pinned-key），因此可以选择性地保持少量 key 复用，使推理变成可流式的过程：随着视频继续输入而持续产出重建结果。这决定了长视频重建能否从离线工具走进入实时管线。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·cs.CV（English）

原文发布：2026-11-16

本期推送：2026-11-17

EcoVGGT: Pinned-Key Inference for Efficient and Streamable Feed-Forward 3D Reconstruction from Long Videos

Abstract

Feed-forward multi-view transformers such as VGGT recover the cameras and geometry of a video in one pass, but the cost of their cross-frame attention grows quadratically with the frame count, and their accuracy drops on long videos. Most remedies approximate attention over all frames within a budget or select a few keys by their content. We hypothesize that the keys of a long video can be chosen without looking at its content, and our experiments on VGGT and π³ support it: a few dozen evenly spread frames can serve as the keys of every frame. We present EcoVGGT, a training-free inference framework whose keys form a Pinned Key Set of 31 such frames. A pin pass stores their tokens in a Scene Cache, and the other frames read it in independent batches that reproduce joint inference with these keys exactly, at a constant cost per frame. An Online Stream updates the pinned frames during recording. Six middle global blocks align the frames and form a reusable VGGT module: the Alignment Score reads their attention to flag failures, and Alignment Refocusing reduces them by fine-tuning only these blocks (3.6 GPU hours). EcoVGGT (π³) matches the success rate of π³ on 1,000-frame ScanNet videos at 13.8 times its speed. With refocusing, EcoVGGT (VGGT) raises the success rate of VGGT from 70% to 82% at 8.5 times its speed on 500 frames. EcoVGGT reconstructs 4,000 frames on one GPU, and EcoVGGT (π³) streams 1,000 frames at 18.6 frames per second with the lowest online absolute trajectory error.

1 Introduction

Feed-forward networks now recover 3D scenes directly from images [54, 24, 51]. Given a video, the Visual Geometry Grounded Transformer (VGGT) [51] predicts the camera pose and dense geometry of every frame in one forward pass, and later models such as π³[56], VGGT-Ω[52], and Depth Anything 3 (DA3) [26] work the same way. Their global blocks make this possible, since cross-frame self-attention lets each view draw on all other views.

We study how such a model can reconstruct every frame of a long video in one coordinate frame at a constant cost per frame. Long videos challenge these models in two ways. First, the cost of cross-frame attention grows quadratically with the number of frames, and its memory grows proportionally with every frame. A two-thousand-frame video at 518 × 392 resolution requires >80 GB GPU memory, so long videos should be split into chunks or subsampled, and subsampling leaves most frames unreconstructed. Second, accuracy suffers even when the video can fit in memory. Our evaluations show that, at 500 frames, the full VGGT keeps its trajectory error within a 0.2 m tolerance in only 70% of 50 ScanNet scenes [10]. Its predicted confidence flags failures barely better than chance (Fig.1c), so users cannot tell which results to trust.

Most existing remedies approximate attention over all frames within a budget, and each of them gives up part of this goal. Streaming variants [65, 66, 62] process each frame once as it arrives and freeze its tokens, so early errors persist. They keep at most half the scenes within tolerance (Tab.1), and InfiniteVGGT misplaces walls in two long videos (Fig.5). Chunked pipelines [14, 16] see one window at a time, so their chain of windows drifts wherever no loop closure corrects it. Token merging [39] keeps every frame in one pass and runs out of memory in most scenes at 2,000 frames. Methods that give each frame a few keys take them at fixed intervals [46, 12, 47] or select them by content, such as diverse views [63, 37] or retrieved frames [66]. Two questions remain open: whether a long video needs attention over all its frames, and whether the keys of each frame must depend on the video content.

We hypothesize that the keys of a long video can be chosen without looking at its content. One shared context of a few dozen frames, spread evenly over the video, can serve as the keys of every frame, and the other frames need not read one another. Our experiments on long indoor videos with VGGT and π³ support three of its predictions. First, with 31 to 125 evenly spread frames as the only keys, VGGT estimates relative rotations more accurately than with all frames, consistent with surplus keys diluting the attention [63, 37] (Fig.1a). With 31 keys, π³ keeps its trajectory error (Tab.1). Second, keys chosen by content perform worse than evenly spread keys. Keys from farthest-point sampling on place-recognition descriptors, as in Good Token Hunting [63], raise the trajectory error of π³ by 9.3% (Tab.5), and the 31 most-attended frames raise the relative rotation error of VGGT over sixfold (Sec.4.3). Third, keys outside the shared set do not help. Extra keys from nearby frames degrade the relative poses (Fig.1b), and prior work finds them poor substitutes for spread keys [63, 59].

If one shared context suffices, a video of any length can be reconstructed at a constant cost per frame, with attention over this context computed exactly. In this work, we propose EcoVGGT, an inference framework with three components that make it Exact, Cached, and Online. A Pinned Key Set of 31 evenly spread frames serves as the only keys, so every frame reads the whole scene in one coordinate frame, and independent batches of the other frames reproduce joint inference with these keys exactly. A pin pass stores the context of the pinned frames once in a Scene Cache, as in keyframe tracking [46], and every batch reads it. During recording, an Online Stream keeps the pinned frames spread over the whole past and caps their number. Beyond efficiency, layer analyses locate frame alignment in a band of middle global blocks [45, 61, 13], and we find that the departure of the band’s attention from uniform identifies the failures of VGGT (AUROC 0.91, Fig.1c). These findings motivate our Alignment Score, which reads this departure to flag failures, and our Alignment Refocusing, which fine-tunes only the band to reduce them.

When running offline, EcoVGGT reconstructs at least as many scenes as its backbones, at a fraction of their cost (Fig.4). With Alignment Refocusing, EcoVGGT (VGGT) raises the success rate on ScanNet from 70% to 82% at 8.5 times the speed on 500 frames and handles 4,000 frames on one GPU. Without training, EcoVGGT (π³) matches the success rate of the full π³ on 1,000 frames at 13.8 times its speed, runs faster at this length than every compared method, and has the lowest online absolute trajectory error (Tabs.1 and 2). On four other indoor datasets, it has the lowest absolute trajectory error of all chunked and streaming methods (Tab.4).

Our contributions are threefold: 1) we observe that a small number of content-agnostic, evenly spread keys outperform keys chosen by content and give VGGT lower relative rotation errors than all frames; 2) EcoVGGT, a training-free inference framework that computes attention over these keys exactly at a constant cost per frame, streams online, and can be directly applied to different backbones, including VGGT, π³, VGGT-Ω, and DA3; 3) a reusable alignment module for VGGT, whose Alignment Refocusing raises the success rate under full attention as well as under the Pinned Key Set, and whose Alignment Score flags failures without training.

2 Related work

Long-video inference

Acceleration methods for multi-view transformers [60, 51, 56, 22, 26] merge tokens [39, 41, 55] as in vision transformers [4], subsample keys and values on a spatial grid [45, 61], or skip weak interactions [49, 13]. They keep every frame in one pass, so cost and memory grow with the video length. VGG-T3[17] retrains the attention to read a fixed-size memory, while FlashVGGT [57] retrains it to read compact descriptors of all frames and a few keyframes. Streaming methods keep a spatial memory [50, 7], a learned state [53, 6], a multi-layer memory [5], or a cache of past keys and values [65, 23, 8], which later variants bound by eviction, frame selection, or retrieval [62, 44, 59, 66, 29, 34, 32, 27, 18]. Chunked pipelines join overlapping windows, offline [14] or incrementally [30, 31], and LASER [16] aligns them by rescaling each depth layer. Without loop closure, an error at one join shifts all later windows (Sec. S8).

Shared keys

Methods in which many frames read a few keys come closest to our hypothesis. KV-Tracker [46] caches the keys and values of keyframes for real-time tracking. SAIL-Recon [12] fine-tunes VGGT so that frames read the cached keys and values of 50 to 100 uniformly sampled anchor frames, while Spark3R [47] keeps those of about 40 frames at a temporal stride and finds them slightly better than random tokens. In KV-Tracker and SAIL-Recon, each frame also reads its own tokens. Good Token Hunting [63] selects one key set for all queries by farthest-point sampling on place-recognition descriptors, while DA-VGGT [37] partitions the frames into chunks of diverse views that share one anchor frame. We test whether the content of the keys matters and find that evenly spread keys outperform keys selected by descriptors on π³ and keys selected by attention on VGGT (Tab.5, Sec. S6). In EcoVGGT, they are the only keys of every frame, since a frame’s own and nearby tokens do not help it (Tab.5, Fig.1b). A pin pass computes these keys once, and independent batches of the other frames reproduce joint inference with them exactly, in one coordinate frame and at a constant cost per frame. EcoVGGT needs no training on π³, VGGT-Ω, and DA3.

Long-context attention

In transformers for text, scaling the logits by the logarithm of the input length restores the focus that the softmax loses over long inputs [9, 35], while StreamingLLM [58] keeps a few initial tokens as permanent keys next to recent ones. Multi-view models lose focus in the same way: the cross-frame attention of VGGT collapses toward rank one over hundreds of frames [39, 25], and redundant views dilute it [37]. Layer analyses find that middle global blocks align the views [45, 61, 13] and attend selectively [34, 32], which they use to thin the attention or the cache. Partial fine-tuning has adapted the image encoder with low-rank adapters for finer geometry [38, 20] and the middle blocks of VGGT for dynamic scenes [64]. Uncertainty estimates use the often overconfident predicted confidence [15], trained adapters [1], or perturbed reruns [33], while VGGT-SLAM 2.0 [31] verifies loop closures with one attention layer. Our Alignment Score reads the attention of the alignment band in one pass to flag failures without training, and our Alignment Refocusing fine-tunes the band’s six blocks alone to align distant views.

3 Method

EcoVGGT organizes VGGT-style inference around one shared context of pinned frames (Fig.2). It computes this context once, reads it exactly, and updates it online. For VGGT, an alignment module refocuses the blocks that align the frames and reads their attention to flag failures (Secs.3.6 and 3.7). We name each version after its backbone, VGGT, π³, VGGT-Ω, or DA3. Analyses in this section use the 50 ScanNet scenes at 500 frames unless noted (Sec.4.1).

3.1 Cross-frame attention

Let a video have N frames, each turned into T tokens of dimension C. The network alternates frame blocks, which mix the tokens within each frame, with L global blocks, which mix them across frames. In one head of a global block, with Xᵢ∈ℝ^T×C the tokens of frame i and X those of all frames, the attention output of frame i is

Oᵢ=softmax((QᵢK^⊤)/(√d))V,

(1)

where W_Q, W_K, and W_V are the head’s projections, Qᵢ=XᵢW_Q, K=XW_K, V=XW_V, and d is the head dimension. Let Hᵢ⁽ˡ⁾ be the tokens of frame i entering global block l∈{0,…,L-1}. For l

Hᵢ⁽ˡ⁺¹⁾=Fₗ₊₁(Gₗ(Hᵢ⁽ˡ⁾; H⁽ˡ⁾)),

(2)

where H⁽ˡ⁾ stacks the tokens of all frames, Fₗ₊₁ is the next frame block, and Gₗ(A;B) is global block l with queries from A and keys and values from B. The tokens Hᵢ⁽⁰⁾ depend on frame i alone, and every prediction head except the camera head of VGGT reads each frame separately. For one query in one head, let a=(a₁,…,aₙ) and u denote its attention over the n keys and the uniform distribution, respectively. We measure the departure from uniform by

KL(u ∥ a)=-\logn-1/n∑ⱼ₌₁ⁿ\logaⱼ,

(3)

a Kullback–Leibler divergence that grows as more keys receive almost no weight. The attention share of one frame on another is the attention that its queries give to all keys of the other, averaged over queries and heads.

On three 100-frame sequences of 7-Scenes [40], the median divergence of VGGT stays near or below 1 up to global block 10, peaks in block 14, and falls below 1 at block 17, a profile that π³ shares (Fig.3a). On 31 spread frames per ScanNet scene, we correlate the attention share of two distant frames (at least four pinned frames apart) with their co-visibility, the overlap of the surfaces that they observe. For VGGT, the rank correlation stays at or below 0.16 in blocks 0 to 9 and reaches 0.66 to 0.68 in blocks 13 to 15 (Fig.3b), so these blocks relate frames by content. We call global blocks 10 to 15, where this correlation rises and peaks, the alignment band and call the later blocks the readout blocks.

Using only 31 to 125 evenly spread frames as keys lowers the relative rotation error of VGGT (Fig.1a), and with 31 keys at 1,000 frames, its median drops from 0.581° to 0.501°. Relative to 125 keys at 500 frames (0.549°), all 500 frames as keys raise this error by 7.2%, whereas 250 keys raise it by 2.6%, consistent with surplus keys diluting the attention once they reach 10 to 20 times the 24-frame training limit [51].

We pin M frames ℙ={p₁,…,p_M} evenly in time, pₖ=1+round((k-1)(N-1)/(M-1)), and restrict the keys and values of every global block to ℙ,

Oᵢ=softmax((QᵢK_ℙ^⊤)/(√d))V_ℙ,

(4)

where K_ℙ and V_ℙ keep the rows of the pinned frames. We use M=31, the smallest tested size at which VGGT and π³ keep their success rates on the evaluation scenes. On 50 training scans, 31 keys match 63 and 125 keys in success rate (Sec. S6). The joint pass of Eq.2 then becomes

Hᵢ⁽ˡ⁺¹⁾=Fₗ₊₁(Gₗ(Hᵢ⁽ˡ⁾; H_ℙ⁽ˡ⁾)),

(5)

where H_ℙ⁽ˡ⁾ stacks the tokens of the pinned frames. Because pinned frames read only one another, a pin pass can process them alone and keep H_ℙ⁽ˡ⁾ at every block. An attach pass then computes any other frame from the kept tokens, in a batch whose frames never read one another.

M²T² (pin pass)+(N-M) M T² (attach passes) = NMT²,

(6)

which is linear in N and a factor of N/M below the N²T² of full attention (16 at 500 frames and 129 at 4,000).

The Online Stream updates the pinned frames during recording (Algorithm S1). Every κ frames, the newest frame becomes a candidate key cₘ=1+mκ, and pass m pins at most M_\max candidates spread evenly over c₀,…,cₘ,

ℙₘ={c_rⱼ}ⱼ₌₀^M_\max-1, rⱼ=round((j m)/(M_\max-1)).

(7)

With a lag of τ passes, this pass attaches and emits the remaining frames up to c_m-τ, so each emitted frame reads keys from the whole past and up to τ+1 later candidates. Every key set contains the first frame, where VGGT fixes the coordinate frame, but each pass normalizes the scale by the frames that it sees. Let Dₖ⁽ᵐ⁾ denote the depth that pass m predicts for frame k, D̂ₖ its emitted depth, and Sₘ⊆ℙₘ those emitted earlier. We rescale pass m>0 with

\begingatheredsₘ=*median_k∈Sₘ(med(D̂ₖ))/(med(Dₖ⁽ᵐ⁾)), D̂ᵢ=sₘDᵢ⁽ᵐ⁾, t̂ᵢ=sₘtᵢ⁽ᵐ⁾,\endgathered

(8)

for every frame i that pass m emits, where med is the pixel median and tᵢ⁽ᵐ⁾ is the camera translation. A rigid transform aligns each pass of π³, which has no reference frame (Sec. S1). The camera head of VGGT reads only the frames of each pass. Each pass handles at most M_\max keys, which bounds its memory, and every frame is emitted within (τ+1) κ frames of its arrival. We use M_\max=32, κ=32 (16 at 500 frames), τ=2 for VGGT, and τ=0 for π³.

3.6 Alignment Refocusing

Our analysis links the remaining failures to the alignment band. With 31 spread keys, the frozen VGGT, which keeps its released weights, succeeds in 72% of the scenes. Its failures occur in large rooms: the ground-truth extent of the camera path separates them from the successes with an AUROC of 0.86. Failed scenes have more distant co-visible pairs among their pinned frames, yet blocks 12 to 15 of the band give these pairs a sixth less attention than in successful scenes. A factor of 1.15 lowers the rotation error of the full VGGT by 2% and 18% at 500 and 1,000 frames, but it sharpens all attention alike. This motivates our Alignment Refocusing, which fine-tunes only the band, 76M parameters or 6.5% of VGGT, to align these pairs. It trains on samples with the structure of inference, so that the band learns to align through pinned keys. Over a whole scan or a random contiguous half, we pin 24 evenly spread frames ℙ and draw 24 random others A that read only these keys, and we minimize the losses of VGGT [51] over the band,

L=λ L_cam(ℙ∪A)+L_depth(ℝ),

(9)

where L_cam and L_depth are the camera and depth losses of VGGT with camera weight λ=5, and the depth loss on only six random frames ℝ of ℙ∪A bounds memory. Training on 195 ScanNet scans of rooms outside our evaluation takes 2,000 AdamW [28] steps (learning rate 10⁻⁵, 3.6 GPU hours).

The band also flags failures: the 90th percentile of Eq.3 over 2,048 random queries and all heads of block 13 (Sec. S9) separates those of the full VGGT at 500 frames from its successes with an AUROC of 0.91 (Fig.1c). For a query q with logits zⱼ=q^⊤kⱼ/√d over keys k₁,…,kₙ, substituting \logaⱼ=zⱼ-\log∑_j^′e^z_j^′ into Eq.3 gives

KL(u ∥ a)=\log∑ⱼ₌₁ⁿe^zⱼ-(q^⊤k̄)/(√d)-\logn,

(10)

where k̄ is the mean key. Attention kernels already compute the first term [11], and the second is one dot product. We define the Alignment Score α as this 90th percentile in the pin pass. Available before any attach pass, it needs no training or ground truth, and a low score flags failure (Sec.4.3).

4 Experiments

一句话：VGGT 这类前馈模型一次恢复相机与几何，但跨帧注意力随帧数平方增长、长视频精度还掉。

要点：

  • 现状：VGGT 之类的前馈多视图 transformer 能一次前向恢复视频的相机与几何，但**跨帧注意力成本随帧数平方增长**，且长视频上精度会下降
  • 常见补救是在预算内近似全帧注意力，或按内容挑选少量 key
  • EcoVGGT 的假设更激进：长视频的 key 可以**不看内容就选**（pinned-key），于是推理可以做成流式

为什么值得看：「流式」是这条能不能进实时管线的分水岭：如果必须拿到整段视频才能重建，就只能离线用。把 key 选择从「看内容」变成「预置」，等于把重建变成可以边录边算的过程。

中文摘要：VGGT 这类前馈多视图 transformer 能一次前向恢复整段视频的相机与几何，但它们的跨帧注意力开销随帧数呈平方增长，长视频上的精度也会下降。现有补救大致两类：在给定预算内近似全帧注意力，或依据内容挑出少量 key。EcoVGGT 提出的假设更激进——长视频的 key 可以不看内容就预先固定（pinned-key），因此可以选择性地保持少量 key 复用，使推理变成可流式的过程：随着视频继续输入而持续产出重建结果。这决定了长视频重建能否从离线工具走进入实时管线。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·cs.CV（English）

原文发布：2026-11-16

本期推送：2026-11-17

EcoVGGT: Pinned-Key Inference for Efficient and Streamable Feed-Forward 3D Reconstruction from Long Videos

Abstract

Feed-forward multi-view transformers such as VGGT recover the cameras and geometry of a video in one pass, but the cost of their cross-frame attention grows quadratically with the frame count, and their accuracy drops on long videos. Most remedies approximate attention over all frames within a budget or select a few keys by their content. We hypothesize that the keys of a long video can be chosen without looking at its content, and our experiments on VGGT and π³ support it: a few dozen evenly spread frames can serve as the keys of every frame. We present EcoVGGT, a training-free inference framework whose keys form a Pinned Key Set of 31 such frames. A pin pass stores their tokens in a Scene Cache, and the other frames read it in independent batches that reproduce joint inference with these keys exactly, at a constant cost per frame. An Online Stream updates the pinned frames during recording. Six middle global blocks align the frames and form a reusable VGGT module: the Alignment Score reads their attention to flag failures, and Alignment Refocusing reduces them by fine-tuning only these blocks (3.6 GPU hours). EcoVGGT (π³) matches the success rate of π³ on 1,000-frame ScanNet videos at 13.8 times its speed. With refocusing, EcoVGGT (VGGT) raises the success rate of VGGT from 70% to 82% at 8.5 times its speed on 500 frames. EcoVGGT reconstructs 4,000 frames on one GPU, and EcoVGGT (π³) streams 1,000 frames at 18.6 frames per second with the lowest online absolute trajectory error.

1 Introduction

Feed-forward networks now recover 3D scenes directly from images [54, 24, 51]. Given a video, the Visual Geometry Grounded Transformer (VGGT) [51] predicts the camera pose and dense geometry of every frame in one forward pass, and later models such as π³[56], VGGT-Ω[52], and Depth Anything 3 (DA3) [26] work the same way. Their global blocks make this possible, since cross-frame self-attention lets each view draw on all other views.

We study how such a model can reconstruct every frame of a long video in one coordinate frame at a constant cost per frame. Long videos challenge these models in two ways. First, the cost of cross-frame attention grows quadratically with the number of frames, and its memory grows proportionally with every frame. A two-thousand-frame video at 518 × 392 resolution requires >80 GB GPU memory, so long videos should be split into chunks or subsampled, and subsampling leaves most frames unreconstructed. Second, accuracy suffers even when the video can fit in memory. Our evaluations show that, at 500 frames, the full VGGT keeps its trajectory error within a 0.2 m tolerance in only 70% of 50 ScanNet scenes [10]. Its predicted confidence flags failures barely better than chance (Fig.1c), so users cannot tell which results to trust.

Most existing remedies approximate attention over all frames within a budget, and each of them gives up part of this goal. Streaming variants [65, 66, 62] process each frame once as it arrives and freeze its tokens, so early errors persist. They keep at most half the scenes within tolerance (Tab.1), and InfiniteVGGT misplaces walls in two long videos (Fig.5). Chunked pipelines [14, 16] see one window at a time, so their chain of windows drifts wherever no loop closure corrects it. Token merging [39] keeps every frame in one pass and runs out of memory in most scenes at 2,000 frames. Methods that give each frame a few keys take them at fixed intervals [46, 12, 47] or select them by content, such as diverse views [63, 37] or retrieved frames [66]. Two questions remain open: whether a long video needs attention over all its frames, and whether the keys of each frame must depend on the video content.

We hypothesize that the keys of a long video can be chosen without looking at its content. One shared context of a few dozen frames, spread evenly over the video, can serve as the keys of every frame, and the other frames need not read one another. Our experiments on long indoor videos with VGGT and π³ support three of its predictions. First, with 31 to 125 evenly spread frames as the only keys, VGGT estimates relative rotations more accurately than with all frames, consistent with surplus keys diluting the attention [63, 37] (Fig.1a). With 31 keys, π³ keeps its trajectory error (Tab.1). Second, keys chosen by content perform worse than evenly spread keys. Keys from farthest-point sampling on place-recognition descriptors, as in Good Token Hunting [63], raise the trajectory error of π³ by 9.3% (Tab.5), and the 31 most-attended frames raise the relative rotation error of VGGT over sixfold (Sec.4.3). Third, keys outside the shared set do not help. Extra keys from nearby frames degrade the relative poses (Fig.1b), and prior work finds them poor substitutes for spread keys [63, 59].

If one shared context suffices, a video of any length can be reconstructed at a constant cost per frame, with attention over this context computed exactly. In this work, we propose EcoVGGT, an inference framework with three components that make it Exact, Cached, and Online. A Pinned Key Set of 31 evenly spread frames serves as the only keys, so every frame reads the whole scene in one coordinate frame, and independent batches of the other frames reproduce joint inference with these keys exactly. A pin pass stores the context of the pinned frames once in a Scene Cache, as in keyframe tracking [46], and every batch reads it. During recording, an Online Stream keeps the pinned frames spread over the whole past and caps their number. Beyond efficiency, layer analyses locate frame alignment in a band of middle global blocks [45, 61, 13], and we find that the departure of the band’s attention from uniform identifies the failures of VGGT (AUROC 0.91, Fig.1c). These findings motivate our Alignment Score, which reads this departure to flag failures, and our Alignment Refocusing, which fine-tunes only the band to reduce them.

When running offline, EcoVGGT reconstructs at least as many scenes as its backbones, at a fraction of their cost (Fig.4). With Alignment Refocusing, EcoVGGT (VGGT) raises the success rate on ScanNet from 70% to 82% at 8.5 times the speed on 500 frames and handles 4,000 frames on one GPU. Without training, EcoVGGT (π³) matches the success rate of the full π³ on 1,000 frames at 13.8 times its speed, runs faster at this length than every compared method, and has the lowest online absolute trajectory error (Tabs.1 and 2). On four other indoor datasets, it has the lowest absolute trajectory error of all chunked and streaming methods (Tab.4).

Our contributions are threefold: 1) we observe that a small number of content-agnostic, evenly spread keys outperform keys chosen by content and give VGGT lower relative rotation errors than all frames; 2) EcoVGGT, a training-free inference framework that computes attention over these keys exactly at a constant cost per frame, streams online, and can be directly applied to different backbones, including VGGT, π³, VGGT-Ω, and DA3; 3) a reusable alignment module for VGGT, whose Alignment Refocusing raises the success rate under full attention as well as under the Pinned Key Set, and whose Alignment Score flags failures without training.

2 Related work

Long-video inference

Acceleration methods for multi-view transformers [60, 51, 56, 22, 26] merge tokens [39, 41, 55] as in vision transformers [4], subsample keys and values on a spatial grid [45, 61], or skip weak interactions [49, 13]. They keep every frame in one pass, so cost and memory grow with the video length. VGG-T3[17] retrains the attention to read a fixed-size memory, while FlashVGGT [57] retrains it to read compact descriptors of all frames and a few keyframes. Streaming methods keep a spatial memory [50, 7], a learned state [53, 6], a multi-layer memory [5], or a cache of past keys and values [65, 23, 8], which later variants bound by eviction, frame selection, or retrieval [62, 44, 59, 66, 29, 34, 32, 27, 18]. Chunked pipelines join overlapping windows, offline [14] or incrementally [30, 31], and LASER [16] aligns them by rescaling each depth layer. Without loop closure, an error at one join shifts all later windows (Sec. S8).

Shared keys

Methods in which many frames read a few keys come closest to our hypothesis. KV-Tracker [46] caches the keys and values of keyframes for real-time tracking. SAIL-Recon [12] fine-tunes VGGT so that frames read the cached keys and values of 50 to 100 uniformly sampled anchor frames, while Spark3R [47] keeps those of about 40 frames at a temporal stride and finds them slightly better than random tokens. In KV-Tracker and SAIL-Recon, each frame also reads its own tokens. Good Token Hunting [63] selects one key set for all queries by farthest-point sampling on place-recognition descriptors, while DA-VGGT [37] partitions the frames into chunks of diverse views that share one anchor frame. We test whether the content of the keys matters and find that evenly spread keys outperform keys selected by descriptors on π³ and keys selected by attention on VGGT (Tab.5, Sec. S6). In EcoVGGT, they are the only keys of every frame, since a frame’s own and nearby tokens do not help it (Tab.5, Fig.1b). A pin pass computes these keys once, and independent batches of the other frames reproduce joint inference with them exactly, in one coordinate frame and at a constant cost per frame. EcoVGGT needs no training on π³, VGGT-Ω, and DA3.

Long-context attention

In transformers for text, scaling the logits by the logarithm of the input length restores the focus that the softmax loses over long inputs [9, 35], while StreamingLLM [58] keeps a few initial tokens as permanent keys next to recent ones. Multi-view models lose focus in the same way: the cross-frame attention of VGGT collapses toward rank one over hundreds of frames [39, 25], and redundant views dilute it [37]. Layer analyses find that middle global blocks align the views [45, 61, 13] and attend selectively [34, 32], which they use to thin the attention or the cache. Partial fine-tuning has adapted the image encoder with low-rank adapters for finer geometry [38, 20] and the middle blocks of VGGT for dynamic scenes [64]. Uncertainty estimates use the often overconfident predicted confidence [15], trained adapters [1], or perturbed reruns [33], while VGGT-SLAM 2.0 [31] verifies loop closures with one attention layer. Our Alignment Score reads the attention of the alignment band in one pass to flag failures without training, and our Alignment Refocusing fine-tunes the band’s six blocks alone to align distant views.
