It trains on samples with the structure of inference, so that the band learns to align through pinned keys. Over a whole scan or a random contiguous half, we pin 24 evenly spread frames ℙ and draw 24 random others A that read only these keys, and we minimize the losses of VGGT [51] over the band,

L=λ L_cam(ℙ∪A)+L_depth(ℝ),

(9)

where L_cam and L_depth are the camera and depth losses of VGGT with camera weight λ=5, and the depth loss on only six random frames ℝ of ℙ∪A bounds memory. Training on 195 ScanNet scans of rooms outside our evaluation takes 2,000 AdamW [28] steps (learning rate 10⁻⁵, 3.6 GPU hours).

3.7 Alignment Score

The band also flags failures: the 90th percentile of Eq.3 over 2,048 random queries and all heads of block 13 (Sec. S9) separates those of the full VGGT at 500 frames from its successes with an AUROC of 0.91 (Fig.1c). For a query q with logits zⱼ=q^⊤kⱼ/√d over keys k₁,…,kₙ, substituting \logaⱼ=zⱼ-\log∑_j^′e^z_j^′ into Eq.3 gives

KL(u ∥ a)=\log∑ⱼ₌₁ⁿe^zⱼ-(q^⊤k̄)/(√d)-\logn,

(10)

where k̄ is the mean key. Attention kernels already compute the first term [11], and the second is one dot product. We define the Alignment Score α as this 90th percentile in the pin pass. Available before any attach pass, it needs no training or ground truth, and a low score flags failure (Sec.4.3).

4 Experiments

item.title: 像素空间视频扩散不必复杂：JVT 只用一个大 patch 的 DiT，不要自编码器、不要级联、不要 U-Net 跳连 ｜ JVT: Just Video Transformer makes pixel-space video diffusion simple
item.description:
一句话：在原始高维视频上直接做扩散很难，现有像素空间方法大多靠专门架构兜底。

要点：

  • 直接对高维原始视频做扩散建模很难，因此现有**像素空间**方法往往依赖专门设计的架构（细节修补器、级联阶段、U-Net 式跳连）
  • JVT 反过来做减法：一个**大 patch 的 DiT 式 transformer**，去掉预训练自编码器、辅助细节器、级联阶段与 U-Net 跳连
  • 论文系统性地考察了视频 patch 的嵌入方式等因素，说明「简单结构 + 正确 patch 化」就能支撑像素空间扩散

为什么值得看：像素空间扩散直接绕开了 VAE 带来的粒度与延迟问题（11-15 那篇 PixVid 就在处理这个），而 JVT 说明它不必用复杂架构实现。两条放在一起看：像素空间正在变成可选项，而不是妥协。

中文摘要：直接在高维原始视频上做扩散建模很困难，因此现有的像素空间方法往往依赖特制的架构组件——预训练自编码器、辅助的细节生成器、级联式多阶段流程，或 U-Net 风格的跳连。JVT（Just Video Transformer）反过来做减法：它是一个结构简单的、大 patch 的 DiT 式 transformer，在像素空间直接做视频扩散，不使用预训练自编码器、辅助细节器、级联阶段与 U-Net 跳连。文中还系统考察了视频 patch 的嵌入方式等设计选择，说明「结构足够简单 + patch 化处理正确」本身就足以支撑像素空间扩散。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·cs.CV（English）

原文发布：2026-11-16

本期推送：2026-11-17

JVT: Just Video Transformer makes
pixel-space video diffusion simple

Abstract

Direct diffusion modeling of high-dimensional raw video data is challenging, and existing pixel-space methods often rely on specialized architectures. We introduce JVT (Just Video Transformer), a simple large-patch DiT-style Transformer for pixel-space video diffusion, without a pretrained autoencoder, auxiliary detailers, cascaded stages, or U-Net-style skip connections. We systematically examine video patch embeddings, register tokens, and adaptive layer normalization to identify design choices that balance generation quality and computational efficiency. The resulting JVT design achieves generation quality competitive with latent diffusion baselines in both class-conditioned and unconditional settings. The pixel-space formulation of JVT also naturally supports joint generation of pixel-aligned modalities. We demonstrate this capability through camera-conditioned RGB-disparity generation, which improves camera following relative to RGB-only baselines and yields explicit scene geometry without an additional reconstruction model at inference. These results highlight the potential of simple DiT-style Transformers for pixel-space video diffusion, and we hope our findings offer useful insights and practical guidance for future research.

1 Introduction

Diffusion and flow-based models have become leading paradigms for visual generative modeling, driven by rapid advances in algorithm designs and model architectures. Early diffusion models [(Ho et al., 2020; Dhariwal and Nichol, 2021)] operate directly on pixels with classical U-Nets [(Ronneberger et al., 2015)], but struggle with efficiency and fidelity at high resolutions. To alleviate this difficulty, latent diffusion moves denoising from pixel space to a compact latent space produced by a separately trained autoencoder [(Rombach et al., 2022)]. Combined with the Diffusion Transformer (DiT) architecture [(Peebles and Xie, 2023)], this formulation has become a standard design for high-resolution visual generation.

Despite its efficiency, latent diffusion is inherently bounded by the autoencoder, including reconstruction error [(Yu et al., 2026; Zheng et al., 2026)], additional training and inference costs [(Leng et al., 2025; Cheng and Yuan, 2025; Wang et al., 2026c)], and limited cross-modal capability for joint modeling [(Bounoua et al., 2024; Qiu et al., 2025)]. Thus recent works revisit pixel-space diffusion and demonstrate competitive quality on image generation [(Li and He, 2026; Yu et al., 2026; Lu et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026b)]. In contrast, video generation is still dominated by latent DiTs [(Ma et al., 2025; Kong et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2025; Wan et al., 2025)], while pixel-space models mostly retain U-Net-style skip connections [(Gu et al., 2024; Bar-Tal et al., 2024; Hoogeboom et al., 2025)] or cascaded generation [(Menapace et al., 2024; Skorokhodov et al., 2024)]. This motivates us to investigate how far a simple DiT-style Transformer can go in direct pixel-space video generation.

We introduce JVT, a pixel-space video generative model built on a simple DiT-style Transformer backbone, without detailers, cascaded stages or U-Net-style skip connections. Following JiT [(Li and He, 2026)], JVT predicts clean videos from noisy pixels under a rectified-flow objective. To make raw videos tractable, we explore variants of video patch embedding for efficient spatiotemporal downsampling. We further examine the design choices of register tokens [(Darcet et al., 2024)] and adaptive layer normalization (AdaLN) [(Peebles and Xie, 2023)], which can carry noise level or class condition and amplify it by register guidance [(Starodubcev et al., 2026)] or classifier-free guidance [(Ho and Salimans, 2021)]. With these design choices, JVT achieves generation quality competitive with latent diffusion baselines in both class-conditioned and unconditional settings.

Pixel-space video modeling also provides a direct interface for jointly generating video and pixel-aligned modalities, which typically requires reusing an RGB-specific autoencoder in latent diffusion [(Ke et al., 2024; Zhu et al., 2025; Huang et al., 2026a)]. We extend JVT to camera-conditioned joint RGB-disparity generation to demonstrate this cross-modal capability. Without an additional reconstruction model at inference, the generated disparity yields a sequence of point clouds in world coordinates, which enables explicit 4D world modeling. Experiments further show that joint RGB-disparity generation improves camera following relative to RGB-only JVT.

The main contributions of this work are as follows:

  • •

    We present JVT, the first pixel-space video diffusion model built on a simple DiT-style Transformer backbone, without detailers, cascaded stages, or U-Net-style skip connections.

  • •

    We systematically study video patch embeddings and conditioning mechanisms, identifying designs that improve the quality-efficiency trade-off. In class-conditioned and unconditional settings, JVT achieves generation quality competitive with latent diffusion baselines.

  • •

    We formulate pixel-aligned joint generation as a native extension of JVT. We further demonstrate this capability through camera-conditioned RGB-disparity video generation, which enables explicit 4D scene representation and improves camera following relative to RGB-only generation.

    • 2 Related Work

    High-resolution pixel-space diffusion. Pixel-space diffusion modeling for high-resolution visual data has long relied on specialized architectures, including cascaded diffusion [(Ho et al., 2022a; Teng et al., 2024)], cross-resolution designs [(Gu et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2025b)], multiscale or U-shaped backbones [(Hoogeboom et al., 2023; Crowson et al., 2024; Hoogeboom et al., 2025; He et al., 2026; Guo et al., 2026)], frequency decomposition [(Ma et al., 2026b; Lin et al., 2026; Ma et al., 2026a)], and auxiliary detail modules [(Wang et al., 2026a; Chen et al., 2026; Yu et al., 2026)]. Though effective, these approaches often introduce additional architectural or training complexity, which can limit efficiency and scalability. Recently, JiT [(Li and He, 2026)] achieves high-resolution image generation competitive with latent diffusion using a simple large-patch DiT-style Transformer. This paradigm is also extended to one-step image generation [(Lu et al., 2026)] and text-to-image generation [(Wang et al., 2026b; Jiang et al., 2026)], further demonstrating the effectiveness.

    Video Transformer architectures. Modern video Transformers largely retain the standard blocks of 2D Vision Transformers (ViTs), making patch embedding the key adaptation to video inputs [(Tong et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2023; Bardes et al., 2024; Assran et al., 2025)]. A common choice is tubelet embedding [(Arnab et al., 2021)], which encodes non-overlapping spatiotemporal patches into tokens via 3D convolution. This architecture is also widely adopted in latent video DiTs, whereas pixel-space video diffusion methods still typically rely on U-shaped architectures [(Gu et al., 2024; Bar-Tal et al., 2024; Hoogeboom et al., 2025)] or cascaded generation [(Menapace et al., 2024; Skorokhodov et al., 2024)]. Our work aims to explore whether a simple DiT-style video Transformer can also support direct pixel-space video generation.

    3 Method

    3.1 Preliminaries

    Though denoising diffusion models commonly use noise, score or velocity prediction [(Dhariwal and Nichol, 2021; Song et al., 2021; Karras et al., 2022; Salimans and Ho, 2022; Lipman et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2023)], JiT proposes clean data prediction and velocity loss supervision for pixel-space diffusion [(Li and He, 2026)]. Following this formulation, JVT predicts clean video x̂₀ from noisy pixels xₜ:

    xₜ=(1-t)x₀+tε, x̂₀=f_θ(xₜ,t,c), v̂=(x̂₀-xₜ)/t,

    		(1)

    where noise ε∼ℕ(0,I), noise level t∈(0,1], and c denotes the available conditioning. Thus the standard rectified-flow velocity loss can be represented as:

    L_MSE=𝔼∥v̂-v∥₂²=𝔼∥(x̂₀-x₀)/t∥₂², v=x₀-ε=(x₀-xₜ)/t.

    		(2)

    3.2 Patch Embedding

    Patch embedding is central to pixel-space DiTs, as it provides the initial downsampling that latent DiTs obtain from an autoencoder. For videos, it also aggregates spatiotemporal information while controlling the token sequence length.

    Following standard video Transformer designs, we use plain tubelet embedding as our baseline. As illustrated in Fig. 3 (a), it uses a single 3D convolution to project each non-overlapping patch of temporal size pₜ and spatial size pₕ×p_w into a C-dimensional token.

    Bottleneck structure. Following JiT [(Li and He, 2026)], we introduce a channel bottleneck into tubelet embedding (Fig. 3 (b)). A 3D convolution first projects each patch into a C_b-dimensional representation, which is then expanded to C channels by a pointwise projection. We typically choose C_b

    Spatiotemporal factorization. Inspired by the factorization principle of depthwise separable convolution [(Chollet, 2017; Howard et al., 2017)], we separate the spatial and temporal operations of tubelet embedding. Specifically, a patch-wise 2D convolution extracts spatial features within each frame, while a frame-wise 1D convolution aggregates temporal information at each spatial location. Applying the spatial operation first yields patch-first embedding (Fig. 3 (c)), while reversing the order yields frame-first embedding (Fig. 3 (d)).

    3.3 Register Tokens

    Register tokens provide additional computational slots in ViTs [(Darcet et al., 2024)] and also support in-context conditioning and improve generation quality in pixel-space image DiTs [(Li and He, 2026; Starodubcev et al., 2026)]. We extend this mechanism to JVT and examine its roles in conditioning and sampling guidance.

    As illustrated in Fig. 2, given L=L₁+L₂ Transformer blocks, register tokens are prepended to the visual sequence after the first L₁ blocks and discarded after the remaining L₂ blocks. Let X^(L₁)∈ℝ^N×C denote the N visual tokens at the insertion point and R₀∈ℝ^ℓᵣ×C the ℓᵣ learnable base registers. With eₜ,e_y∈ℝ^C denoting the noise level and class embeddings, respectively, we construct the register tokens and augmented sequence as

    R=R₀+Repeat(eᵣ,ℓᵣ), X̃^(L₁)=Concat(R,X^(L₁)),

    		(3)

    where eᵣ∈{0,eₜ,e_y,eₜ+e_y} and Repeat(eᵣ,ℓᵣ) replicates eᵣ across the ℓᵣ register positions. Setting eᵣ=0 preserves R=R₀ without adding a conditioning embedding, which is different from removing the registers. For eᵣ∈{eₜ,e_y,eₜ+e_y}, the register tokens provide an additional conditioning pathway alongside AdaLN.

    Register guidance. We also apply register guidance (RG) [(Starodubcev et al., 2026)] during sampling. For the same noisy input and condition, let vᵣ and vₙᵣ denote the velocity predictions of the same model with and without registers, respectively. RG amplifies the register contribution through

    v_rg=vᵣ+w_rg(vᵣ-vₙᵣ), w_rg≥0.

    		(4)

    For conditional generation, let vᵤ denote the unconditional velocity prediction with registers retained. Combining RG with classifier-free guidance (CFG) [(Ho and Salimans, 2021)] gives

    v_cfg+rg=vᵤ+w_cfg(vᵣ-vᵤ)+w_rg(vᵣ-vₙᵣ).

    		(5)

    The scales w_cfg and w_rg separately weight the CFG and RG terms: setting w_rg=0 recovers CFG, while w_cfg=1 recovers RG in Eq. (4). Unlike the original RG procedure [(Starodubcev et al., 2026)], which randomly drops registers during training, we keep them active throughout training and remove them only to compute vₙᵣ during sampling. Our experiments show that RG remains effective without register dropout during training.

    3.4 Pixel-aligned Joint Generation

    Pixel-aligned signals about geometry, motion, and semantic structure provide complementary cues for video generation. By channel-wise concatenating RGB frames with these signals [(Ke et al., 2024)], diffusion models can jointly generate RGB content and spatially aligned auxiliary modalities [(Zhu et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2025a; Huang et al., 2026a)].

    Pixel-space modeling allows these modalities to be represented on a shared spatiotemporal grid without an RGB-specific autoencoder. After modality-specific normalization, we concatenate an RGB video x_rgb∈ℝ^T×3×H×W with M pixel-aligned modalities along the channel dimension:

    x₀=[x_rgb;x⁽¹⁾;…;x^(M)]∈ℝ^T×Cⱼₒᵢₙₜ×H×W,

    		(6)

    where x⁽ᵐ⁾∈ℝ^T×Cₘ×H×W denotes the m-th aligned modality and Cⱼₒᵢₙₜ=3+∑ₘ₌₁^MCₘ is the total number of channels. These modalities may include depth, surface normals, ray maps, segmentation masks, and optical flow. All modalities share the same noise level and are predicted jointly during denoising.

    We instantiate this formulation with RGB and disparity, a reparameterization of depth, for camera-conditioned video generation (Sec. 4.3). At inference, we convert the predicted disparity back to depth and unproject it using the camera parameters. Combined with the generated RGB frames, this yields a sequence of colored point clouds without an additional reconstruction model.

    4 Experiments

    4.1 Main Results

    Datasets. For class-conditioned generation and unconditional generation, we conduct experiments on four datasets: UCF-101 [(Soomro et al., 2012)], FaceForensics [(Rössler et al., 2018)], SkyTimelapse [(Xiong et al., 2018)], and Taichi-HD [(Siarohin et al., 2019)]. Following settings of previous works [(Skorokhodov et al., 2022; Ma et al., 2025)], we use both training and test splits of UCF-101, and only the training split of the other datasets. We randomly extract 16-frame video clips with a frame interval of 3, and resize all video frames to 256×256 resolution for training.

    Evaluation metrics. We evaluate generation quality with Fréchet Video Distance (FVD) [(Unterthiner et al., 2019)], using 2,048 generated samples. For efficiency metrics, we report parameter count, floating point operations (FLOPs), peak allocated GPU memory and inference latency. Additional details about these metrics are given in Appendix (A.2, A.4).

    Baselines. Our main baseline is Latte [(Ma et al., 2025)], a representative DiT-based latent diffusion model. Other competing methods include GAN-based methods [(Skorokhodov et al., 2022; Yu et al., 2022)], autoregressive models [(Yan et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2024a)], U-Net-based latent diffusion [(He et al., 2022; Yu et al., 2023b)] and DiT-based latent diffusion [(Liu et al., 2024)].

    Tab. 1 reports class-conditioned results on UCF-101 and unconditional results on the four datasets. JVT outperforms all competing methods in the table, demonstrating the effectiveness of direct pixel-space video modeling. Additional qualitative results are provided in Fig. 8 of the Appendix.

    4.2 Ablation Study

    Video patch embedding. We compare the tubelet, patch-first, and frame-first embeddings introduced in Sec. 3.2 while varying the bottleneck width C_b. Under identical training settings, all bottlenecked variants in Tab. 2 achieve lower final training loss than the plain tubelet baseline. With an appropriate choice of C_b, tubelet and patch-first embeddings also improve FVD while reducing computational cost. Taking both generation quality and efficiency into consideration, we adopt patch-first embedding with C_b=32 as the default configuration for JVT. Further patch embedding ablation details are provided in Appendix A.3.

    Register tokens and guidance. In Tab. 3, we ablate both the information carried by register tokens and the effect of register guidance (RG) in class-conditioned generation. Under the default 50-step Euler sampling setup, adding registers without RG yields no FVD improvement over the register-free baseline. With RG, however, all tested register variants outperform this baseline, regardless of the conditioning information they carry. The 50-step Heun and 100-step Euler results further show that RG retains its advantage over higher-NFE baselines using more sampling steps or a higher-order solver, consistent with findings of prior works [(Reynaud et al., 2024; Lu et al., 2025; Salajegheh and Mudur, 2026)].

    Although prior studies demonstrate the effectiveness of in-context class conditioning for pixel-space image generation [(Starodubcev et al., 2026; Li and He, 2026; Lu et al., 2026)], we observe no clear benefit from any of the three variants of register-based conditioning in Tab. 3. Instead, registers with eᵣ=0 achieve the lowest FVD of 129.2. These results suggest that, under this sampling setup, the benefits of register tokens depend on RG, rather than register-based conditioning..

    As shown in Tab. 1, RG works well on UCF-101, but brings no obvious gains on the other 3 datasets. Without register guidance, JVT variants with and without registers exhibit broadly similar FVD scores and intermediate feature-map smoothness. However, as illustrated in Fig. 4, visual tokens attend strongly to register tokens immediately after their insertion (L₁=9) on UCF-101, while this interaction is noticeably weaker on FaceForensics, SkyTimelapse, and Taichi-HD.

    This dataset-dependent difference may be attributed to the global semantics encoded by register tokens [(Starodubcev et al., 2026)]. UCF-101 spans 101 action categories and exhibits greater semantic diversity than the other three datasets. We hypothesize that this diversity, together with stronger patch-to-register interactions, makes the register-enabled prediction vᵣ a more informative guide for its register-free counterpart vₙᵣ. In contrast, the more homogeneous semantics of the other datasets may limit the benefits of RG.

    Adaptive layer normalization. Standard DiTs inject noise level and class information through adaptive layer normalization (AdaLN) [(Peebles and Xie, 2023)]. However, recent works start to explore AdaLN-free DiTs for image generation, using in-context tokens, cross-attention, or multimodal joint attention for conditioning [(Geng et al., 2026; Lu et al., 2026; Zeng et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026b)]. In Tab. 4, we examine whether register-based conditioning offers a reliable alternative to AdaLN in JVT. Relative to the baseline, neither adding class-conditioned registers nor removing noise level conditioning improves FVD. With class-only conditioning, replacing AdaLN with register tokens further worsens FVD to 156.3. We also observe no clear efficiency gain from removing AdaLN. Unconditional ablations show no consistent FVD improvement from jointly removing noise level conditioning and AdaLN (Appendix A.3, Tab. 11). These results support retaining standard AdaLN as JVT’s default conditioning mechanism.

    4.3 Camera-conditioned Video Generation

    We instantiate the pixel-aligned joint generation framework in Sec. 3.4 for camera-conditioned video generation. Given an initial RGB frame and a target camera trajectory, we jointly generate RGB frames and aligned disparity maps. After recovering depth from disparity, the camera parameters allow the predictions to be unprojected into a sequence of colored point clouds, providing an explicit 4D representation of the generated scene, as shown in Fig. 5.

    Experimental setting. We conduct 8-frame camera-conditioned video generation experiments on RealEstate10K [(Zhou et al., 2018)] at a resolution of 256×256. As dense depth annotations are unavailable, a frozen lightweight 3D reconstruction model, Pi3X [(Wang et al., 2026d)] supplies depth targets online during training. Following prior works [(Song et al., 2026; Zhu et al., 2025)], we reversibly transform depth D to square-root disparity d=(D+1)^-1/2 and concatenate it with RGB as a four-channel target.

    Evaluation. We evaluate RGB video quality using FVD, and assess camera following by comparing Pi3X-estimated relative poses with the target camera trajectory. Following prior works [(Wang et al., 2024b; Wang et al., 2025a; Wang et al., 2026d)], we report relative rotation accuracy (RRA), relative translation accuracy (RTA), and AUC as camera-following metrics. Specifically, RRA and RTA measure the percentages of evaluated frame pairs whose rotation and translation-direction errors fall below a given threshold, respectively, while AUC summarizes their joint error distribution. We use thresholds of 5^∘ and 30^∘.

    We compare JVT with pixel-space U-ViT models [(Song et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2026)] and a latent-space DiT [(Huang et al., 2026b)]. As shown in Tab. 5, both JVT variants achieve lower FVD than these baselines. Joint RGB-disparity generation achieves the highest RTA and AUC among all compared methods, with only a slight increase in FVD relative to RGB-only JVT. The qualitative results in Fig. 6 further illustrate the differences in camera following.

    Across methods, RRA is consistently high, whereas RTA remains substantially lower. This gap highlights a key limitation of these camera-conditioned video generators: they can follow prescribed camera rotations relatively reliably, but are less accurate at reproducing camera translations. Joint RGB-disparity generation narrows this gap, suggesting that explicit depth cues help the model relate camera motion to scene geometry. Within a unified pixel-space generative framework, JVT natively supports this joint modeling of RGB and geometry and improves camera following.

    5 Conclusion

    We demonstrate pixel-space video generation with a simple DiT-style Transformer, achieving generation quality competitive with latent diffusion baselines in both class-conditioned and unconditional video generation benchmarks. Our ablations study suggests patch-first embedding for spatiotemporal tokenization and standard AdaLN for conditioning. For the register mechanism, register-free JVT provides an acceptable baseline, while register guidance can offer additional gains, particularly on the more diverse UCF-101 dataset.

    Pixel-space modeling makes pixel-aligned joint generation straightforward by representing RGB and aligned modalities on a common spatiotemporal grid, without encoding them into a shared pretrained latent space. When extending JVT to camera-conditioned joint RGB-disparity generation, we find camera following is improved relative to RGB-only baselines, with a small FVD trade-off.

    These findings highlight the potential of simple DiT-style Transformers for pixel-space video generation and pixel-aligned joint modeling. We hope our empirical findings help guide future efforts to scale pixel-space video generation to larger model size, more datasets, longer videos and higher resolutions.

    （参考文献见原文。）

    Appendix A Appendix

    A.1 Implementation Details

    Our implementation follows the pixel-space clean-data prediction design of JiT [(Li and He, 2026)], with video generation and camera conditioning implemented in the DFoT framework [(Song et al., 2025)]. Tab. 6 specifies model and optimization configurations.

    Register tokens.

    As shown in Fig. 4, the register mechanism brings clear gains on UCF-101 but only limited benefits on the other datasets, so we use register tokens only for class-conditioned and unconditional video generation on UCF-101. The register initialization ablation in Tab. 3 further shows no gain from injecting the timestep or class embedding into the register tokens, and we therefore just set eᵣ=0 when registers are used. The base registers R₀ are learnable tokens initialized i.i.d. from a zero-mean Gaussian with standard deviation 0.02. All register-equipped variants are sampled with register guidance, whose scale is selected by a linear search with a step size of 0.1.

    Training details. All models are trained from scratch. Following JiT [(Li and He, 2026)], we use clean data prediction and velocity MSE loss. For noise sampling, we sample noise level t_base from logit-normal distribution [(Esser et al., 2024)] and shift it with noise shift s, as shown in Eq. (7). Our full-scale training of JVT use a global batch size of 256 with 8 NVIDIA 80GB GPUs, while some ablations use a batch size of 40 on a single GPU (Fig. 7).

    t=(s·t_base)/(1+(s-1)·t_base)

    		(7)

    For camera-conditioned generation, we sample the video noise independently for each frame, following DFoT [(Song et al., 2025)]. We also adopt the data augmentations of the DFoT dataloader: horizontal flipping and temporal reversal, each applied with probability 0.5, and back-and-forth augmentation with probability 0.1.

    Sampling configurations. Tab. 7 specifies the exact sampling configuration of each main result. We use the Euler solver for class-conditioned and camera-conditioned generation, and the Heun solver for unconditional generation. All samplers run for 50 denoising steps, with the timestep schedule shifted by the noise shift s (Eq. (7)). Depending on the task, we apply classifier-free guidance (CFG) [(Ho and Salimans, 2021)], register guidance (RG) [(Starodubcev et al., 2026)], or history guidance (HG) [(Song et al., 2025)]. The CFG scale is selected by a linear search with a step size of 1, and the RG scale with a step size of 0.1. For FVD evaluation, we generate 2,048 clips per method and use the same number of real clips as the reference.

    Geometry annotation for RealEstate10K. As in Sec. 4.3, dense depth annotations are unavailable for RealEstate10K, so we use a frozen Pi3X [(Wang et al., 2026d)] to supply depth pseudo-labels online during training. For each training clip, Pi3X is conditioned on the prescribed camera intrinsics and extrinsics as priors. Since Pi3X predicts scale-invariant geometry and affine-invariant cameras, we estimate the global scale of the predicted depth by aligning the predicted cameras with the ground-truth cameras. The aligned depth is clamped to a minimum of 10⁻⁵ and, following prior works [(Song et al., 2026; Zhu et al., 2025)], reversibly transformed to square-root disparity d=(D+1)^-1/2, which is concatenated with RGB as a four-channel target.

    A.2 Efficiency Evaluation Details

    The efficiency experiments use JVT-XL with 28 Transformer blocks, width 1,152, 16 attention heads, and spatial patch size 16. Each case processes one 16-frame 256×256 video in pixel space. With a temporal downsampling factor of 4, the denoiser receives 1,024 visual tokens. The register-enabled configuration inserts 32 in-context register tokens after the first 9 blocks, resulting in 1,056 tokens for the remaining blocks.

    Sampling uses Euler integration with 50 steps. Register-enabled cases include no guidance, CFG, RG, and CFG+RG, while register-disabled cases include no guidance and CFG. These four guidance settings use one, two, two, and three denoiser-forward equivalents per step, respectively.

    All measurements use bfloat16 with TF32 enabled and torch.compile disabled on one NVIDIA 4090 GPU. Each case runs in a fresh Python process. Denoiser latency uses 20 warm-up iterations followed by 100 timed iterations, and sampling latency uses 5 warm-up samples followed by 20 timed samples. The complete matrix is repeated in three independent sweeps. We record model parameters, FLOPs, baseline and peak allocated GPU memory, incremental peak memory, latency statistics, and throughput. FLOPs for one denoiser forward pass are counted with torch.utils.flop_counter.FlopCounterMode. Sampling FLOPs are computed from the matching denoiser FLOPs, 50 sampling steps, and the number of denoiser-forward equivalents per step.

    Tab. 8 covers the ten embedding configurations in Tab. 2, with additional register-free measurements for five of them. Tab. 9 reports the corresponding 30 sampling measurements.

    A.3 Additional Ablations

    Figure 7 gives the bottleneck width sweep curve. In this experiment, we use batch size of 40, different from the full-scale experiments in Tab. 2 with global batch size 256. For tubelet and patch-first embedding, FVD varies non-monotonically with C_b: an overly narrow bottleneck may discard task-relevant spatiotemporal information, whereas an excessively wide bottleneck offers limited additional benefit. As for frame-first embedding, FVD improves progressively as C_b increases, but the efficiency metrics declines sharply.

    Tab. 10 and Tab. 11 repeat the register and AdaLN ablations of Tab. 3 and Tab. 4 (Sec. 4.2) for unconditional video generation. As shown in Tab. 10, the gains from registers are dataset-dependent: register guidance substantially improves UCF-101 but brings marginal or no improvement on FaceForensics, SkyTimelapse and Taichi-HD. The AdaLN ablation in Tab. 11 leads to the same conclusion as in the class-conditioned case: simply removing AdaLN without scaling parameters commonly degrades FVD, supporting standard AdaLN as the default conditioning mechanism.

    Prior work on text-to-image generation has shown that, under matched parameter counts, AdaLN-free variants can outperform their standard AdaLN counterparts [(Wang et al., 2026b)]. However, such a parameter-matched comparison is not compute-matched: AdaLN accounts for a considerable fraction of the model parameters, yet it is merely a linear layer with linear computational complexity. Matching the parameter count of an AdaLN-free variant to the baseline therefore substantially enlarges the quadratic-complexity attention blocks, leading to a marked increase in overall computation. For this reason, the AdaLN-free variants in Tab. 4 and Tab. 11 are instead compared against standard JVT with the same number of Transformer layers.

    A.4 Additional FVD Results

    Training strategies and algorithm designs greatly affect model performance. Some methods adopt the image-video joint training strategy proposed in VDM [(Ho et al., 2022b)], which markedly improves video generation quality and can also be incorporated into our method. Tab. 13 compares our method without the joint training strategy against these methods. We further compare our method with recent hybrid approaches of autoregressive modeling and diffusion, and show the results in Tab. 14.

    Different evaluation protocols can also directly influence the reported FVD scores. Following StyleGAN-V [(Skorokhodov et al., 2022)] and Latte [(Ma et al., 2025)], we compute FVD using 2048 generated video samples (FVD@2048), whereas several other methods use 10000 samples (FVD@10000). Since the original FVD paper [(Unterthiner et al., 2019)] shows that the number of samples used for evaluation can greatly affect the FVD score, we additionally report our FVD@10000 result in Tab. 15.
item.content:encoded:
一句话：在原始高维视频上直接做扩散很难，现有像素空间方法大多靠专门架构兜底。

要点：

  • 直接对高维原始视频做扩散建模很难，因此现有**像素空间**方法往往依赖专门设计的架构（细节修补器、级联阶段、U-Net 式跳连）
  • JVT 反过来做减法：一个**大 patch 的 DiT 式 transformer**，去掉预训练自编码器、辅助细节器、级联阶段与 U-Net 跳连
  • 论文系统性地考察了视频 patch 的嵌入方式等因素，说明「简单结构 + 正确 patch 化」就能支撑像素空间扩散

为什么值得看：像素空间扩散直接绕开了 VAE 带来的粒度与延迟问题（11-15 那篇 PixVid 就在处理这个），而 JVT 说明它不必用复杂架构实现。两条放在一起看：像素空间正在变成可选项，而不是妥协。

中文摘要：直接在高维原始视频上做扩散建模很困难，因此现有的像素空间方法往往依赖特制的架构组件——预训练自编码器、辅助的细节生成器、级联式多阶段流程，或 U-Net 风格的跳连。JVT（Just Video Transformer）反过来做减法：它是一个结构简单的、大 patch 的 DiT 式 transformer，在像素空间直接做视频扩散，不使用预训练自编码器、辅助细节器、级联阶段与 U-Net 跳连。文中还系统考察了视频 patch 的嵌入方式等设计选择，说明「结构足够简单 + patch 化处理正确」本身就足以支撑像素空间扩散。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·cs.CV（English）

原文发布：2026-11-16

本期推送：2026-11-17

JVT: Just Video Transformer makes
pixel-space video diffusion simple

Abstract

Direct diffusion modeling of high-dimensional raw video data is challenging, and existing pixel-space methods often rely on specialized architectures. We introduce JVT (Just Video Transformer), a simple large-patch DiT-style Transformer for pixel-space video diffusion, without a pretrained autoencoder, auxiliary detailers, cascaded stages, or U-Net-style skip connections. We systematically examine video patch embeddings, register tokens, and adaptive layer normalization to identify design choices that balance generation quality and computational efficiency. The resulting JVT design achieves generation quality competitive with latent diffusion baselines in both class-conditioned and unconditional settings. The pixel-space formulation of JVT also naturally supports joint generation of pixel-aligned modalities. We demonstrate this capability through camera-conditioned RGB-disparity generation, which improves camera following relative to RGB-only baselines and yields explicit scene geometry without an additional reconstruction model at inference. These results highlight the potential of simple DiT-style Transformers for pixel-space video diffusion, and we hope our findings offer useful insights and practical guidance for future research.

1 Introduction

Diffusion and flow-based models have become leading paradigms for visual generative modeling, driven by rapid advances in algorithm designs and model architectures. Early diffusion models [(Ho et al., 2020; Dhariwal and Nichol, 2021)] operate directly on pixels with classical U-Nets [(Ronneberger et al., 2015)], but struggle with efficiency and fidelity at high resolutions. To alleviate this difficulty, latent diffusion moves denoising from pixel space to a compact latent space produced by a separately trained autoencoder [(Rombach et al., 2022)]. Combined with the Diffusion Transformer (DiT) architecture [(Peebles and Xie, 2023)], this formulation has become a standard design for high-resolution visual generation.

Despite its efficiency, latent diffusion is inherently bounded by the autoencoder, including reconstruction error [(Yu et al., 2026; Zheng et al., 2026)], additional training and inference costs [(Leng et al., 2025; Cheng and Yuan, 2025; Wang et al., 2026c)], and limited cross-modal capability for joint modeling [(Bounoua et al., 2024; Qiu et al., 2025)]. Thus recent works revisit pixel-space diffusion and demonstrate competitive quality on image generation [(Li and He, 2026; Yu et al., 2026; Lu et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026b)]. In contrast, video generation is still dominated by latent DiTs [(Ma et al., 2025; Kong et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2025; Wan et al., 2025)], while pixel-space models mostly retain U-Net-style skip connections [(Gu et al., 2024; Bar-Tal et al., 2024; Hoogeboom et al., 2025)] or cascaded generation [(Menapace et al., 2024; Skorokhodov et al., 2024)]. This motivates us to investigate how far a simple DiT-style Transformer can go in direct pixel-space video generation.

We introduce JVT, a pixel-space video generative model built on a simple DiT-style Transformer backbone, without detailers, cascaded stages or U-Net-style skip connections. Following JiT [(Li and He, 2026)], JVT predicts clean videos from noisy pixels under a rectified-flow objective. To make raw videos tractable, we explore variants of video patch embedding for efficient spatiotemporal downsampling. We further examine the design choices of register tokens [(Darcet et al., 2024)] and adaptive layer normalization (AdaLN) [(Peebles and Xie, 2023)], which can carry noise level or class condition and amplify it by register guidance [(Starodubcev et al., 2026)] or classifier-free guidance [(Ho and Salimans, 2021)]. With these design choices, JVT achieves generation quality competitive with latent diffusion baselines in both class-conditioned and unconditional settings.

Pixel-space video modeling also provides a direct interface for jointly generating video and pixel-aligned modalities, which typically requires reusing an RGB-specific autoencoder in latent diffusion [(Ke et al., 2024; Zhu et al., 2025; Huang et al., 2026a)]. We extend JVT to camera-conditioned joint RGB-disparity generation to demonstrate this cross-modal capability. Without an additional reconstruction model at inference, the generated disparity yields a sequence of point clouds in world coordinates, which enables explicit 4D world modeling. Experiments further show that joint RGB-disparity generation improves camera following relative to RGB-only JVT.

The main contributions of this work are as follows:

  • •

    We present JVT, the first pixel-space video diffusion model built on a simple DiT-style Transformer backbone, without detailers, cascaded stages, or U-Net-style skip connections.

  • •

    We systematically study video patch embeddings and conditioning mechanisms, identifying designs that improve the quality-efficiency trade-off. In class-conditioned and unconditional settings, JVT achieves generation quality competitive with latent diffusion baselines.

  • •

    We formulate pixel-aligned joint generation as a native extension of JVT. We further demonstrate this capability through camera-conditioned RGB-disparity video generation, which enables explicit 4D scene representation and improves camera following relative to RGB-only generation.

    • 2 Related Work

    High-resolution pixel-space diffusion. Pixel-space diffusion modeling for high-resolution visual data has long relied on specialized architectures, including cascaded diffusion [(Ho et al., 2022a; Teng et al., 2024)], cross-resolution designs [(Gu et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2025b)], multiscale or U-shaped backbones [(Hoogeboom et al., 2023; Crowson et al., 2024; Hoogeboom et al., 2025; He et al., 2026; Guo et al., 2026)], frequency decomposition [(Ma et al., 2026b; Lin et al., 2026; Ma et al., 2026a)], and auxiliary detail modules [(Wang et al., 2026a; Chen et al., 2026; Yu et al., 2026)]. Though effective, these approaches often introduce additional architectural or training complexity, which can limit efficiency and scalability. Recently, JiT [(Li and He, 2026)] achieves high-resolution image generation competitive with latent diffusion using a simple large-patch DiT-style Transformer. This paradigm is also extended to one-step image generation [(Lu et al., 2026)] and text-to-image generation [(Wang et al., 2026b; Jiang et al., 2026)], further demonstrating the effectiveness.

    Video Transformer architectures. Modern video Transformers largely retain the standard blocks of 2D Vision Transformers (ViTs), making patch embedding the key adaptation to video inputs [(Tong et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2023; Bardes et al., 2024; Assran et al., 2025)]. A common choice is tubelet embedding [(Arnab et al., 2021)], which encodes non-overlapping spatiotemporal patches into tokens via 3D convolution. This architecture is also widely adopted in latent video DiTs, whereas pixel-space video diffusion methods still typically rely on U-shaped architectures [(Gu et al., 2024; Bar-Tal et al., 2024; Hoogeboom et al., 2025)] or cascaded generation [(Menapace et al., 2024; Skorokhodov et al., 2024)]. Our work aims to explore whether a simple DiT-style video Transformer can also support direct pixel-space video generation.

    3 Method

    3.1 Preliminaries

    Though denoising diffusion models commonly use noise, score or velocity prediction [(Dhariwal and Nichol, 2021; Song et al., 2021; Karras et al., 2022; Salimans and Ho, 2022; Lipman et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2023)], JiT proposes clean data prediction and velocity loss supervision for pixel-space diffusion [(Li and He, 2026)]. Following this formulation, JVT predicts clean video x̂₀ from noisy pixels xₜ:

    xₜ=(1-t)x₀+tε, x̂₀=f_θ(xₜ,t,c), v̂=(x̂₀-xₜ)/t,

    		(1)

    where noise ε∼ℕ(0,I), noise level t∈(0,1], and c denotes the available conditioning. Thus the standard rectified-flow velocity loss can be represented as:

    L_MSE=𝔼∥v̂-v∥₂²=𝔼∥(x̂₀-x₀)/t∥₂², v=x₀-ε=(x₀-xₜ)/t.

    		(2)

    3.2 Patch Embedding

    Patch embedding is central to pixel-space DiTs, as it provides the initial downsampling that latent DiTs obtain from an autoencoder. For videos, it also aggregates spatiotemporal information while controlling the token sequence length.

    Following standard video Transformer designs, we use plain tubelet embedding as our baseline. As illustrated in Fig. 3 (a), it uses a single 3D convolution to project each non-overlapping patch of temporal size pₜ and spatial size pₕ×p_w into a C-dimensional token.

    Bottleneck structure. Following JiT [(Li and He, 2026)], we introduce a channel bottleneck into tubelet embedding (Fig. 3 (b)). A 3D convolution first projects each patch into a C_b-dimensional representation, which is then expanded to C channels by a pointwise projection. We typically choose C_b

    Spatiotemporal factorization. Inspired by the factorization principle of depthwise separable convolution [(Chollet, 2017; Howard et al., 2017)], we separate the spatial and temporal operations of tubelet embedding. Specifically, a patch-wise 2D convolution extracts spatial features within each frame, while a frame-wise 1D convolution aggregates temporal information at each spatial location. Applying the spatial operation first yields patch-first embedding (Fig. 3 (c)), while reversing the order yields frame-first embedding (Fig. 3 (d)).

    3.3 Register Tokens

    Register tokens provide additional computational slots in ViTs [(Darcet et al., 2024)] and also support in-context conditioning and improve generation quality in pixel-space image DiTs [(Li and He, 2026; Starodubcev et al., 2026)]. We extend this mechanism to JVT and examine its roles in conditioning and sampling guidance.

    As illustrated in Fig. 2, given L=L₁+L₂ Transformer blocks, register tokens are prepended to the visual sequence after the first L₁ blocks and discarded after the remaining L₂ blocks. Let X^(L₁)∈ℝ^N×C denote the N visual tokens at the insertion point and R₀∈ℝ^ℓᵣ×C the ℓᵣ learnable base registers. With eₜ,e_y∈ℝ^C denoting the noise level and class embeddings, respectively, we construct the register tokens and augmented sequence as

    R=R₀+Repeat(eᵣ,ℓᵣ), X̃^(L₁)=Concat(R,X^(L₁)),

    		(3)

    where eᵣ∈{0,eₜ,e_y,eₜ+e_y} and Repeat(eᵣ,ℓᵣ) replicates eᵣ across the ℓᵣ register positions. Setting eᵣ=0 preserves R=R₀ without adding a conditioning embedding, which is different from removing the registers. For eᵣ∈{eₜ,e_y,eₜ+e_y}, the register tokens provide an additional conditioning pathway alongside AdaLN.

    Register guidance. We also apply register guidance (RG) [(Starodubcev et al., 2026)] during sampling. For the same noisy input and condition, let vᵣ and vₙᵣ denote the velocity predictions of the same model with and without registers, respectively. RG amplifies the register contribution through

    v_rg=vᵣ+w_rg(vᵣ-vₙᵣ), w_rg≥0.

    		(4)

    For conditional generation, let vᵤ denote the unconditional velocity prediction with registers retained. Combining RG with classifier-free guidance (CFG) [(Ho and Salimans, 2021)] gives

    v_cfg+rg=vᵤ+w_cfg(vᵣ-vᵤ)+w_rg(vᵣ-vₙᵣ).

    		(5)

    The scales w_cfg and w_rg separately weight the CFG and RG terms: setting w_rg=0 recovers CFG, while w_cfg=1 recovers RG in Eq. (4). Unlike the original RG procedure [(Starodubcev et al., 2026)], which randomly drops registers during training, we keep them active throughout training and remove them only to compute vₙᵣ during sampling. Our experiments show that RG remains effective without register dropout during training.

    3.4 Pixel-aligned Joint Generation

    Pixel-aligned signals about geometry, motion, and semantic structure provide complementary cues for video generation. By channel-wise concatenating RGB frames with these signals [(Ke et al., 2024)], diffusion models can jointly generate RGB content and spatially aligned auxiliary modalities [(Zhu et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2025a; Huang et al., 2026a)].

    Pixel-space modeling allows these modalities to be represented on a shared spatiotemporal grid without an RGB-specific autoencoder. After modality-specific normalization, we concatenate an RGB video x_rgb∈ℝ^T×3×H×W with M pixel-aligned modalities along the channel dimension:

    x₀=[x_rgb;x⁽¹⁾;…;x^(M)]∈ℝ^T×Cⱼₒᵢₙₜ×H×W,

    		(6)

    where x⁽ᵐ⁾∈ℝ^T×Cₘ×H×W denotes the m-th aligned modality and Cⱼₒᵢₙₜ=3+∑ₘ₌₁^MCₘ is the total number of channels. These modalities may include depth, surface normals, ray maps, segmentation masks, and optical flow. All modalities share the same noise level and are predicted jointly during denoising.

    We instantiate this formulation with RGB and disparity, a reparameterization of depth, for camera-conditioned video generation (Sec. 4.3). At inference, we convert the predicted disparity back to depth and unproject it using the camera parameters. Combined with the generated RGB frames, this yields a sequence of colored point clouds without an additional reconstruction model.

    4 Experiments

    4.1 Main Results

    Datasets. For class-conditioned generation and unconditional generation, we conduct experiments on four datasets: UCF-101 [(Soomro et al., 2012)], FaceForensics [(Rössler et al., 2018)], SkyTimelapse [(Xiong et al., 2018)], and Taichi-HD [(Siarohin et al., 2019)]. Following settings of previous works [(Skorokhodov et al., 2022; Ma et al., 2025)], we use both training and test splits of UCF-101, and only the training split of the other datasets. We randomly extract 16-frame video clips with a frame interval of 3, and resize all video frames to 256×256 resolution for training.

    Evaluation metrics. We evaluate generation quality with Fréchet Video Distance (FVD) [(Unterthiner et al., 2019)], using 2,048 generated samples. For efficiency metrics, we report parameter count, floating point operations (FLOPs), peak allocated GPU memory and inference latency. Additional details about these metrics are given in Appendix (A.2, A.4).

    Baselines. Our main baseline is Latte [(Ma et al., 2025)], a representative DiT-based latent diffusion model. Other competing methods include GAN-based methods [(Skorokhodov et al., 2022; Yu et al., 2022)], autoregressive models [(Yan et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2024a)], U-Net-based latent diffusion [(He et al., 2022; Yu et al., 2023b)] and DiT-based latent diffusion [(Liu et al., 2024)].

    Tab. 1 reports class-conditioned results on UCF-101 and unconditional results on the four datasets. JVT outperforms all competing methods in the table, demonstrating the effectiveness of direct pixel-space video modeling. Additional qualitative results are provided in Fig. 8 of the Appendix.

    4.2 Ablation Study

    Video patch embedding. We compare the tubelet, patch-first, and frame-first embeddings introduced in Sec. 3.2 while varying the bottleneck width C_b. Under identical training settings, all bottlenecked variants in Tab. 2 achieve lower final training loss than the plain tubelet baseline. With an appropriate choice of C_b, tubelet and patch-first embeddings also improve FVD while reducing computational cost. Taking both generation quality and efficiency into consideration, we adopt patch-first embedding with C_b=32 as the default configuration for JVT. Further patch embedding ablation details are provided in Appendix A.3.

    Register tokens and guidance. In Tab. 3, we ablate both the information carried by register tokens and the effect of register guidance (RG) in class-conditioned generation. Under the default 50-step Euler sampling setup, adding registers without RG yields no FVD improvement over the register-free baseline. With RG, however, all tested register variants outperform this baseline, regardless of the conditioning information they carry. The 50-step Heun and 100-step Euler results further show that RG retains its advantage over higher-NFE baselines using more sampling steps or a higher-order solver, consistent with findings of prior works [(Reynaud et al., 2024; Lu et al., 2025; Salajegheh and Mudur, 2026)].

    Although prior studies demonstrate the effectiveness of in-context class conditioning for pixel-space image generation [(Starodubcev et al., 2026; Li and He, 2026; Lu et al., 2026)], we observe no clear benefit from any of the three variants of register-based conditioning in Tab. 3. Instead, registers with eᵣ=0 achieve the lowest FVD of 129.2. These results suggest that, under this sampling setup, the benefits of register tokens depend on RG, rather than register-based conditioning..

    As shown in Tab. 1, RG works well on UCF-101, but brings no obvious gains on the other 3 datasets. Without register guidance, JVT variants with and without registers exhibit broadly similar FVD scores and intermediate feature-map smoothness. However, as illustrated in Fig. 4, visual tokens attend strongly to register tokens immediately after their insertion (L₁=9) on UCF-101, while this interaction is noticeably weaker on FaceForensics, SkyTimelapse, and Taichi-HD.

    This dataset-dependent difference may be attributed to the global semantics encoded by register tokens [(Starodubcev et al., 2026)]. UCF-101 spans 101 action categories and exhibits greater semantic diversity than the other three datasets. We hypothesize that this diversity, together with stronger patch-to-register interactions, makes the register-enabled prediction vᵣ a more informative guide for its register-free counterpart vₙᵣ. In contrast, the more homogeneous semantics of the other datasets may limit the benefits of RG.

    Adaptive layer normalization. Standard DiTs inject noise level and class information through adaptive layer normalization (AdaLN) [(Peebles and Xie, 2023)]. However, recent works start to explore AdaLN-free DiTs for image generation, using in-context tokens, cross-attention, or multimodal joint attention for conditioning [(Geng et al., 2026; Lu et al., 2026; Zeng et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026b)]. In Tab. 4, we examine whether register-based conditioning offers a reliable alternative to AdaLN in JVT. Relative to the baseline, neither adding class-conditioned registers nor removing noise level conditioning improves FVD. With class-only conditioning, replacing AdaLN with register tokens further worsens FVD to 156.3. We also observe no clear efficiency gain from removing AdaLN. Unconditional ablations show no consistent FVD improvement from jointly removing noise level conditioning and AdaLN (Appendix A.3, Tab. 11). These results support retaining standard AdaLN as JVT’s default conditioning mechanism.

    4.3 Camera-conditioned Video Generation

    We instantiate the pixel-aligned joint generation framework in Sec. 3.4 for camera-conditioned video generation. Given an initial RGB frame and a target camera trajectory, we jointly generate RGB frames and aligned disparity maps. After recovering depth from disparity, the camera parameters allow the predictions to be unprojected into a sequence of colored point clouds, providing an explicit 4D representation of the generated scene, as shown in Fig. 5.

    Experimental setting. We conduct 8-frame camera-conditioned video generation experiments on RealEstate10K [(Zhou et al., 2018)] at a resolution of 256×256. As dense depth annotations are unavailable, a frozen lightweight 3D reconstruction model, Pi3X [(Wang et al., 2026d)] supplies depth targets online during training. Following prior works [(Song et al., 2026; Zhu et al., 2025)], we reversibly transform depth D to square-root disparity d=(D+1)^-1/2 and concatenate it with RGB as a four-channel target.

    Evaluation. We evaluate RGB video quality using FVD, and assess camera following by comparing Pi3X-estimated relative poses with the target camera trajectory. Following prior works [(Wang et al., 2024b; Wang et al., 2025a; Wang et al., 2026d)], we report relative rotation accuracy (RRA), relative translation accuracy (RTA), and AUC as camera-following metrics. Specifically, RRA and RTA measure the percentages of evaluated frame pairs whose rotation and translation-direction errors fall below a given threshold, respectively, while AUC summarizes their joint error distribution. We use thresholds of 5^∘ and 30^∘.

    We compare JVT with pixel-space U-ViT models [(Song et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2026)] and a latent-space DiT [(Huang et al., 2026b)]. As shown in Tab. 5, both JVT variants achieve lower FVD than these baselines. Joint RGB-disparity generation achieves the highest RTA and AUC among all compared methods, with only a slight increase in FVD relative to RGB-only JVT. The qualitative results in Fig. 6 further illustrate the differences in camera following.

    Across methods, RRA is consistently high, whereas RTA remains substantially lower. This gap highlights a key limitation of these camera-conditioned video generators: they can follow prescribed camera rotations relatively reliably, but are less accurate at reproducing camera translations. Joint RGB-disparity generation narrows this gap, suggesting that explicit depth cues help the model relate camera motion to scene geometry. Within a unified pixel-space generative framework, JVT natively supports this joint modeling of RGB and geometry and improves camera following.

    5 Conclusion

    We demonstrate pixel-space video generation with a simple DiT-style Transformer, achieving generation quality competitive with latent diffusion baselines in both class-conditioned and unconditional video generation benchmarks. Our ablations study suggests patch-first embedding for spatiotemporal tokenization and standard AdaLN for conditioning. For the register mechanism, register-free JVT provides an acceptable baseline, while register guidance can offer additional gains, particularly on the more diverse UCF-101 dataset.

    Pixel-space modeling makes pixel-aligned joint generation straightforward by representing RGB and aligned modalities on a common spatiotemporal grid, without encoding them into a shared pretrained latent space. When extending JVT to camera-conditioned joint RGB-disparity generation, we find camera following is improved relative to RGB-only baselines, with a small FVD trade-off.

    These findings highlight the potential of simple DiT-style Transformers for pixel-space video generation and pixel-aligned joint modeling. We hope our empirical findings help guide future efforts to scale pixel-space video generation to larger model size, more datasets, longer videos and higher resolutions.

    （参考文献见原文。）

    Appendix A Appendix

    A.1 Implementation Details

    Our implementation follows the pixel-space clean-data prediction design of JiT [(Li and He, 2026)], with video generation and camera conditioning implemented in the DFoT framework [(Song et al., 2025)]. Tab. 6 specifies model and optimization configurations.

    Register tokens.

    As shown in Fig. 4, the register mechanism brings clear gains on UCF-101 but only limited benefits on the other datasets, so we use register tokens only for class-conditioned and unconditional video generation on UCF-101. The register initialization ablation in Tab. 3 further shows no gain from injecting the timestep or class embedding into the register tokens, and we therefore just set eᵣ=0 when registers are used. The base registers R₀ are learnable tokens initialized i.i.d. from a zero-mean Gaussian with standard deviation 0.02. All register-equipped variants are sampled with register guidance, whose scale is selected by a linear search with a step size of 0.1.

    Training details. All models are trained from scratch. Following JiT [(Li and He, 2026)], we use clean data prediction and velocity MSE loss. For noise sampling, we sample noise level t_base from logit-normal distribution [(Esser et al., 2024)] and shift it with noise shift s, as shown in Eq. (7). Our full-scale training of JVT use a global batch size of 256 with 8 NVIDIA 80GB GPUs, while some ablations use a batch size of 40 on a single GPU (Fig. 7).

    t=(s·t_base)/(1+(s-1)·t_base)

    		(7)

    For camera-conditioned generation, we sample the video noise independently for each frame, following DFoT [(Song et al., 2025)]. We also adopt the data augmentations of the DFoT dataloader: horizontal flipping and temporal reversal, each applied with probability 0.5, and back-and-forth augmentation with probability 0.1.

    Sampling configurations. Tab. 7 specifies the exact sampling configuration of each main result. We use the Euler solver for class-conditioned and camera-conditioned generation, and the Heun solver for unconditional generation. All samplers run for 50 denoising steps, with the timestep schedule shifted by the noise shift s (Eq. (7)). Depending on the task, we apply classifier-free guidance (CFG) [(Ho and Salimans, 2021)], register guidance (RG) [(Starodubcev et al., 2026)], or history guidance (HG) [(Song et al., 2025)]. The CFG scale is selected by a linear search with a step size of 1, and the RG scale with a step size of 0.1. For FVD evaluation, we generate 2,048 clips per method and use the same number of real clips as the reference.

    Geometry annotation for RealEstate10K. As in Sec. 4.3, dense depth annotations are unavailable for RealEstate10K, so we use a frozen Pi3X [(Wang et al., 2026d)] to supply depth pseudo-labels online during training. For each training clip, Pi3X is conditioned on the prescribed camera intrinsics and extrinsics as priors. Since Pi3X predicts scale-invariant geometry and affine-invariant cameras, we estimate the global scale of the predicted depth by aligning the predicted cameras with the ground-truth cameras. The aligned depth is clamped to a minimum of 10⁻⁵ and, following prior works [(Song et al., 2026; Zhu et al., 2025)], reversibly transformed to square-root disparity d=(D+1)^-1/2, which is concatenated with RGB as a four-channel target.

    A.2 Efficiency Evaluation Details

    The efficiency experiments use JVT-XL with 28 Transformer blocks, width 1,152, 16 attention heads, and spatial patch size 16. Each case processes one 16-frame 256×256 video in pixel space. With a temporal downsampling factor of 4, the denoiser receives 1,024 visual tokens. The register-enabled configuration inserts 32 in-context register tokens after the first 9 blocks, resulting in 1,056 tokens for the remaining blocks.

    Sampling uses Euler integration with 50 steps. Register-enabled cases include no guidance, CFG, RG, and CFG+RG, while register-disabled cases include no guidance and CFG. These four guidance settings use one, two, two, and three denoiser-forward equivalents per step, respectively.

    All measurements use bfloat16 with TF32 enabled and torch.compile disabled on one NVIDIA 4090 GPU. Each case runs in a fresh Python process. Denoiser latency uses 20 warm-up iterations followed by 100 timed iterations, and sampling latency uses 5 warm-up samples followed by 20 timed samples. The complete matrix is repeated in three independent sweeps. We record model parameters, FLOPs, baseline and peak allocated GPU memory, incremental peak memory, latency statistics, and throughput. FLOPs for one denoiser forward pass are counted with torch.utils.flop_counter.FlopCounterMode. Sampling FLOPs are computed from the matching denoiser FLOPs, 50 sampling steps, and the number of denoiser-forward equivalents per step.

    Tab. 8 covers the ten embedding configurations in Tab. 2, with additional register-free measurements for five of them. Tab. 9 reports the corresponding 30 sampling measurements.

    A.3 Additional Ablations

    Figure 7 gives the bottleneck width sweep curve. In this experiment, we use batch size of 40, different from the full-scale experiments in Tab. 2 with global batch size 256. For tubelet and patch-first embedding, FVD varies non-monotonically with C_b: an overly narrow bottleneck may discard task-relevant spatiotemporal information, whereas an excessively wide bottleneck offers limited additional benefit. As for frame-first embedding, FVD improves progressively as C_b increases, but the efficiency metrics declines sharply.

    Tab. 10 and Tab. 11 repeat the register and AdaLN ablations of Tab. 3 and Tab. 4 (Sec. 4.2) for unconditional video generation. As shown in Tab. 10, the gains from registers are dataset-dependent: register guidance substantially improves UCF-101 but brings marginal or no improvement on FaceForensics, SkyTimelapse and Taichi-HD. The AdaLN ablation in Tab. 11 leads to the same conclusion as in the class-conditioned case: simply removing AdaLN without scaling parameters commonly degrades FVD, supporting standard AdaLN as the default conditioning mechanism.

    Prior work on text-to-image generation has shown that, under matched parameter counts, AdaLN-free variants can outperform their standard AdaLN counterparts [(Wang et al., 2026b)]. However, such a parameter-matched comparison is not compute-matched: AdaLN accounts for a considerable fraction of the model parameters, yet it is merely a linear layer with linear computational complexity. Matching the parameter count of an AdaLN-free variant to the baseline therefore substantially enlarges the quadratic-complexity attention blocks, leading to a marked increase in overall computation. For this reason, the AdaLN-free variants in Tab. 4 and Tab. 11 are instead compared against standard JVT with the same number of Transformer layers.

    A.4 Additional FVD Results

    Training strategies and algorithm designs greatly affect model performance. Some methods adopt the image-video joint training strategy proposed in VDM [(Ho et al., 2022b)], which markedly improves video generation quality and can also be incorporated into our method. Tab. 13 compares our method without the joint training strategy against these methods. We further compare our method with recent hybrid approaches of autoregressive modeling and diffusion, and show the results in Tab. 14.

    Different evaluation protocols can also directly influence the reported FVD scores. Following StyleGAN-V [(Skorokhodov et al., 2022)] and Latte [(Ma et al., 2025)], we compute FVD using 2048 generated video samples (FVD@2048), whereas several other methods use 10000 samples (FVD@10000). Since the original FVD paper [(Unterthiner et al., 2019)] shows that the number of samples used for evaluation can greatly affect the FVD score, we additionally report our FVD@10000 result in Tab. 15.

item.title: AMD 把 FSR 4.1.2 推进 UE 插件：支持 UE 5.3–5.8，且后续版本可随驱动升级、不必重发游戏 ｜ AMD FSR UE plugin updated with FSR Upscaling 4.1.2
item.description:
一句话：一条容易忽略的工程口径：插件走 FSR API，于是新版本可以靠 Adrenalin 驱动下发。

要点：

  • 覆盖面：AMD FSR 的 **Unreal Engine 插件更新到 4.1.2**，把 SDK 2.4 的更新带进 **UE 5.3 到 5.8**；ML 版 FSR Upscaling 从 8 月的 RX 7000 扩到 **RX 6000（RDNA 2）**，并首次支持部分带 Radeon 核显的 Ryzen 处理器（游戏本、mini-PC、掌机）
  • 集成口径：插件通过 **AMD FSR API** 集成，因此游戏**可以随 AMD Software: Adrenalin Edition 驱动更新获得更新的 FSR 版本，不必为每个版本重发游戏**
  • 同批还包括更平滑的帧生成与 Radeon Anti-Lag 2 的改进

为什么值得看：「新版本可以靠驱动下发」这件事对运营的意义大于任何画质提升：它把上采样从「每次都要发版」变成「跟着驱动走」。加上 UE 5.3–5.8 的版本覆盖，这条是引擎团队真正会照抄的集成口径。

中文摘要：AMD 把 FSR 的 Unreal Engine 插件更新到 4.1.2 版，把 FSR「Redstone」SDK 2.4 的更新带进 Unreal Engine 5.3 到 5.8。这次更新让基于机器学习的 FSR Upscaling 覆盖更多 AMD 硬件：继 8 月扩到 RX 7000 系列之后，现在也支持 RX 6000 系列（RDNA 2）独显，并首次支持部分带 Radeon 核显的 AMD Ryzen 处理器（见于游戏本、mini-PC 与掌机）。同样重要的是集成口径：插件通过 AMD FSR API 集成，因此使用它的游戏可以随 AMD Software: Adrenalin Edition 的驱动更新获得更新的 FSR 版本，而无需为每个版本重新发版。此外这批更新还带来更平滑的帧生成与 Radeon Anti-Lag 2 的改进。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：AMD GPUOpen（English）

原文发布：2026-11-16

本期推送：2026-11-17

Home » Learn » AMD FSR UE plugin updated with FSR Upscaling 4.1.2 Share on Bluesky Share on Mastadon Share on LinkedIn Share on Twitter/X Share on Reddit Share on Facebook Share on Whatsapp Share via Email AMD FSR UE plugin updated with FSR Upscaling 4.1.2 Originally posted: November 16, 2026 Alexander Blake-Davies

Plugin updated with AMD FSR™ Upscaling 4.1.2, adding AMD Radeon™ RX 6000 Series and select AMD Ryzen™ processor support.

The AMD FSR™ Unreal® Engine plugin has been updated to version 4.1.2, bringing the latest updates from the AMD FSR “Redstone” SDK 2.4 to Unreal Engine 5.3 up to 5.8. With this release, ML-based FSR Upscaling runs on a much wider range of AMD hardware, so more of your players can benefit from it on more of the devices they play on. And because the plugin integrates FSR through the AMD FSR API, games built with it can also receive newer FSR versions through AMD Software: Adrenalin Edition™ driver updates, without a game-side update for each release.

ML upscaling for more Unreal Engine players

AMD FSR™ Upscaling is our ML-powered upscaler, delivering a substantial boost in game performance together with significant image quality improvements. In August, the plugin extended it to AMD Radeon™ RX 7000 Series GPUs. With version 4.1.2, it now also runs on AMD Radeon RX 6000 Series (AMD RDNA™ 2 architecture) discrete GPUs and, for the first time, on select AMD Ryzen™ processors with integrated Radeon graphics, found in gaming laptops, mini-PCs and handheld gaming devices.

FSR Upscaling 4.1.2 uses two INT8 models to cover this hardware. AMD Radeon RX 6000 Series GPUs and AMD Ryzen AI Max processors run the full model. A second, highly optimized model, less than half the size, is purpose-built for more constrained integrated graphics and brings ML-based upscaling to thin-and-light laptops and handhelds. Model selection is automatic and based on the target hardware. Results vary by game, resolution, quality mode and hardware.

For Unreal Engine developers, that means a single plugin integration brings ML-based upscaling to players on AMD Radeon RX 9000, RX 7000 and RX 6000 Series graphics cards and on supported AMD Ryzen-powered laptops and handhelds, with analytical AMD FSR 3 as the fallback on other hardware. See the plugin guide’s Requirements section for the full hardware list.

The plugin supports DirectX® 12. Vulkan® support, added to AMD FSR Upscaling and AMD FSR Frame Generation in the AMD FSR SDK 2.4, isn’t currently available in the plugin, so stay tuned to GPUOpen for future plugin updates.

Smoother frame generation on AMD Radeon RX 9000 Series GPUs

The plugin also includes AMD FSR™ Frame Generation 4.0.2 and the new FSR Frame Generation Swapchain 4.0.0, which adds Driver-Assisted Frame Pacing on AMD Radeon™ RX 9000 Series GPUs. On compatible hardware, final presentation timing is delegated to the AMD display driver, which schedules the present closer to the display pipeline for smoother frame delivery and lower CPU overhead.

Driver-Assisted Frame Pacing requires AMD Software: Adrenalin Edition™ 26.10.1 or later, and works with the plugin’s default OverrideSwapChainDX12 setting of true. AMD FSR Frame Generation 4.0.2 requires Windows® 11. See the AMD FSR Frame Generation page for the full list of requirements.

AMD Radeon Anti-Lag 2 plugin update

The AMD Radeon™ Anti-Lag 2 Unreal® Engine plugin has also been updated to version 2.0.6 with performance and stability improvements. It reduces end-to-end system latency in GPU-bound scenarios and integrates with the AMD FSR™ plugin to function correctly with FSR Frame Generation enabled. It can now also be downloaded directly from the AMD FSR Unreal Engine plugin guide.

More information Learn more about AMD FSR Upscaling and AMD FSR Frame Generation. Download the plugin and get started with the AMD FSR Unreal Engine plugin guide. Read about everything new in FSR “Redstone” in our AMD FSR SDK 2.4 blog. Learn more about and download the latest AMD Radeon Anti-Lag 2 Unreal Engine plugin. Discuss the plugin update on the AMD Developer Community. Sign up to our AMD Developer Newsletter for the latest updates. Footnotes

It delivers significant image quality improvements with reduced ghosting, better particle preservation, and superior detail. AMD FSR Upscaling 4.1.2 Comes to XBOX AMD FSR™ Upscaling 4.1.2 is now available on XBOX® Series X|S with the October 2026 GDK. AMD FSR™ Redstone expands with the latest AMD FSR™ SDK 2.1 AMD FSR 'Redstone' SDK 2.1 enables developers to integrate FSR features into games with easy-to-use APIs and access to advanced neural rendering technologies. item.title: SDF 转网格只要几秒：FOMOS 走纯几何的特征导向网格化，不靠 Marching Cubes 也不靠神经网络 ｜ FOMOS: Feature-Oriented Meshing of SDFs
item.description:
一句话：Marching Cubes 出密集低质三角面，Neural Dual Contouring 又牺牲特征——中间还有路。

要点：

  • 对比对象很具体：现有方法里，**Marching Cubes** 会产生密集、质量差的三角化；**Neural Dual Contouring** 这类方法则会在特征保持上做妥协
  • FOMOS 是**纯几何**方法，做的是「特征导向」的 SDF 网格化，不引入神经组件
  • 结果指标是网格质量与运行时间同时改善，把 SDF 网格化压到**数秒级**

为什么值得看：SDF 是生成式 3D 与仿真之间的通用货币，但「SDF → 可用网格」这一步长期是瓶颈：要么面数爆炸，要么特征被抹平。能在数秒内出高质量、保特征的网格，直接决定生成资产能不能进引擎。

1. Introduction

A Signed Distance Field (SDF) is a scalar function that, for any given point in space, returns the distance to the nearest point on a given boundary, with the sign indicating whether the point lies inside or outside the boundary. Although these methods are simple and easy to implement and use, their reliance on uniform sampling prioritizes volumetric coverage over geometric fidelity. This often leads to the omission of important edges, corners, or surface curvature variations, as it does not explicitly preserve these features. Consequently, it introduces approximation errors in critical applications such as computational fluid dynamics (CFD) and finite element methods (FEM), which reduce simulation accuracy. Although it is possible to implement workarounds using a very dense grid sampling followed by feature-aware remeshing, such solutions are both computationally expensive and require significant peak memory as volumetric data grows with cubic complexity. Furthermore, such workarounds are suboptimal as they do not account for the global shape structure.

While traditional approaches, such as Marching Cubes and Dual Contouring (along with their numerous variants), rely on grids, recent techniques have investigated grid-free meshing using learned representations and optimization techniques [(Sellán et al., 2023; Sellán et al., 2024)]. However, all of these methods, as shown in Figure 1, are prone to over-smoothing, and some impose restrictions on the topology. The focus of this work is, therefore, to automatically and precisely mesh SDFs without making any topological assumptions. The core challenge is to develop efficient techniques for estimating features that are defined in a global sense. Our approach directly addresses the fundamental relationship between SDFs and features that must be explicitly preserved to achieve a high-fidelity reconstruction.

Our core idea is to adopt an ε-sampling framework that determines the sampling density according to the local feature size (LFS), defined as the distance from a surface point to the medial axis [(Amenta et al., 1998)] (please see Section 3.1 for a formal definition). This choice addresses key limitations of conventional sampling strategies: uniform-length sampling uses a fixed spatial scale regardless of local geometric complexity, whereas curvature-aware sampling relies solely on surface curvature alone, which may not fully capture the scale of thin structures or closely spaced surface regions (particularly useful for volumetric meshing). In contrast, ε-sampling based on LFS accounts for both local curvature and the spatial proximity of surface regions, providing a principled basis to preserve fine geometric details while avoiding unnecessary sampling in less complex regions [(Amenta and Bern, 1998; Boissonnat and Oudot, 2005)]. To achieve this, we introduce a new technique for computing the local feature size (LFS), and subsequently incorporate an iterative refinement process to add points that meet that sampling condition, thereby preserving and capturing features of arbitrary size. We demonstrate that our method outperforms the state of the art in both quality and runtime, further enabling instant in-memory meshing of SDFs with huge grid sizes of 10240³, and illustrate the advantages of feature-based meshing by running FEM simulations on its volumetric interior.

  • •

    We introduce a novel algorithm for computing interior and exterior medial axis samples (which we term medial scaffolds) directly from a generic signed distance function (SDF), and demonstrate its performance to be on par with or better than state-of-the-art mesh-based medial axis computation techniques.

  • •

    We introduce FOMOS, an LFS-based adaptive SDF meshing technique that reduces the time and memory complexity of discrete SDF meshing from cubic to quadratic, achieves state-of-the-art performance, and guarantees a manifold output mesh homeomorphic to the target surface.

  • •

    We extend our meshing framework to generate manifold meshes from huge truncated signed distance fields (TSDFs) and to create near-instantaneous SDF previews.

    • 2. Related Work

    The related works for feature-aware meshing of SDFs can be classified into two categories: Algorithms for computing the medial axis (as we and most works in literature prevalently use the medial axis for estimating LFS), and SDF meshing algorithms (algorithms for creating meshes from signed distance functions). To our knowledge, our end-to-end algorithm is the first to take an SDF as input and directly mesh it based on the local feature size rather than a grid.

    Medial Axis Approximation.

    The main challenge in local feature sizing functions is its dual demand of geometric fidelity and computational efficiency. The foundations of works in this direction lie in either curvature- or shape-diameter-driven adaptations [(Persson, 2006; Shapira et al., 2008)] or in local feature size estimation. As the local feature size (LFS) is defined as the distance to the closest point on the medial axis [(Amenta et al., 1998)], most works in this direction rely on approximate medial axis computation, requiring global knowledge of the shape. Hence, in this section, we discuss various methods in the literature for computing the medial axis.

    Due to its usefulness in shape analysis, early works in medial axis computation date back to the late 1960s [(Blum, 1967)]. However, due to its highly unstable nature and high geometric complexity, later works (in our context) explored the connection between a subset of easily computable Voronoi vertices and the medial axis [(Amenta et al., 2001; Boissonnat and Cazals, 2001)]. Though theoretically valid when the boundary samples approach infinity, it cannot produce a clean medial axis from real-world inputs for practical usage. This led to several works focusing on pruning the extraneous branches from the medial axis [(Amenta and Kolluri, 2001; Dey and Zhao, 2004; Miklos et al., 2010; Yan et al., 2018)], employing restricted power diagram [(Wang et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2024)] and simplifying the medial axis [(Li et al., 2015; Huang et al., 2024; Sun et al., 2015; Guo et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2026a)], but these usually require user-defined parameters. Another line of work focuses on computing medial axis points by shrinking spheres [(Ma et al., 2012; Jalba et al., 2012; Dou et al., 2022)], but assumes the closest points on the surface are known and well-defined. Recent methods utilize deep learning to predict the medial axis [(Rebain et al., 2019; Lin et al., 2021; Pepe et al., 2025; Kong et al., 2026)]. Despite these advances, medial axis computation remains costly and non-robust, making it unsuitable for our needs. In addition, unlike typical point cloud and mesh representations, the SDF representation we are handling poses additional challenges as it lacks explicit topology and exhibits gradient sensitivity near sharp features and in under-resolved regions. It is also worth noting that, although not directly related to or applicable to our objective, time-consuming LFS computations on point clouds [(Fu et al., 2024)] and 2D Bézier curves [(Ohrhallinger et al., 2023)] have recently been studied in the literature. A closely related method [(Persson, 2006)] detects the medial axis as the shock set of an SDF approximated by polynomials along grid-cell edges; however, its cubic computational complexity limits its suitability for the fast, high-resolution meshing targeted in our work.

    Unlike these methods, we prioritize computing a medial scaffold as a set of estimated medial centers over precise medial axis computation, focusing solely on meshing an SDF. These medial scaffolds are then used to estimate a more precise LFS. Furthermore, the medial scaffolds can be computed arbitrarily sparsely, while still precisely meshing using the entire SDF, resulting in an output-sensitive mesh generation time, enabling instant previews with fewer triangles.

    While widely used in geometry processing, SDFs are often converted to meshes to facilitate further processing. The classical approach, Marching Cubes [(Lorensen and Cline, 1987; Chernyaev, 1995)], grids the SDF and applies a look-up table to generate triangulated surfaces following a predefined set of rules. This is further improved in various directions, for instance, to resolve ambiguities [(Lorensen and Cline, 1998)], capture sharp features [(Kobbelt et al., 2001; Ju et al., 2002)], and to enhance memory efficiency [(Vega et al., 2019)]. However, these techniques often result in non-manifold surfaces and poor-quality triangles, limiting their utility in many further applications (see Figure 1). Recent deep learning variants, Neural Marching Cubes [(Chen and Zhang, 2021)] and Neural Dual Contouring [(Chen et al., 2022)], being the most prominent among them, learn the tessellation templates and vertex positions to reconstruct higher-quality meshes with improved feature preservation. Although not their primary focus, some learning-based methods reconstruct surfaces from point clouds using an SDF as an intermediate representation [(Zhang et al., 2025; Ren et al., 2023; Zhou et al., 2024)]. However, their generalization to complex, previously unseen geometries may be limited (as illustrated in Figure 1), they are often time-consuming, and they often result in low-quality triangles.
