Recent deep learning variants, Neural Marching Cubes [(Chen and Zhang, 2021)] and Neural Dual Contouring [(Chen et al., 2022)], being the most prominent among them, learn the tessellation templates and vertex positions to reconstruct higher-quality meshes with improved feature preservation. In this line of work, Deep Marching Cubes [(Liao et al., 2018)], MeshSDF [(Remelli et al., 2020)], and FlexiCubes [(Shen et al., 2023)] introduced techniques to offer differentiable isosurfacing procedures. Although not their primary focus, some learning-based methods reconstruct surfaces from point clouds using an SDF as an intermediate representation [(Zhang et al., 2025; Ren et al., 2023; Zhou et al., 2024)]. However, their generalization to complex, previously unseen geometries may be limited (as illustrated in Figure 1), they are often time-consuming, and they often result in low-quality triangles.

    Despite the surge in deep learning-based techniques, geometric algorithms remain popular due to their simplicity and generalizability; a comprehensive literature review is available in [(De Araújo et al., 2015)]. A more recent work uses a shrinkwrap or inflation method that iteratively deforms an initial mesh towards the desired surface [(Hanocka et al., 2020; Bukenberger and Lensch, 2021)]. A global approach, Reach for the Spheres (RFTS) [(Sellán et al., 2023)], shrink-wraps an initial mesh around the SDF to fit the surface using a gradient flow (note that topology changes are not allowed during the process). Its successor, Reach for the Arcs (RFTA) [(Sellán et al., 2024)], manages to handle non-zero genus objects and is somewhat faster, but reconstructs many bad triangles. Other approaches focus on adaptive sampling to reduce the cost of implicit-surface extraction. McGrids [(Ren et al., 2024)] uses iterative Monte Carlo sampling to reduce implicit-field queries, but incurs additional grid-construction overhead, produces bad quality triangles, and may require denser sampling to recover sharp features than methods that exploit normal information. Similarly, power-diagram-based extraction [(Wang et al., 2026b)] adaptively refines the extracted surface according to approximation error, but does not explicitly incorporate local feature size into its refinement criterion or directly optimize triangle quality. Another related approach [(Kohlbrenner and Alexa, 2025)] follows a similar direction, but computes the largest empty sphere around every voxel using polyhedral approximations. As shown in Figure 1, although these techniques work very well, they are particularly designed for sparse inputs (e.g., 30³) and require a significant amount of time and/or memory for large inputs, rendering them unsuitable for interactive applications such as RibbonSculpt [(Sureshkumar et al., 2025)], which is the focus of our work. In addition, the results of existing methods are not specifically designed for feature-preserving sampling and often produce a large number of (mostly redundant) triangles. Furthermore, they are designed specifically for SDFs represented on discrete grids, while ours can also handle continuous SDFs (for which we sample the boundary discretely, e.g., but not necessarily, on a grid).

    3. Method

    The main technical challenge we are addressing is the LFS computation from SDFs. We then use it with a meshing algorithm to generate the desired surface/volume meshes from the SDFs. Thanks to the inherent property of feature-sized sampling constructed using the LFS, the resulting meshes are sampled proportionally to this local feature sizing function. In this section, after giving some definitions, we describe how we create a mesh for the zero surface of the SDF with feature-proportional triangle sizes. Then we show how to extend our method to a light-weight variant that handles huge inputs.

    3.1. Background and Definitions

    First, we recall a few basic definitions in the continuous case to facilitate further understanding. Let the boundary Ω be a set of simple closed smooth (twice differentiable) 2-manifolds in ℝ³,

  • (1)

    The medial axis M of Ω is defined as the set of all points having at least two closest points in Ω[(Blum, 1967)]

  • (2)

    The local feature size \mboxlfs(p) at a point p∈Ω is the Euclidean distance from p to the closest point in M[(Ruppert, 1993)]

  • (3)

    The union of the centers of all medial balls of Ω also forms the medial axis M of Ω, and their radii are an upper bound of the local feature size at the points where they touch Ω.

  • (4)

    Given a closed boundary, medial balls B(c,r) can be classified as non-overlapping interior and exterior balls.

  • (5)

    The surface Ω is called ε-sampled by a point set S if for each point p∈Ω, ∃s∈S\textbackslashp such that |p,s|<ε·\mboxlfs(p), with the |·,·| operator denoting the Euclidean distance, for ε∈(0,1].

    • In our case, we define H as a 0-isosurface (φ(x)=0) of a signed distance function (SDF) φ:ℝ³→ℝ, with φ(x) as |x,H| with interior negative, and our medial scaffold M̂ as set of medial centers.

    Overview of our method.

    Our method takes an SDF as input and generates a mesh satisfying the ε-sampling condition. We adopt this meshing algorithm [(Boissonnat and Oudot, 2005)], customizing it to incorporate our novel LFS computation from the SDFs. Our method consists of three main steps: (1) Computing the medial scaffold that is required for (2) computing the LFS, which is used in turn for (3) LFS-based meshing. We first elaborate on our method in theory, then give implementation details, and finally, analyze its accuracy.

    3.2. Our Algorithm for the Continuous Case

    Since we assume H to be smooth, we can fit maximally inscribed balls B(c,r) such that they touch (tangentially) at least 2 points in H, without r vanishing. Since such a touching point p is tangent to H, we can determine a B(c,r) tangent to H at p by varying r until it fulfills the criteria both of being empty of H and touching at least one other point q∈H. We exploit the fact that φ(c) directly gives us the (signed) distance to the closest point x on H, with x=c-φ(c)∇φ(c).     After all medial balls have been computed, the union of their centers forms the medial axis M, and we can compute \mboxlfs(p)=|p,m| for p∈H to its closest point m∈M. Then, an ε-sampled point set S∈H can be generated by adding samples s∈H to S near points p∈H while ∃p:|p,s|≥ε·\mboxlfs(p).

    However, since we cannot test an arbitrary number of medial balls or samples, we describe a practical implementation below that, for the sake of simplicity, takes an SDF defined on a uniform grid as input, without loss of generality. Our algorithm begins by computing a discrete set of sample points on the medial axis, which we term the medial scaffold and denote by M̂.

    3.3. Computing the medial scaffold

    The core contribution of FOMOS is the efficient computation of medial axis points directly from the zero surface of an SDF, rather than its volume, reducing both time and space complexity from cubic to quadratic (except for filtering initial footpoints). Note that for the gridded SDF, H is C²-continuous everywhere except at cell boundaries (C⁰). First, we compute a dense, uniformly distributed set of discrete footpoint samples on H. For that, we only consider SDF grid values near the surface (φ smaller than the cell diameter, i.e., only at the corners of cells that contain the surface). These grid points are then projected onto H using gradient descent, iteratively refining the position of each point by computing the gradient ∇φ(pᵏ), and then moving towards pᵏ⁺¹=pᵏ-φ(pᵏ)∇φ(pᵏ). This directed movement rapidly (on average, 2.5-3.5 iterations) converges to near the surface, φ(p)<μ, with a precision of μ=10⁻²d, where d is the grid cell diagonal d=√3|e| for a cell edge e.
